assignment.title: Colorectal — polyps, colon and rectal cancer

taxonomy.title: Colorectal — polyps, colon and rectal cancer
taxonomy.scopeIn: Colorectal screening, colonoscopy adequacy and polypectomy, benign subepithelial colon lesions, malignant polyps, colon/rectal staging, surgery and response assessment.
taxonomy.scopeOut: Anal SCC belongs to anal-cancer. Germline testing interpretation belongs to oncology-genetics-principles. Polyposis operative extent stays here.
taxonomy.priorityReason: Large clinical breadth and consequential oncologic decisions justify high research priority.
researchAgenda: Rectal local staging and multimodal treatment sequence
Colonoscopy adequacy, polypectomy and surgical anatomy
taxonomy.coverageReason: Live identities cover part of this scope. The research agenda flags breadth to check, and the topic worker must judge redundancy and question quality.
taxonomy.testingWeightBasis: Owner-directed editorial estimate of general-surgery testing relevance. No exam percentages or official blueprint weights are asserted.

programRelease.catalogRegistryMeaning: 610 registered concept identities include 156 with no live node. Active coverage uses the 454 primaryConceptId identities actually scored in default-release nodes.

concepts.displayName: Oncologic regional resection for colon cancer
concepts.learningObjective: Select resection of the tumor-bearing colon with its regional lymphatic drainage for localized resectable colon cancer.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Preoperative cross-sectional staging for colon cancer
concepts.learningObjective: Select contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis before treatment planning for confirmed colon cancer.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Complete colon staging from actual prior imaging
concepts.learningObjective: Retain adequate prior staging while selecting targeted characterization or missing-region imaging from the actual coverage and unresolved findings of outside examinations.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Management of a clearly characterized asymptomatic colonic lipoma
concepts.learningObjective: Choose no lipoma-directed treatment or dedicated surveillance for a clearly characterized asymptomatic colonic lipoma and recognize features that make that pathway inapplicable.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.learningObjective: Recognize the characteristic soft, yellowish, deformable subepithelial phenotype of a colonic lipoma while preserving the boundary that an absent cushion sign does not exclude it.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Reconcile mucosal sampling with a characteristic subepithelial lesion
concepts.learningObjective: Interpret whether a negative surface specimen samples the EUS-defined layer and decide whether a characteristic colonic lipoma needs further tissue confirmation.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Distinguish clinical characterization from histologic confirmation
concepts.learningObjective: Use the EUS-defined lesion layer and the actual submitted tissue to document whether a clinically characterized fatty submucosal lesion has histologic confirmation, without equating that status with a need for another biopsy.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Histologic confirmation of a colorectal lesion
concepts.learningObjective: Identify histologic examination of sampled lesion tissue as the confirming evidence after colonoscopy identifies a suspicious colorectal lesion.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Diagnostic colonoscopy after a positive FIT
concepts.learningObjective: Select diagnostic colonoscopy after a positive screening FIT while recognizing that the stool result alone does not diagnose colorectal cancer.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: IPAA referral for uncontrolled rectal FAP burden
concepts.learningObjective: Select restorative proctocolectomy/IPAA referral when rectal adenomas cannot be controlled endoscopically and restoration is appropriate.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.learningObjective: Refer a fit patient with adverse malignant-polyp histology or uncertain clearance for oncologic segmental resection.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.learningObjective: Recognize when complete endoscopic excision is adequate treatment for a favorable malignant colon polyp.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: A clear polypectomy site and regional oncologic risk
concepts.learningObjective: Distinguish clearance of the local invasive-polyp site from the regional oncologic question created by adverse invasive histology.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.learningObjective: Distinguish pretreatment staging from post-treatment local response evidence before offering organ-preserving rectal-cancer follow-up.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.learningObjective: Integrate post-treatment examination, endoscopy and MRI before offering an organ-preserving response-management strategy.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.learningObjective: Interpret head and stalk dimensions separately to select a pedunculated-polyp resection sequence.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Multimodal response assessment after rectal cancer treatment
concepts.learningObjective: Select combined digital rectal examination, endoscopy, and rectal-protocol MRI after neoadjuvant treatment.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Selected watch-and-wait after clinical complete response
concepts.learningObjective: Recognize intensive-surveillance watch-and-wait as an acceptable nonsurgical option for a fully informed adherent patient with a clinical complete response in an experienced program.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.learningObjective: Select an adequately prepared repeat colonoscopy when the whole-colon examination cannot support the intended assessment, with review of preparation failure rather than a fixed repeat timetable.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Choose cold snare for a small colorectal polyp
concepts.learningObjective: Choose cold snare for a supplied accessible 4 mm or 7 mm nonpedunculated colorectal polyp without invasive features in an outside endoscopic removal plan.

recordedHolds.reason: The recorded complete-response watch-and-wait option does not establish near-complete-response timing or the threshold for resection.
recordedHolds.ownerQuestion: At eight weeks after rectal-cancer neoadjuvant treatment, if a small ulcer and equivocal MRI signal are shrinking without a palpable nodule, should the key be another response assessment rather than total mesorectal excision?

recordedHolds.reason: The same cold-snare answer applies before and after the residual observation; forceps/hot-forceps competitors remain weak. New wide-stalk construct addresses a different reviewed slot instead.

withheldTeachingPoints.taskTextShort: Mandatory same-day or next-day repeat after inadequate preparation
withheldTeachingPoints.reason: ESGE reports limited/conflicting same-day/next-day evidence. Both sources support an adequately prepared repeat; the disputed scheduling extension is withheld, not averaged into a fixed rule.
Fixed Barrett intervals, sedation-driving clearance times and laxative regimens are outside the selected one-decision objectives and are not authored.

cues.phrase: normal colonic mucosa

decision.title: Distinguish clinical characterization from histologic confirmation
fairness: The learner must infer actual specimen depth from epithelium, crypts and lamina propria instead of accepting 'bite-on-bite' or 'benign' as proof of lesion sampling, then distinguish compatibility with the imaging from lesional confirmation. Moderate resident application with two linked evidence inferences.

The technique name creates a credible overconfidence error. The actual constituent list is necessary; it no longer explicitly names absent fat/submucosa or supplies an interpretation label. All options concern the same imaged lesion, with balanced components and comparable wording.

The keyed distinction is defensible. A benign surface sample need not contradict the classic imaged submucosal phenotype and does not prove its histology. This does not assert that bite-on-bite biopsy never reaches lesions or mandate another biopsy.

The list of constituents is interpreted as the actual tissue represented in the submitted levels. If that is not intended as a complete specimen description, clarification would be needed, but no positive lesional tissue is otherwise supplied. No prior feedback precedes this node.
The local single-source provenance limitation remains; clinical sign-off of the exact GI/pathology formulation is still required. No new quantitative rule is introduced.

Sequence check: new feedback says 'nor a reason by itself to repeat sampling', which discourages the unchanged B22 repeat-endoscopy distractor before that question appears. This is a partial scaffold, not a full solution of surveillance/removal versus no lesion-directed care. B22 remains preservation-only and its prior easy rating is carried forward; do not represent the sequence as independent assessment of repeat-biopsy reasoning.
suggestions: Keep discussion of whether to repeat sampling until after the management question when independent assessment of that alternative is intended. Feedback on this interpretation can end with what the specimen does and does not establish.

decision.title: A clear polypectomy site and regional oncologic risk
fairness: Matching specimen provenance to the correct colonic site is consequential, and interpretation of invasion/vascular involvement must then override reassurance from a clear local margin and imaging. The complete two-by-two option matrix has no component-frequency advantage.
Regional oncologic resection of the sigmoid lesion is the best offered discussion for the represented pathology and functional status; scar excision would not address regional oncologic risk.

Importance: high for malignant-polyp management and avoiding wrong-site treatment. Realism: reconciling two polypectomy specimens and a misleadingly conspicuous tattoo is a credible clinic planning problem.

The malignant wording necessarily identifies the relevant specimen but does not choose regional surgery over local scar treatment without clinical reasoning. Normal nodal imaging should remain because it tests a real misconception.
suggestions: Retain the specimen-location map, margin finding and vascular-channel observation.

Improve the option grammar to concrete procedures such as 'Oncologic sigmoid colectomy with regional lymphadenectomy,' with comparable wording for each alternative; this is a wording refinement rather than a substantive verdict blocker.

decision.title: Colon lesion review
fairness: Node node.n4.colonic-wall-pattern-after-mucosal-biopsy.v1: no decisive nonmedical wording overlap, option outlier, convergence, absolute or diagnosis label is apparent. The yellow, compressible mound and layer-specific findings require clinical interpretation rather than matching an option's words.

The learner must reconcile a superficial specimen that did not sample the lesion with the independent wall-layer and current endoscopic phenotype, then decide whether more tissue or resection is warranted. Deeper sampling is a credible temptation after an inadequate specimen; resection is a distinct overtreatment error.

Leaving the mound is the defensible best offered action for the asymptomatic, concordantly benign-appearing submucosal lesion. This does not treat the prior mucosal specimen as proof of a benign deep lesion or assert histologic certainty from it. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified from the supplied fields.

Phase fits: although the miniprobe study is recorded from earlier, the current scope confirms the surface behavior and the choice is whether to sample, resect or leave the lesion during this examination. The negative sampling option is clinically substantive rather than a grammatical giveaway.
suggestions: Retain the distinction between sampled surface and imaged deep layer, the concordant current findings and the absence of attributable symptoms.

Obtain clinician confirmation that the complete phenotype supports observation in this exact version; do not generalize it to all unsampled subepithelial lesions or add a diagnosis label before the choice.

question.stem: Which treatment plan should be discussed for {patientName}'s resection site?

answerChoices.label: Segmental colectomy with removal of the draining mesentery
answerChoices.rationale: Interprets the adverse invasive-polyp feature and recognizes a regional-node risk that a clear-looking scar or negative CT cannot remove.

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic full-thickness excision centered on the resection scar
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Addresses potential local residual disease but does not provide regional nodal treatment/staging for this adverse histology.

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic scar surveillance with repeat targeted tissue sampling
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Overweights endoscopic/CT reassurance and does not address the adverse histologic feature that changes the adequacy of polypectomy.

question.explanation: An endoscopically removed malignant polyp is not automatically cured by a clear-looking scar. The supplied adverse invasive feature supports discussion of oncologic resection with the regional mesentery. CT-negative nodes do not exclude microscopic disease. Exact bowel extent, especially for a transverse lesion, remains an anatomic operative decision.

visibleSequence.stem: Which imaging plan should complete {patientName}'s pretreatment assessment?

answerChoices.label: Chest CT with intravenous-contrast abdominal and pelvic CT
answerChoices.rationale: Provides anatomic staging not supplied by a negative PET uptake summary and localization CT.

answerChoices.label: Repeat whole-body FDG PET with low-dose localization CT
answerChoices.rationale: Repeats the same metabolic/localization approach rather than obtaining the missing diagnostic anatomic assessment.

answerChoices.label: Hepatic ultrasound with review of the existing localization CT
answerChoices.rationale: Adds a liver survey but continues to rely on the localization study for the remaining distant assessment.

visibleSequence.explanation: Read both the coverage and acquisition of the prior study. Standard colon-cancer distant staging includes thoracic CT and adequate contrast-enhanced abdominal/pelvic assessment; a negative radiograph, organ ultrasound or PET uptake/localization report does not automatically supply that assessment. MRI is a legitimate abdominal alternative in appropriate pathways, not inherently a wrong test.

visibleSequence.stem: Which staging pathway should precede further treatment planning for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Chest CT with contrast-enhanced abdominal and pelvic CT
answerChoices.rationale: Provides the conventional systemic staging pathway after recognition of invasive adverse polyp histology.

answerChoices.label: Chest radiographs with contrast-enhanced abdominal and pelvic CT
answerChoices.rationale: Covers the same broad body regions but substitutes a less suitable thoracic examination for staging.

answerChoices.label: Whole-body FDG PET-CT with regional anatomic review
answerChoices.rationale: Treats an advanced metabolic survey as the routine initial staging pathway, rather than reserving it for appropriate selected questions.

visibleSequence.explanation: The pathology, not the scar's appearance, establishes the need for invasive-cancer staging. CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis is a standard initial pathway. Chest radiography is not the equivalent thoracic assessment, and PET-CT is not routine initial staging. MRI-based alternatives can be appropriate in selected settings and are not falsely offered as invalid here.

question.stem: Which imaging plan should complete {patientName}'s pretreatment assessment?

answerChoices.label: Thoracic CT to complete the existing cross-sectional staging
answerChoices.rationale: Completes the unassessed thorax rather than treating lung bases/chest radiography as full thoracic CT.

answerChoices.label: Hepatic MRI to complete the existing cross-sectional staging
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Adds liver characterization despite no indeterminate lesion and leaves the thoracic staging gap.

answerChoices.label: Whole-body FDG PET-CT to replace the existing staging pathway
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Escalates to routine metabolic staging rather than completing the standard anatomic assessment.

question.explanation: Read both the coverage and acquisition of the prior study. Standard colon-cancer distant staging includes thoracic CT and adequate contrast-enhanced abdominal/pelvic assessment; a negative radiograph, organ ultrasound or PET uptake/localization report does not automatically supply that assessment. MRI is a legitimate abdominal alternative in appropriate pathways, not inherently a wrong test.

visibleSequence.stem: Which investigation should complete {patientName}'s pretreatment assessment?

answerChoices.label: Liver MRI with contrast
answerChoices.rationale: Dedicated liver characterization addresses the actual unresolved staging finding without discarding adequate coverage elsewhere.

answerChoices.label: Whole-body FDG PET-CT
answerChoices.rationale: Routine metabolic imaging does not substitute for appropriate anatomic characterization of this indeterminate liver finding.

answerChoices.label: Image-guided liver biopsy
answerChoices.rationale: Tissue can be appropriate in selected indeterminate lesions, but dedicated noninvasive characterization is the preferred next problem-solving step for this small single-phase finding before committing to sampling.

visibleSequence.explanation: A complete staging examination may leave a focal lesion unresolved. Dedicated liver MRI is an appropriate next characterization study for a subcentimeter single-phase CT finding in known extrahepatic cancer. PET sensitivity and the value/feasibility of biopsy differ from targeted anatomic characterization; neither is universally forbidden. Retain the adequate prior staging.

visibleSequence.stem: Which staging pathway should precede further treatment planning for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Chest CT with contrast-enhanced abdominal and pelvic CT
answerChoices.rationale: Provides the conventional systemic staging pathway after recognition of invasive adverse polyp histology.

answerChoices.label: Chest radiographs with contrast-enhanced abdominal and pelvic CT
answerChoices.rationale: Covers the same broad body regions but substitutes a less suitable thoracic examination for staging.

answerChoices.label: Whole-body FDG PET-CT with regional anatomic review
answerChoices.rationale: Treats an advanced metabolic survey as the routine initial staging pathway, rather than reserving it for appropriate selected questions.

visibleSequence.explanation: The pathology, not the scar's appearance, establishes the need for invasive-cancer staging. CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis is a standard initial pathway. Chest radiography is not the equivalent thoracic assessment, and PET-CT is not routine initial staging. MRI-based alternatives can be appropriate in selected settings and are not falsely offered as invalid here.

question.stem: Which broad treatment plan should be discussed with {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Resection of the involved colon with its regional lymphatic drainage
answerChoices.rationale: Addresses incompletely assessed invasive disease and regional risk after a malignant polyp with an involved deep margin, despite a clear scar and normal-size CT nodes.

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic full-thickness removal of the colon scar and local wall
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Could improve local wall assessment, but is not the preferred substitute for oncologic regional resection in this fit patient with involved/indeterminate invasive clearance.

answerChoices.distractorRationale: Mistakes a scar and reassuring CT for proof of local invasive clearance and microscopic node negativity.

question.explanation: The deep invasive front is transected and local depth/clearance cannot be adequately assessed. In a surgically suitable patient, this is not the low-risk, completely excised malignant-polyp group. Discuss oncologic resection including regional lymphatic drainage; neither a clear scar nor normal-size CT nodes establishes clearance. This is a broad planning choice, not specification of the exact transverse-colon operation.

node.currentUpdate: Staging CT shows no distant deposits and no enlarged regional nodes. Preoperative assessment finds the patient suitable for elective colon surgery.
node.stem: Which broad treatment plan should be discussed with {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Resection of the involved colon with its regional lymphatic drainage
answerChoices.rationale: Addresses incompletely assessed invasive disease and regional risk after a malignant polyp with an involved deep margin, despite a clear scar and normal-size CT nodes.

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic full-thickness removal of the colon scar and local wall
answerChoices.rationale: Could improve local wall assessment, but is not the preferred substitute for oncologic regional resection in this fit patient with involved/indeterminate invasive clearance.

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic colon scar surveillance with targeted mucosal tissue sampling
answerChoices.rationale: Mistakes a scar and reassuring CT for proof of local invasive clearance and microscopic node negativity.

node.explanation: The deep invasive front is transected and local depth/clearance cannot be adequately assessed. In a surgically suitable patient, this is not the low-risk, completely excised malignant-polyp group. Discuss oncologic resection including regional lymphatic drainage; neither a clear scar nor normal-size CT nodes establishes clearance. This is a broad planning choice, not specification of the exact transverse-colon operation.

visibleSequence.currentUpdate: The current outside assessment includes a chest radiograph and abdominal ultrasound. The reports describe no focal lung opacity, no focal hepatic mass and no ascites.
visibleSequence.stem: Which imaging plan should complete {patientName}'s pretreatment assessment?

answerChoices.label: Chest CT with intravenous-contrast abdominal and pelvic CT
answerChoices.rationale: Obtains the standard cross-sectional staging despite reassuring lower-sensitivity preliminary studies.

answerChoices.label: Abdominal and pelvic MRI with the current chest radiograph
answerChoices.rationale: Offers valid abdominal cross-sectional imaging but retains radiography rather than adequate thoracic staging.

answerChoices.label: Whole-body FDG PET-CT with the current chest radiograph
answerChoices.rationale: Substitutes routine metabolic imaging for the standard anatomic pathway without an established metastatic decision problem.

visibleSequence.explanation: Read both the coverage and acquisition of the prior study. Standard colon-cancer distant staging includes thoracic CT and adequate contrast-enhanced abdominal/pelvic assessment; a negative radiograph, organ ultrasound or PET uptake/localization report does not automatically supply that assessment. MRI is a legitimate abdominal alternative in appropriate pathways, not inherently a wrong test.

visibleSequence.stem: Which plan should complete {patientName}'s pretreatment imaging assessment?

answerChoices.label: Diagnostic whole-chest CT
answerChoices.rationale: The prior examination did not cover the whole chest; preserve the diagnostic abdominal/pelvic work and complete the unresolved thoracic assessment.

answerChoices.label: Chest radiography
answerChoices.rationale: A radiograph does not replace diagnostic thoracic CT for the incompletely assessed lung finding and staging coverage.

answerChoices.label: FDG PET with low-dose localization CT
answerChoices.rationale: Metabolic assessment with localization CT is not the same as the required diagnostic thoracic acquisition, particularly for a small nodule.

visibleSequence.explanation: Use the studies that actually answer each regional question. Diagnostic abdominal/pelvic MRI can be retained, but a partial lower-chest cardiac acquisition does not cover the upper lungs or fully assess the edge nodule. The later staging report is supplied only after completion of the diagnostic chest study.

question.stem: Which examination should complete {patientName}'s pretreatment imaging assessment?

answerChoices.label: Chest CT with thin-section inspiratory lung acquisitions
answerChoices.rationale: This provides a full diagnostic lung examination beyond the cardiac field while retaining adequate abdominal/pelvic MRI rather than repeating it.

answerChoices.label: FDG PET/CT with a low-dose free-breathing CT acquisition
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This is a real staging modality, but its metabolic result and low-dose free-breathing CT do not replace the indicated diagnostic chest acquisition.

answerChoices.label: Chest radiography with posteroanterior and lateral acquisitions
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A normal radiograph would not supply equivalent cross-sectional assessment of the lungs or of the partly imaged solid nodule.

question.explanation: Interpret what each prior and proposed acquisition can establish. Adequate abdominal/pelvic MRI can be retained, while the cardiac CT has not supplied a diagnostic examination of the lungs. Obtain the chest CT acquisition; routine PET with low-dose free-breathing CT or radiographs are not interchangeable substitutes. No nodule-size threshold or automatic metastatic diagnosis is inferred.

planningContext.task: Which examination should complete {patientName}'s pretreatment imaging assessment?
planningContext.presentation: {patientName}, a 54-year-old woman, visits the clinic after endoscopic removal of a polyp in the transverse colon. The site now appears as a scar. Moderately differentiated malignant glands extend through the muscularis mucosae into submucosa and reach the cauterized deep edge. The pathology report lists invasion depth as not measurable. No lymphovascular invasion is identified in the sampled sections.

node.currentUpdate: Abdominal and pelvic MRI includes the liver, mesentery and pelvic nodal stations with contrast-enhanced sequences. A separate cardiac CT runs from below the carina to the diaphragm and shows a small solid nodule near its cranial edge. The receiving center can obtain chest CT, chest radiography or FDG PET/CT.
node.stem: Which examination should complete {patientName}'s pretreatment imaging assessment?

answerChoices.label: Chest CT with thin-section inspiratory lung acquisitions
answerChoices.rationale: This provides a full diagnostic lung examination beyond the cardiac field while retaining adequate abdominal/pelvic MRI rather than repeating it.

answerChoices.label: FDG PET/CT with a low-dose free-breathing CT acquisition
answerChoices.rationale: This is a real staging modality, but its metabolic result and low-dose free-breathing CT do not replace the indicated diagnostic chest acquisition.

answerChoices.label: Chest radiography with posteroanterior and lateral acquisitions
answerChoices.rationale: A normal radiograph would not supply equivalent cross-sectional assessment of the lungs or of the partly imaged solid nodule.

node.explanation: Interpret what each prior and proposed acquisition can establish. Adequate abdominal/pelvic MRI can be retained, while the cardiac CT has not supplied a diagnostic examination of the lungs. Obtain the chest CT acquisition; routine PET with low-dose free-breathing CT or radiographs are not interchangeable substitutes. No nodule-size threshold or automatic metastatic diagnosis is inferred.

visibleSequence.currentUpdate: A previous forceps specimen is reported as normal colonic mucosa. The submitted sections contain colonic crypts and lamina propria.
visibleSequence.stem: Which interpretation of the outside specimen should accompany {patientName}'s imaging assessment?

answerChoices.label: Compatible with imaging; lesional histology remains unconfirmed
answerChoices.rationale: The constituents correspond to the overlying mucosa, not a tissue diagnosis of the deeper imaged mass. A locally normal surface specimen does not contradict the integrated classic imaging phenotype.

answerChoices.label: Compatible with imaging; lesional histology is confirmed
answerChoices.rationale: The surface finding can be compatible, but it does not itself represent the imaged third-layer mass. Agreement is not the same as lesional tissue confirmation.

answerChoices.label: Inconsistent with imaging; lesional histology remains unconfirmed
answerChoices.rationale: The lack of a lesional specimen is recognized, but ordinary mucosa above the lesion is not evidence that the imaging characterization is wrong.

answerChoices.label: Inconsistent with imaging; lesional histology is confirmed
answerChoices.rationale: This both overstates what was sampled and treats a compatible surface finding as a conflicting lesional diagnosis.

visibleSequence.explanation: Identify what tissue the crypts and lamina propria represent, then judge concordance separately from confirmation. Overlying mucosa can be normal above the classic imaged third-layer lesion. It neither histologically confirms that mass nor contradicts its integrated characterization. This distinction does not create an indication for another biopsy or change the passed management premise.
visibleSequence.teachingPoint: Identify what tissue the crypts and lamina propria represent, then judge concordance separately from confirmation. visibleSequence.stem: Which diagnosis best integrates {patientName}'s endoscopic and wall-layer findings?

answerChoices.label: Colonic lipoma
answerChoices.rationale: Combines compressibility/yellow surface with a uniform hyperechoic submucosal lesion.

answerChoices.label: Colonic lymphangioma
answerChoices.rationale: Can be deformable and submucosal, but ordinarily has fluid-containing/cystic internal spaces rather than the supplied uniform bright solid pattern.

answerChoices.label: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
answerChoices.rationale: Is a plausible solid subepithelial alternative, but the usual muscularis-propria hypoechoic pattern differs from these observations.

visibleSequence.explanation: Interpret the wall layer and internal echo pattern before integrating the endoscopic behavior. A uniform hyperechoic submucosal lesion with this surface behavior supports lipoma; compressibility by itself is not the whole assessment.

visibleSequence.currentUpdate: A previous forceps specimen was reported as normal colonic mucosa. Its slide contains epithelium, crypts and lamina propria, ending above the submucosal plane. The current endoscopic and wall-layer observations are documented above.
visibleSequence.stem: Which tissue-assessment plan should be recorded for {patientName}'s lesion?

answerChoices.label: No additional lesion tissue sampling
answerChoices.rationale: The normal surface biopsy is compatible with a characteristic submucosal lipoma; it does not require invasive confirmation.

answerChoices.label: EUS-guided core biopsy of the lesion
answerChoices.rationale: Core tissue is appropriate for selected indeterminate or higher-risk subepithelial lesions, but is not needed solely to reconfirm the characteristic lipoma pattern shown here.

answerChoices.label: Repeat deep-forceps biopsy of the lesion
answerChoices.rationale: A deeper forceps attempt might obtain submucosa, but another tissue procedure is unnecessary when the characteristic imaging and examination already establish an asymptomatic lipoma.

visibleSequence.explanation: Interpret a negative specimen by the layer it contains. Normal mucosa does not erase a submucosal lesion. For a characteristic lipoma, normal mucosal biopsies do not mandate another lesion specimen.
visibleSequence.teachingPoint: Interpret a negative specimen by the layer it contains. Normal mucosa does not erase a submucosal lesion. For a characteristic lipoma, normal mucosal biopsies do not mandate another lesion specimen.

question.stem: Which interpretation of the outside specimen should accompany {patientName}'s imaging assessment?

answerChoices.label: Compatible with imaging; lesional histology remains unconfirmed
answerChoices.rationale: The constituents correspond to the overlying mucosa, not a tissue diagnosis of the deeper imaged mass. A locally normal surface specimen does not contradict the integrated classic imaging phenotype.

answerChoices.label: Compatible with imaging; lesional histology is confirmed
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The surface finding can be compatible, but it does not itself represent the imaged third-layer mass. Agreement is not the same as lesional tissue confirmation.

answerChoices.label: Inconsistent with imaging; lesional histology remains unconfirmed
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The lack of a lesional specimen is recognized, but ordinary mucosa above the lesion is not evidence that the imaging characterization is wrong.

answerChoices.label: Inconsistent with imaging; lesional histology is confirmed
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This both overstates what was sampled and treats a compatible surface finding as a conflicting lesional diagnosis.

question.explanation: Identify what tissue the crypts and lamina propria represent, then judge concordance separately from confirmation. Overlying mucosa can be normal above the classic imaged third-layer lesion. It neither histologically confirms that mass nor contradicts its integrated characterization. This distinction does not create an indication for another biopsy or change the passed management premise.
question.teachingPoint: Identify what tissue the crypts and lamina propria represent, then judge concordance separately from confirmation. answerChoices.rationale: The specimen's actual constituents, rather than its technique label, establish the represented compartment. Normal surface tissue is compatible with the deeper imaged lesion but does not provide its histologic confirmation.

answerChoices.label: Compatible with imaging; lesional histology is confirmed
answerChoices.rationale: This credits the benign or bite-on-bite label as proof that the imaged mass was sampled, without using the listed tissue constituents.

answerChoices.label: Inconsistent with imaging; lesional histology remains unconfirmed
answerChoices.rationale: The mass is unconfirmed histologically, but a benign overlying mucosal specimen does not conflict with the integrated classic imaging characterization.

answerChoices.label: Inconsistent with imaging; lesional histology is confirmed
answerChoices.rationale: This treats a technique label as proof of lesional tissue and then misreads the benign surface result as a conflicting diagnosis.

visibleSequence.explanation: The technique name does not establish the depth reached in this particular submitted specimen. The constituents represent surface mucosa. That can agree with the overlying surface of the classic imaged lesion while leaving lesional histology unconfirmed. This is neither a universal criticism of bite-on-bite biopsy nor a reason by itself to repeat sampling.

visibleSequence.stem: Which diagnosis best integrates {patientName}'s endoscopic and wall-layer findings?

answerChoices.label: Colonic lipoma
answerChoices.rationale: Combines compressibility/yellow surface with a uniform hyperechoic submucosal lesion.

answerChoices.label: Colonic lymphangioma
answerChoices.rationale: Can be deformable and submucosal, but ordinarily has fluid-containing/cystic internal spaces rather than the supplied uniform bright solid pattern.

answerChoices.label: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
answerChoices.rationale: Is a plausible solid subepithelial alternative, but the usual muscularis-propria hypoechoic pattern differs from these observations.

visibleSequence.explanation: Interpret the wall layer and internal echo pattern before integrating the endoscopic behavior. A uniform hyperechoic submucosal lesion with this surface behavior supports lipoma; compressibility by itself is not the whole assessment.

visibleSequence.stem: Which tissue-assessment plan should be recorded for {patientName}'s lesion?

answerChoices.label: No additional lesion tissue sampling
answerChoices.rationale: The named biopsy technique did not reach the lesion, but a characteristic lipoma appearance does not require tissue confirmation merely because surface mucosa is normal.

answerChoices.label: EUS-guided core biopsy of the lesion
answerChoices.rationale: Core tissue is appropriate for selected indeterminate or higher-risk subepithelial lesions, but is not needed solely to reconfirm the characteristic lipoma pattern shown here.

answerChoices.label: Repeat deep-forceps biopsy of the lesion
answerChoices.rationale: A deeper forceps attempt might obtain submucosa, but another tissue procedure is unnecessary when the characteristic imaging and examination already establish an asymptomatic lipoma.

visibleSequence.explanation: Interpret a negative specimen by the layer it contains. Normal mucosa does not erase a submucosal lesion. For a characteristic lipoma, normal mucosal biopsies do not mandate another lesion specimen.
visibleSequence.teachingPoint: Interpret a negative specimen by the layer it contains. Normal mucosa does not erase a submucosal lesion. For a characteristic lipoma, normal mucosal biopsies do not mandate another lesion specimen.

question.stem: Which interpretation of the outside specimen should accompany {patientName}'s imaging assessment?

answerChoices.label: Compatible with imaging; lesional histology remains unconfirmed
answerChoices.rationale: The specimen's actual constituents, rather than its technique label, establish the represented compartment. Normal surface tissue is compatible with the deeper imaged lesion but does not provide its histologic confirmation.

answerChoices.label: Compatible with imaging; lesional histology is confirmed
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This credits the benign or bite-on-bite label as proof that the imaged mass was sampled, without using the listed tissue constituents.

answerChoices.label: Inconsistent with imaging; lesional histology remains unconfirmed
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The mass is unconfirmed histologically, but a benign overlying mucosal specimen does not conflict with the integrated classic imaging characterization.

answerChoices.label: Inconsistent with imaging; lesional histology is confirmed
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This treats a technique label as proof of lesional tissue and then misreads the benign surface result as a conflicting diagnosis.

question.explanation: The technique name does not establish the depth reached in this particular submitted specimen. The constituents represent surface mucosa. That can agree with the overlying surface of the classic imaged lesion while leaving lesional histology unconfirmed. This is neither a universal criticism of bite-on-bite biopsy nor a reason by itself to repeat sampling.

question.stem: Which treatment plan should be discussed for {patientName}'s represented pathology?
question.explanation: Read the histology and its mapped site, not just the marker or the healed surface. Invasive glands in an endothelial-lined channel are the adverse feature relevant to regional oncologic resection. The clear local edge does not remove that concern, and the correct specimen maps it to the sigmoid colon. Discuss the corresponding segmental resection with its draining mesentery, subject to the patient's operative assessment and preferences.

cells: Ascending colon, tattoo placed

Sigmoid colon, en-bloc specimen

answerChoices.label: Sigmoid colon with regional oncologic colectomy
answerChoices.rationale: The adverse invasive finding belongs to the sigmoid specimen and creates a regional oncologic question despite the locally clear edge and scar.

answerChoices.label: Ascending colon with regional oncologic colectomy
answerChoices.rationale: A visible tattoo is not a substitute for reconciling the container with the adverse invasive pathology.

answerChoices.label: Sigmoid colon with full-thickness endoscopic scar excision
answerChoices.rationale: A further local procedure does not address the regional-risk finding already represented in the removed specimen.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A further local procedure does not address the regional-risk finding already represented in the removed specimen.

answerChoices.label: Ascending colon with full-thickness endoscopic scar excision

answerChoices.rationale: The adverse invasive finding belongs to the sigmoid specimen and creates a regional oncologic question despite the locally clear edge and scar.

answerChoices.label: Ascending colon with regional oncologic colectomy
answerChoices.rationale: A visible tattoo is not a substitute for reconciling the container with the adverse invasive pathology.

answerChoices.label: Sigmoid colon with full-thickness endoscopic scar excision
answerChoices.rationale: A further local procedure does not address the regional-risk finding already represented in the removed specimen.

answerChoices.label: Ascending colon with full-thickness endoscopic scar excision
answerChoices.rationale: This acts locally on the tattooed noninvasive site while failing to address the separate adverse invasive specimen mapped to the sigmoid.

node.explanation: Read the histology and its mapped site, not just the marker or the healed surface. Invasive glands in an endothelial-lined channel are the adverse feature relevant to regional oncologic resection. The clear local edge does not remove that concern, and the correct specimen maps it to the sigmoid colon. Discuss the corresponding segmental resection with its draining mesentery, subject to the patient's operative assessment and preferences.

question.stem: What should the endoscopist do with {patientName}'s mound during this examination?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Earlier specimen
items.value: Colonic surface mucosa; no submucosal tissue is present in the fragment.

items.label: Recorded miniprobe study
items.value: The mound is homogeneous and bright, confined to the submucosal layer; the muscle layer beneath it is continuous.

items.label: Current colonoscopic view
items.value: A smooth yellow mound indents under gentle closed-forceps pressure and returns to shape; the overlying surface is intact.

answerChoices.label: Leave the mound without further sampling
answerChoices.rationale: The integrated phenotype supports a clear asymptomatic lipoma; the overlying mucosal fragment does not make it necessary to obtain another sample.

answerChoices.label: Obtain deeper bite-on-bite mucosal samples
answerChoices.rationale: A prior specimen lacking submucosa does not automatically justify another sample when the integrated phenotype is already characteristic.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A prior specimen lacking submucosa does not automatically justify another sample when the integrated phenotype is already characteristic.

answerChoices.label: Remove the mound by endoscopic resection
answerChoices.rationale: An incidental clearly characterized lipoma does not require resection merely to obtain histology.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: An incidental clearly characterized lipoma does not require resection merely to obtain histology.

question.explanation: The earlier fragment describes mucosa, not the submucosal mound. That sampling limitation does not overturn a characteristic soft yellow, homogeneous bright submucosal phenotype. A clearly characterized asymptomatic lipoma does not need another biopsy or lipoma-directed resection. Symptoms, ulceration or uncertainty would change the assessment.

planningContext.task: What should the endoscopist do with {patientName}'s mound during this examination?
planningContext.presentation: {patientName}, a 68-year-old man, is undergoing colonoscopy to reassess an incidental colonic mound sampled during an earlier examination. He has no symptoms attributable to the lesion.

node.stem: What should the endoscopist do with {patientName}'s mound during this examination?

answerChoices.label: Leave the mound without further sampling
answerChoices.rationale: The integrated phenotype supports a clear asymptomatic lipoma; the overlying mucosal fragment does not make it necessary to obtain another sample.

answerChoices.label: Obtain deeper bite-on-bite mucosal samples
answerChoices.rationale: A prior specimen lacking submucosa does not automatically justify another sample when the integrated phenotype is already characteristic.

answerChoices.label: Remove the mound by endoscopic resection
answerChoices.rationale: An incidental clearly characterized lipoma does not require resection merely to obtain histology.

node.explanation: The earlier fragment describes mucosa, not the submucosal mound. That sampling limitation does not overturn a characteristic soft yellow, homogeneous bright submucosal phenotype. A clearly characterized asymptomatic lipoma does not need another biopsy or lipoma-directed resection. Symptoms, ulceration or uncertainty would change the assessment.

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Earlier specimen
items.value: Colonic surface mucosa; no submucosal tissue is present in the fragment.

items.label: Recorded miniprobe study
items.value: The mound is homogeneous and bright, confined to the submucosal layer; the muscle layer beneath it is continuous.

items.label: Current colonoscopic view
items.value: A smooth yellow mound indents under gentle closed-forceps pressure and returns to shape; the overlying surface is intact.

David did not finish the preparation because the instructions were unclear. He remains suitable for another examination.

question.stem: A previously incidental colonic lipoma is being managed without lesion-specific treatment. Which new finding most clearly makes that observation-only plan inappropriate?

answerChoices.label: Continued absence of symptoms
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Continued asymptomatic status does not leave the approved observation pathway.

answerChoices.label: An unchanged smooth surface
answerChoices.distractorRationale: An unchanged nonconcerning surface does not independently require lesion-directed treatment.

answerChoices.label: No evidence of obstruction
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Absence of obstruction remains compatible with the approved asymptomatic pathway.

question.explanation: Bleeding or ulceration moves the lesion outside the approved asymptomatic observation pathway and warrants further evaluation for individualized treatment. This question does not prescribe a particular resection technique.

question.stem: Which patient is the best candidate for no lipoma-directed treatment or dedicated surveillance?

answerChoices.label: A patient with a clearly characterized, asymptomatic colonic lipoma and no bleeding, ulceration, obstruction, or pain
A patient with an indeterminate firm subepithelial lesion
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Diagnostic uncertainty places this patient outside the approved observation-only lipoma pathway.

answerChoices.label: A patient with an ulcerated lesion and recurrent bleeding
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Ulceration and bleeding require further individualized evaluation rather than the approved asymptomatic observation pathway.

answerChoices.label: A patient with a lesion causing obstructive symptoms
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Clinically significant symptoms place this patient outside the approved asymptomatic observation pathway.

question.explanation: The no-intervention pathway applies only when the diagnosis is clear and the lipoma is asymptomatic and uncomplicated.

question.stem: Which colonoscopy description most strongly supports a colonic lipoma?

answerChoices.label: A smooth, yellowish subepithelial lesion that indents with gentle pressure and regains its shape
An irregular ulcerated mucosal mass that bleeds with contact
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This is a concerning mucosal phenotype rather than the approved characteristic lipoma profile.

answerChoices.label: A firm noncompressible subepithelial lesion with an atypical surface
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This lacks the approved soft, deformable lipoma characteristics.

answerChoices.label: A blue, serpiginous vascular-appearing structure
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This vascular-appearing profile is not the approved characteristic lipoma phenotype.

question.explanation: The soft yellowish lesion with a positive cushion or pillow sign is the characteristic profile among these options.

question.stem: A colonic subepithelial lesion does not indent when gently probed. Which interpretation is most accurate?

answerChoices.label: An absent cushion or pillow sign does not by itself exclude lipoma; the full lesion assessment must guide further evaluation
Lipoma has been excluded
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The approved boundary is that the sign has limited sensitivity and its absence is not exclusionary.

answerChoices.label: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor has been confirmed
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A negative cushion sign does not establish a different histologic diagnosis.

answerChoices.label: The patient requires immediate colectomy
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The maneuver alone neither establishes a diagnosis nor dictates an operation.

question.explanation: The cushion or pillow sign is highly supportive when present but has limited sensitivity. A negative maneuver is not diagnostic of another lesion and does not independently dictate treatment.

visibleSequence.stem: Which operative plan should be recommended for {patientName}'s colon cancer?

answerChoices.label: Segmental colectomy with lymphadenectomy
answerChoices.rationale: Removes the tumor-bearing segment with its lymphatic drainage; normal node size on CT does not establish pathologic node negativity.

answerChoices.label: Local full-thickness excision of the tumour
answerChoices.rationale: Underweights the need for regional oncologic resection and nodal assessment of an invasive tumor not suitable for endoscopic removal.

answerChoices.label: Total abdominal colectomy with lymphadenectomy
answerChoices.rationale: Extends bowel removal beyond the supplied single tumor without an additional indication for total colectomy.

question.stem: Which staging pathway should precede further treatment planning for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Chest CT with contrast-enhanced abdominal and pelvic CT
answerChoices.rationale: Provides the conventional systemic staging pathway after recognition of invasive adverse polyp histology.

answerChoices.label: Chest radiographs with contrast-enhanced abdominal and pelvic CT
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Covers the same broad body regions but substitutes a less suitable thoracic examination for staging.

question.explanation: The pathology, not the scar's appearance, establishes the need for invasive-cancer staging. CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis is a standard initial pathway. Chest radiography is not the equivalent thoracic assessment, and PET-CT is not routine initial staging. MRI-based alternatives can be appropriate in selected settings and are not falsely offered as invalid here.

visibleSequence.stem: Which treatment plan should be discussed for {patientName}'s resection site?

answerChoices.label: Segmental colectomy with removal of the draining mesentery
answerChoices.rationale: Interprets the adverse invasive-polyp feature and recognizes a regional-node risk that a clear-looking scar or negative CT cannot remove.

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic full-thickness excision centered on the resection scar
answerChoices.rationale: Addresses potential local residual disease but does not provide regional nodal treatment/staging for this adverse histology.

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic scar surveillance with repeat targeted tissue sampling
answerChoices.rationale: Overweights endoscopic/CT reassurance and does not address the adverse histologic feature that changes the adequacy of polypectomy.

visibleSequence.explanation: An endoscopically removed malignant polyp is not automatically cured by a clear-looking scar. The supplied adverse invasive feature supports discussion of oncologic resection with the regional mesentery. CT-negative nodes do not exclude microscopic disease. Exact bowel extent, especially for a transverse lesion, remains an anatomic operative decision.

question.explanation: The pathology, not the scar's appearance, establishes the need for invasive-cancer staging. CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis is a standard initial pathway. Chest radiography is not the equivalent thoracic assessment, and PET-CT is not routine initial staging. MRI-based alternatives can be appropriate in selected settings and are not falsely offered as invalid here.

visibleSequence.stem: Which operative plan should be recommended for {patientName}'s colon cancer?

answerChoices.label: Segmental colectomy with lymphadenectomy
answerChoices.rationale: Removes the tumor-bearing segment with its lymphatic drainage; normal node size on CT does not establish pathologic node negativity.

answerChoices.label: Local full-thickness excision of the tumour
answerChoices.rationale: Underweights the need for regional oncologic resection and nodal assessment of an invasive tumor not suitable for endoscopic removal.

answerChoices.label: Total abdominal colectomy with lymphadenectomy
answerChoices.rationale: Extends bowel removal beyond the supplied single tumor without an additional indication for total colectomy.

question.stem: Which staging pathway should precede further treatment planning for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Chest CT with contrast-enhanced abdominal and pelvic CT
answerChoices.rationale: Provides the conventional systemic staging pathway after recognition of invasive adverse polyp histology.

answerChoices.label: Chest radiographs with contrast-enhanced abdominal and pelvic CT
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Covers the same broad body regions but substitutes a less suitable thoracic examination for staging.

answerChoices.label: Whole-body FDG PET-CT with regional anatomic review
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Treats an advanced metabolic survey as the routine initial staging pathway, rather than reserving it for appropriate selected questions.

question.explanation: The pathology, not the scar's appearance, establishes the need for invasive-cancer staging. CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis is a standard initial pathway. Chest radiography is not the equivalent thoracic assessment, and PET-CT is not routine initial staging. MRI-based alternatives can be appropriate in selected settings and are not falsely offered as invalid here.

visibleSequence.stem: Which treatment plan should be discussed for {patientName}'s resection site?

answerChoices.label: Segmental colectomy with removal of the draining mesentery
answerChoices.rationale: Interprets the adverse invasive-polyp feature and recognizes a regional-node risk that a clear-looking scar or negative CT cannot remove.

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic full-thickness excision centered on the resection scar
answerChoices.rationale: Addresses potential local residual disease but does not provide regional nodal treatment/staging for this adverse histology.

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic scar surveillance with repeat targeted tissue sampling
answerChoices.rationale: Overweights endoscopic/CT reassurance and does not address the adverse histologic feature that changes the adequacy of polypectomy.

visibleSequence.explanation: An endoscopically removed malignant polyp is not automatically cured by a clear-looking scar. The supplied adverse invasive feature supports discussion of oncologic resection with the regional mesentery. CT-negative nodes do not exclude microscopic disease. Exact bowel extent, especially for a transverse lesion, remains an anatomic operative decision.

question.stem: Which imaging plan should complete {patientName}'s pretreatment assessment?

answerChoices.label: IV-contrast abdominopelvic CT with the existing chest CT
answerChoices.rationale: Supplies the still-needed enhancement assessment while retaining adequate thoracic coverage.

answerChoices.label: Abdominal and pelvic ultrasound with the existing chest CT
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Mistakes a broad sonographic survey for the standard cross-sectional distant staging pathway.

answerChoices.label: Whole-body FDG PET-CT with the existing chest CT
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Uses routine metabolic staging as a replacement for the missing contrast-enhanced abdominal/pelvic assessment.

question.explanation: Read both the coverage and acquisition of the prior study. Standard colon-cancer distant staging includes thoracic CT and adequate contrast-enhanced abdominal/pelvic assessment; a negative radiograph, organ ultrasound or PET uptake/localization report does not automatically supply that assessment. MRI is a legitimate abdominal alternative in appropriate pathways, not inherently a wrong test.

visibleSequence.stem: Which diagnosis best explains {patientName}'s colonic lesion at endoscopy?

answerChoices.label: Colonic lipoma
answerChoices.rationale: A soft, yellowish subepithelial lesion that indents and rebounds demonstrates a characteristic cushion or pillow-sign phenotype that strongly supports colonic lipoma.

answerChoices.label: Adenomatous polyp
answerChoices.rationale: This does not match the approved soft subepithelial cushion-sign phenotype.

answerChoices.label: Colonic neuroendocrine tumor
answerChoices.rationale: A neuroendocrine tumor is not identified by the approved combination of a soft yellowish lesion and positive cushion sign.

answerChoices.label: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
answerChoices.rationale: This does not match the approved soft deformable lipoma phenotype.

answerChoices.label: Adenomatous polyp
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This does not match the approved soft subepithelial cushion-sign phenotype.

answerChoices.label: Colonic neuroendocrine tumor
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A neuroendocrine tumor is not identified by the approved combination of a soft yellowish lesion and positive cushion sign.

answerChoices.label: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This does not match the approved soft deformable lipoma phenotype.

question.stem: Which diagnosis best integrates {patientName}'s endoscopic and wall-layer findings?

answerChoices.label: Colonic lipoma
answerChoices.rationale: Combines compressibility/yellow surface with a uniform hyperechoic submucosal lesion.

answerChoices.label: Colonic lymphangioma
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Can be deformable and submucosal, but ordinarily has fluid-containing/cystic internal spaces rather than the supplied uniform bright solid pattern.

answerChoices.label: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Is a plausible solid subepithelial alternative, but the usual muscularis-propria hypoechoic pattern differs from these observations.

question.explanation: Interpret the wall layer and internal echo pattern before integrating the endoscopic behavior. A uniform hyperechoic submucosal lesion with this surface behavior supports lipoma; compressibility by itself is not the whole assessment.
question.teachingPoint: Interpret the wall layer and internal echo pattern before integrating the endoscopic behavior. A uniform hyperechoic submucosal lesion with this surface behavior supports lipoma; compressibility by itself is not the whole assessment.

question.stem: Which tissue-assessment plan should be recorded for {patientName}'s lesion?

answerChoices.label: No additional lesion tissue sampling
answerChoices.rationale: The normal surface biopsy is compatible with a characteristic submucosal lipoma; it does not require invasive confirmation.

answerChoices.label: EUS-guided core biopsy of the lesion
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Core tissue is appropriate for selected indeterminate or higher-risk subepithelial lesions, but is not needed solely to reconfirm the characteristic lipoma pattern shown here.

answerChoices.label: Repeat deep-forceps biopsy of the lesion
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A deeper forceps attempt might obtain submucosa, but another tissue procedure is unnecessary when the characteristic imaging and examination already establish an asymptomatic lipoma.

question.explanation: Interpret a negative specimen by the layer it contains. Normal mucosa does not erase a submucosal lesion. For a characteristic lipoma, normal mucosal biopsies do not mandate another lesion specimen.

question.stem: Which diagnosis best integrates {patientName}'s endoscopic and wall-layer findings?

answerChoices.label: Colonic lipoma
answerChoices.rationale: Combines compressibility/yellow surface with a uniform hyperechoic submucosal lesion.

answerChoices.label: Colonic lymphangioma
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Can be deformable and submucosal, but ordinarily has fluid-containing/cystic internal spaces rather than the supplied uniform bright solid pattern.

answerChoices.label: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Is a plausible solid subepithelial alternative, but the usual muscularis-propria hypoechoic pattern differs from these observations.

question.explanation: Interpret the wall layer and internal echo pattern before integrating the endoscopic behavior. A uniform hyperechoic submucosal lesion with this surface behavior supports lipoma; compressibility by itself is not the whole assessment.

question.stem: Which tissue-assessment plan should be recorded for {patientName}'s lesion?

answerChoices.label: No additional lesion tissue sampling
answerChoices.rationale: The named biopsy technique did not reach the lesion, but a characteristic lipoma appearance does not require tissue confirmation merely because surface mucosa is normal.

answerChoices.label: EUS-guided core biopsy of the lesion
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Core tissue is appropriate for selected indeterminate or higher-risk subepithelial lesions, but is not needed solely to reconfirm the characteristic lipoma pattern shown here.

answerChoices.label: Repeat deep-forceps biopsy of the lesion
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A deeper forceps attempt might obtain submucosa, but another tissue procedure is unnecessary when the characteristic imaging and examination already establish an asymptomatic lipoma.

question.explanation: Interpret a negative specimen by the layer it contains. Normal mucosa does not erase a submucosal lesion. For a characteristic lipoma, normal mucosal biopsies do not mandate another lesion specimen.

question.stem: Which local-margin interpretation and next oncologic purpose match {patientName}'s completed excision?

answerChoices.label: Clear local margin and regional oncologic assessment
answerChoices.rationale: A locally clear excision does not remove the adverse-histology indication for assessing an oncologic regional resection.

answerChoices.label: Clear local margin and routine local surveillance
answerChoices.rationale: Surveillance of the local site does not address the separate regional resection question raised by the invasive histology.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Surveillance of the local site does not address the separate regional resection question raised by the invasive histology.

answerChoices.label: Involved local margin and regional oncologic assessment
answerChoices.rationale: Regional assessment remains indicated, but lymphovascular invasion does not make the explicitly clear cut-surface margin involved.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Regional assessment remains indicated, but lymphovascular invasion does not make the explicitly clear cut-surface margin involved.

answerChoices.label: Involved local margin and routine local surveillance
answerChoices.rationale: This misreads the clear margin and leaves the adverse invasive feature without its regional oncologic assessment.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This misreads the clear margin and leaves the adverse invasive feature without its regional oncologic assessment.

question.explanation: The report describes two different properties: local margin clearance and an adverse invasive feature. In a fit patient, lymphovascular invasion supports oncologic segmental-resection assessment despite a clean scar. Colon oncologic resection includes the tumor-bearing segment and its regional lymphatic territory; further local sampling is not a substitute for that question.

question.stem: Which management plan best fits {patientName}'s combined findings and informed preference?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Digital examination
items.value: Soft, smooth scar; no palpable nodule.

items.label: Endoscopy
items.value: Flat white scar with small telangiectatic vessels; no ulcer or nodular component.

items.label: Rectal-protocol MRI
items.value: Thin low-T2 scar at the treated site without a focal diffusion-restricting component; the previously enlarged mesorectal nodes are no longer enlarged.

items.label: Systemic restaging
items.value: No distant disease identified.

items.label: Discussion and follow-up
items.value: After discussion of regrowth risk and salvage surgery, she prefers avoiding immediate rectal resection and agrees to the experienced program's intensive examination, endoscopy and imaging schedule.

answerChoices.label: Watch-and-wait under the organ-preservation protocol
answerChoices.rationale: Concordant post-treatment observations support the clinical-complete-response pathway rather than reliance on a single scar. In an informed patient able to follow an experienced program, watch-and-wait is a reasonable selected option.

answerChoices.label: Total mesorectal excision at the next operative opportunity
answerChoices.rationale: Resection remains a cancer treatment option, but it does not match this selected response pathway and informed preference when watch-and-wait conditions are met.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Resection remains a cancer treatment option, but it does not match this selected response pathway and informed preference when watch-and-wait conditions are met.

answerChoices.label: Transanal excision of the treated scar
answerChoices.rationale: This adds a local operation without a represented focal residual lesion that requires excision; it is not the offered surveillance pathway supported by these combined findings.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This adds a local operation without a represented focal residual lesion that requires excision; it is not the offered surveillance pathway supported by these combined findings.

question.explanation: The decision depends on current concordant examination, endoscopic and rectal-MRI findings, not a pretreatment attachment or a scar by itself. Those findings support consideration of clinical complete response. With informed preference and intensive follow-up in an experienced program, watch-and-wait is a reasonable offered strategy. It is not equivalent to proof of pathological eradication or ordinary symptom-led observation, and the individual staging and response assessment require clinical sign-off.

question.stem: Which resection technique should be selected for {patientName}'s lesion?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Initial view
items.value: A 4-mm mucosal head appears perched above a narrow segment.

items.label: View after the fold is straightened
items.value: The narrow segment broadens into the adjacent normal fold. The lesion itself has a short broad mucosal attachment, without a separate stalk, depression or ulceration. An open snare can encompass its edge.

answerChoices.label: Cold snare polypectomy
answerChoices.rationale: The apparent stalk is the underlying fold; the actual lesion fits the supplied small nonpedunculated cold-snare category.

answerChoices.label: Hot snare polypectomy
answerChoices.rationale: The first apparent silhouette should not be treated as the established stalk morphology once the actual attachment is demonstrated.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The first apparent silhouette should not be treated as the established stalk morphology once the actual attachment is demonstrated.

answerChoices.label: Hot biopsy-forceps polypectomy
answerChoices.rationale: Hot biopsy forceps are discouraged for diminutive colorectal-polyp excision; the changed view does not create an indication for them.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Hot biopsy forceps are discouraged for diminutive colorectal-polyp excision; the changed view does not create an indication for them.

question.explanation: Use the attachment after the fold is displayed, rather than the initial silhouette. This is an accessible diminutive nonpedunculated lesion, for which cold snare is preferred. Hot biopsy forceps are discouraged because of resection, specimen and thermal-injury concerns. No pedunculated-polyp algorithm is taught here.

question.stem: Which resection sequence should be used for {patientName}’s polyp?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed clinical record; fictional observations

items.label: Current view
items.value: A rounded 18-mm head hangs from a distinct 12-mm-wide stalk. Surface vessels run up the stalk into the head; the adjacent colonic wall is separate from the stalk.

items.label: Medication record
items.value: He takes no antithrombotic medication and has no known bleeding disorder.

answerChoices.label: Detachable-loop ligation followed by hot-snare transection
answerChoices.rationale: The stalk meets the directly sourced wide-stalk criterion even though the head is below the separate head-size trigger.

answerChoices.label: Hot-snare transection followed by rescue clipping
answerChoices.rationale: This waits for bleeding despite the stalk meeting a prophylaxis criterion. A smaller head does not remove that indication.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This waits for bleeding despite the stalk meeting a prophylaxis criterion. A smaller head does not remove that indication.

answerChoices.label: Cold-snare excision with intact specimen retrieval
answerChoices.rationale: A nonpedunculated cold-snare rule does not select treatment for this thick stalk.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A nonpedunculated cold-snare rule does not select treatment for this thick stalk.

question.explanation: Classify the lesion as pedunculated and assess its stalk separately from its head. ESGE recommends hot-snare removal and suggests preventive stalk treatment when the stalk is at least 1 cm wide or the head is at least 2 cm. This lesion meets the stalk criterion. Loop placement followed by hot-snare transection is the best offered sequence. Injection-based prevention can also be appropriate and is not offered as an incorrect option.

planningContext.presentation: {patientName}, a 63-year-old man, is undergoing screening colonoscopy. The endoscopist has reached a mobile sigmoid polyp and is deciding how to remove it.

node.stem: Which resection sequence should be used for {patientName}’s polyp?

answerChoices.label: Detachable-loop ligation followed by hot-snare transection
answerChoices.rationale: The stalk meets the directly sourced wide-stalk criterion even though the head is below the separate head-size trigger.

answerChoices.label: Hot-snare transection followed by rescue clipping
answerChoices.rationale: This waits for bleeding despite the stalk meeting a prophylaxis criterion. A smaller head does not remove that indication.

answerChoices.label: Cold-snare excision with intact specimen retrieval
answerChoices.rationale: A nonpedunculated cold-snare rule does not select treatment for this thick stalk.

node.explanation: Classify the lesion as pedunculated and assess its stalk separately from its head. ESGE recommends hot-snare removal and suggests preventive stalk treatment when the stalk is at least 1 cm wide or the head is at least 2 cm. This lesion meets the stalk criterion. Loop placement followed by hot-snare transection is the best offered sequence. Injection-based prevention can also be appropriate and is not offered as an incorrect option.

decision.title: Distinguish clinical characterization from histologic confirmation

cues.phrase: normal colonic mucosa
cues.why: Partial compatibility cue: it echoes the earlier intact surface and makes an 'Inconsistent with imaging' answer less attractive. It does not distinguish the two compatible options or establish that the deeper lesion was sampled; the tissue-depth inference remains necessary.

fairness: The resident must identify crypts and lamina propria as mucosal constituents, relate that sample to the third-layer mass, and distinguish a compatible surface result from histologic proof of the lesion. Moderate at the lower end; two substantive linked evidence interpretations remain.

The explicit absent-fat/submucosa teaching sentence and already-excluded mucosal-diagnosis distractors are removed. Both compatibility and confirmation assertions occur twice, so neither caution nor an option-length/grammar outlier selects the complete key.

Normal overlying mucosa can be compatible with the supplied imaging without histologically confirming the mass. No equally defensible distractor or confident medical error was identified, reading the listed specimen constituents as the reported sampled tissue.
The update passes the deletion test for confirmation status. It does not create a need for repeat biopsy or change the frozen management premise. There is no prior feedback before this node.

The specific tissue-provenance claim records one adequate ESGE source plus an anatomical application; the broader imaging phenotype has separate prior mappings. This is an offline editorial assessment and not new clinical approval.

Sequence check: the new feedback adds 'This distinction does not create an indication for another biopsy or change the passed management premise.' The latter is authoring metadata in learner-facing text and should be removed. It does not directly select among B21's surveillance/removal/no-follow-up options; the standalone interpretation PASS is not a fresh approval of the later item's difficulty.
suggestions: Remove 'or change the passed management premise' from learner-facing feedback. Preserve the clinical distinction without referring to review status; the frozen B21 fields should remain unchanged.

reasons: Retain the exact independently passed version and visible case fields. Original decision B21-context in docs/research/question-batch1-adversarial-review6-20261102.json is authoritative for editorial history; this audit grants no new PASS or clinical approval.

Crypts and lamina propria must be related to the imaged third-layer lesion before distinguishing compatibility from tissue proof. Preserve the moderate-at-lower-end and authoring-status feedback-cleanup caveats for manager review.
