rankedConcepts.title: Malignant-polyp adequacy and regional risk
rankedConcepts.decision: Choose local follow-up, further local treatment or regional resection from a represented invasive-polyp specimen.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Intact versus fragmented specimen, actual invasive front, vascular channels, budding and cut edges.
rankedConcepts.closestError: Treat a clear scar or margin as proof that regional risk is absent.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Undertreatment of microscopic regional disease or unnecessary colectomy.
rankedConcepts.relevance: Frequent practical preoperative decision with several credible near-misses; editorial testing relevance is high, not an exam-frequency assertion.
rankedConcepts.testingWeightBasis: Qualitative owner-directed editorial relevance estimate, not recalled questions, an official exam blueprint percentage or measured learner performance.

rankedConcepts.title: Rectal local staging and neoadjuvant sequence
rankedConcepts.decision: Choose the remaining local staging examination and treatment sequence from actual pelvic extent.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Tumor relative to muscle, mesorectal fascia and peritoneal reflection; current distant staging.
rankedConcepts.closestError: Apply colon-like surgery-first or a uniform rectal-radiation pathway without interpreting anatomy.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Inadequate local planning or unnecessary multimodal treatment.
rankedConcepts.relevance: High-consequence core surgical oncology; existing assigned live content had response items but no full local-stage-to-sequence chain.
rankedConcepts.testingWeightBasis: Qualitative owner-directed editorial relevance estimate, not recalled questions, an official exam blueprint percentage or measured learner performance.

rankedConcepts.title: Early rectal local excision and completion treatment
rankedConcepts.decision: Clarify early depth and revise local-excision plans when final pathology reaches muscle.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Size, circumference, tissue grade, wall-layer uncertainty, actual excision depth and clear edges.
rankedConcepts.closestError: Equate a clear local edge and normal-sized nodes with completed regional treatment.
rankedConcepts.relevance: Tests a common surgical de-escalation boundary; no assigned original early-rectal chain.
rankedConcepts.testingWeightBasis: Qualitative owner-directed editorial relevance estimate, not recalled questions, an official exam blueprint percentage or measured learner performance.

rankedConcepts.title: Current rectal response evidence and acquisition quality
rankedConcepts.decision: Determine which response evidence is current, actually acquired, retrievable or genuinely inadequate.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Treatment dates, acquisition logs, T2/diffusion quality, current examination/endoscopy and discordant reports.
rankedConcepts.closestError: Accept a complete-looking transfer or repeat imaging that was already acquired.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Incorrect response classification, duplicate testing or an unearned organ-preservation decision.
rankedConcepts.relevance: Existing combination-recognition siblings are redundant; new variants vary actual provenance and acquisition rather than patient names.
rankedConcepts.testingWeightBasis: Qualitative owner-directed editorial relevance estimate, not recalled questions, an official exam blueprint percentage or measured learner performance.

rankedConcepts.title: Persistent disease and regrowth after rectal treatment
rankedConcepts.decision: Distinguish persistent or recurrent disease from an eligible complete-response observation pathway.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Progressive palpable/MRI mural findings despite superficial negative tissue; later biopsy-proven depth and distant staging.
rankedConcepts.closestError: Allow preference or negative surface biopsies to override mural disease.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Delay oncologic treatment or deliver insufficient local salvage.
rankedConcepts.relevance: High clinical consequence; replaces an answer-cued nonsurgical-option exercise. The shrinking equivocal eight-week owner boundary remains held.
rankedConcepts.testingWeightBasis: Qualitative owner-directed editorial relevance estimate, not recalled questions, an official exam blueprint percentage or measured learner performance.

rankedConcepts.title: Regional colon operations and adjacent-organ interface
rankedConcepts.decision: Plan regional resection and preserve a potentially involved adjacent-organ interface.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Site, adherence, curative intent, local planes and distant disease.
rankedConcepts.closestError: Peel an adherent tumor off bladder or infer pathology-negative invasion from appearance.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Tumor violation or compromised local margins.
rankedConcepts.relevance: Frozen regional-resection questions remain useful; an adjacent-organ decision fills a distinct operative gap.
rankedConcepts.testingWeightBasis: Qualitative owner-directed editorial relevance estimate, not recalled questions, an official exam blueprint percentage or measured learner performance.

rankedConcepts.title: Postoperative regional staging and adjuvant planning
rankedConcepts.decision: Improve incomplete regional pathology and apply a confirmed tumor deposit to postoperative intent.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Actual node count, retained specimen, discontinuous pericolic deposit and distant staging.
rankedConcepts.closestError: Count negative nodes but ignore specimen adequacy or deposit-defined regional disease.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Understaging or omission of adjuvant discussion.
rankedConcepts.relevance: High-yield surgical pathology-to-plan reasoning absent from assigned originals; exact regimen duration and molecular selection remain outside the draft.
rankedConcepts.testingWeightBasis: Qualitative owner-directed editorial relevance estimate, not recalled questions, an official exam blueprint percentage or measured learner performance.

rankedConcepts.title: FAP rectal burden, function and reconstruction
rankedConcepts.decision: Choose whether the rectum can be retained and whether a restored outlet is appropriate.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Documented clearing attempts, residual dysplastic field, current continence and informed priorities.
rankedConcepts.closestError: Select IRA or IPAA reflexively from a syndrome label or an earlier operation.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Retained uncontrolled disease or poor functional reconstruction.
rankedConcepts.relevance: Preserves the existing operative concept while adding rectal-sparing and poor-function boundaries; germline interpretation remains with the genetics topic.
rankedConcepts.testingWeightBasis: Qualitative owner-directed editorial relevance estimate, not recalled questions, an official exam blueprint percentage or measured learner performance.

rankedConcepts.title: Complete a positive FIT evaluation
rankedConcepts.decision: Complete an unresolved positive screen despite a later discordant negative screen.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Original result, later test role, diagnostic work performed and colonoscopy suitability.
rankedConcepts.closestError: Use the latest screen as a diagnostic cancellation.
rankedConcepts.relevance: Core completion rule gains a meaningful record-role conflict rather than four cosmetic screening narratives.
rankedConcepts.testingWeightBasis: Qualitative owner-directed editorial relevance estimate, not recalled questions, an official exam blueprint percentage or measured learner performance.

rankedConcepts.title: Colonoscopy reach versus adequate mucosal examination
rankedConcepts.decision: Complete the poorly seen colon rather than accept cecal reach or a routine interval.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Regional visibility after washing, scope endpoint and positive-screen indication.
rankedConcepts.closestError: Treat anatomic completion as adequate diagnostic visualization.
rankedConcepts.relevance: Practical high-value quality distinction; exact same-day/next-day scheduling remains withheld.
rankedConcepts.testingWeightBasis: Qualitative owner-directed editorial relevance estimate, not recalled questions, an official exam blueprint percentage or measured learner performance.

rankedConcepts.title: Technical complexity and advanced endoscopic referral
rankedConcepts.decision: Refer technically complex or scarred lesions without assuming size/nonlifting proves invasive cancer.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Surface assessment, incomplete attempts, cautery/tattoo location and nonlifting chronology.
rankedConcepts.closestError: Operate automatically or repeat routine partial attempts.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Unnecessary surgery or unsafe/incomplete endoscopic treatment.
rankedConcepts.relevance: Consequential referral decisions replace repeated simple cold-snare rules. Stalk-prophylaxis and other basic technique versions remain visible quality parks.
rankedConcepts.testingWeightBasis: Qualitative owner-directed editorial relevance estimate, not recalled questions, an official exam blueprint percentage or measured learner performance.

rankedConcepts.title: Resection mode, dysplasia and serial surveillance
rankedConcepts.decision: Choose USMSTF follow-up from the actual lesion, method and prior examinations.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Lesion versus fragment counts, size, dysplasia, intact versus piecemeal removal and earlier baseline findings.
rankedConcepts.closestError: Use latest-exam-only, size-only or fragment-count shortcuts.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Delayed recurrence detection or unnecessary surveillance.
rankedConcepts.relevance: A major uncovered set of testable decisions; interval facts are explicitly USMSTF-scoped and directly sourced.
rankedConcepts.testingWeightBasis: Qualitative owner-directed editorial relevance estimate, not recalled questions, an official exam blueprint percentage or measured learner performance.

rankedConcepts.title: Meaningful tissue confirmation
rankedConcepts.decision: Resolve whether submitted tissue represents a persistent mucosal lesion before choosing the next diagnostic action.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Procedure-to-specimen map, constituents and persistent visible target.
rankedConcepts.closestError: Treat a benign adjacent sample as the lesion diagnosis.
rankedConcepts.consequence: False reassurance or unnecessary reprocessing of off-target tissue.
rankedConcepts.relevance: Replaces a low-value histology label with an explicit new clinical construct version.
rankedConcepts.testingWeightBasis: Qualitative owner-directed editorial relevance estimate, not recalled questions, an official exam blueprint percentage or measured learner performance.

rankedConcepts.title: Colon staging from actual acquisitions
rankedConcepts.decision: Complete systemic staging or characterize a focal unresolved finding without discarding adequate prior imaging.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Actual scan extent, contrast/protocol details and lesion characterization.
rankedConcepts.closestError: Treat PET localization CT, chest radiography or partial cardiac CT as equivalent full staging.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Incomplete staging or unnecessary repeat work.
rankedConcepts.relevance: Exact independently passed same-case versions are already useful; preserve their original evidence mappings and avoid another cosmetic draft.
rankedConcepts.testingWeightBasis: Qualitative owner-directed editorial relevance estimate, not recalled questions, an official exam blueprint percentage or measured learner performance.

rankedConcepts.title: Metastatic primary strategy and a changed complication state
rankedConcepts.decision: Choose initial systemic treatment for an uncomplicated incurable primary, then change objective when perforation occurs.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Resectability, patency, symptoms and later outside-hospital free gas/fluid with peritonitis.
rankedConcepts.closestError: Carry an earlier correct systemic-first strategy or a stenting option into perforation.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Unnecessary prophylactic surgery or failed source control.
rankedConcepts.relevance: Tests treatment intent and chronology. Hospital events are current clinic chart reviews, requiring no new runtime setting.
rankedConcepts.testingWeightBasis: Qualitative owner-directed editorial relevance estimate, not recalled questions, an official exam blueprint percentage or measured learner performance.

rankedConcepts.title: Subepithelial phenotype versus represented tissue
rankedConcepts.decision: Separate a compatible surface sample from histologic confirmation and a lesion-directed treatment indication.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Wall layer, echo pattern, deformability and actual specimen constituents.
rankedConcepts.closestError: Treat normal surface histology as proof or contradiction of a deeper lesion.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Unnecessary biopsy/resection or false diagnostic certainty.
rankedConcepts.relevance: Current exact PASS versions already test provenance; preserve easy management and sequence caveats rather than duplicate a classic pillow-sign recognition item.
rankedConcepts.testingWeightBasis: Qualitative owner-directed editorial relevance estimate, not recalled questions, an official exam blueprint percentage or measured learner performance.

rankedConcepts.title: Additional colorectal operative anatomy and complications
rankedConcepts.decision: Identify a supported operative-plane or postoperative-complication decision before creating a new case.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Required future evidence: operative planes, structures at risk, anastomotic findings and actual postoperative course.
rankedConcepts.closestError: Invent a nerve, ureter or anastomotic-leak rule from general topic familiarity.
rankedConcepts.consequence: An unsupported difficult-looking question rather than a defensible teaching decision.
rankedConcepts.relevance: Remaining gap: vascular/ureter/autonomic anatomy and anastomotic leak/functional complications were surveyed as relevant scope but no additional independently verified comparison is emitted. Manager may dispatch a later bounded source pass.

after.currentUpdate: Additional pathology finds a total of 15 negative nodes. after.currentUpdate: The August screening FIT was positive and a September repeat was negative. An October colonoscopy reached the cecum and found no lesion. Its withdrawal record describes adherent stool covering much of the ascending and transverse mucosa after irrigation and suction; the distal mucosa was visible. The summary calls the colonoscopy negative.
after.task: Which next colorectal investigation should be arranged for {patientName} after these outside results?

reviewOptions.rationale: The proximal mucosa was not adequately evaluated. The positive FIT still needs a complete diagnostic colonoscopy despite the repeat FIT and negative summary.

after.explanation: Read the withdrawal observations before accepting the negative summary. Cecal reach did not establish adequate proximal inspection, so the positive FIT remains incompletely evaluated. Repeat prepared colonoscopy addresses that deficit; repeating FIT does not.

reviewOptions.label: Repeat colonoscopy in ten years
reviewOptions.rationale: Preparation is judged after cleansing. A complete normal examination with adequate final visualization supports the usual ten-year interval in this scoped screening setting.

reviewOptions.label: Repeat colonoscopy within one year
reviewOptions.rationale: The final withdrawal record establishes that cleaning resolved the obscuration; an inadequacy-driven early repeat is not supported.
reviewOptions.distractorRationale: The final withdrawal record establishes that cleaning resolved the obscuration; an inadequacy-driven early repeat is not supported.

reviewOptions.label: Repeat colonoscopy in three years
reviewOptions.rationale: An intermediate interval does not replace classification of the final examination, and no advanced adenoma was found.
reviewOptions.distractorRationale: An intermediate interval does not replace classification of the final examination, and no advanced adenoma was found.

after.explanation: Insertion quality and final withdrawal quality are different observations. After cleansing, every segment was visible and normal. That final examination supports standard screening timing; an initially dirty view does not independently create an early-repeat indication.

distractorRationales.rationale: The final withdrawal record establishes that cleaning resolved the obscuration; an inadequacy-driven early repeat is not supported.
An intermediate interval does not replace classification of the final examination, and no advanced adenoma was found.

manualAuthorGate.cueAttack: Replaced the editorially signaled bad report and the completed-sigmoidoscopy foil. All options now name colonoscopy timing. The learner must reconcile insertion and withdrawal rather than match the word inadequate to repeat.
manualAuthorGate.stage: Three next-colonoscopy plans for the same completed screening examination.
steps: Determine whether the initial obscuration persisted after endoscopist cleaning.
Use the resulting complete normal examination, rather than insertion appearance, to select standard screening timing.
manualAuthorGate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: an inadequacy heuristic competes with the final visualization record. No unsupported numerical cleanliness score is required.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: Every segment became fully visible on withdrawal after cleaning; the initially dirty view did not persist.

fiveChecks.record: Replaced two attachment-division near-duplicates with three distinct operative extents. The task is a conditional surgical plan, not a guarantee of final margin status. No endoscopic mucosal-negative claim is used to exclude outer-wall involvement.
Three combined colorectal/bladder operative plans at the same planning stage.

Infer that the firm cancer-bladder interface must remain en bloc regardless of whether pathology later shows invasion. Then: Use dome-limited attachment, separate neck/trigone and a usable remnant to distinguish partial from total cystectomy planning.
Moderate prediction: either preserving all bladder by interface division or overextending en-bloc surgery to total cystectomy is a credible resident error.

optionAudit.temptation: Match the organ extent to the involved dome while preserving the tumor interface.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: A focal dome attachment can be removed en bloc with a bladder portion while retaining uninvolved neck, trigone and reservoir; the plan still requires an achievable clear margin.
optionAudit.reasonableWhen: The attached bladder portion can be removed with negative margins and useful remaining bladder.

optionAudit.temptation: Equate any bladder adherence with a need to remove the whole bladder.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: The represented attachment is focal at the dome; the record does not show neck/trigone involvement or loss of a usable remaining bladder requiring total removal.
optionAudit.reasonableWhen: Extent or location prevents clear-margin partial resection with a usable bladder.

optionAudit.temptation: Assume focal attachment can be peeled away to preserve bladder.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: An adherent cancer interface should not be divided to decide whether the adhesion is malignant; partial bladder resection preserves an en-bloc specimen.
optionAudit.reasonableWhen: No true tumor-organ attachment exists and an uninvolved plane is established without dividing an adherent cancer interface.

after.currentUpdate: The outside multidisciplinary team records diffuse bilobar liver and pulmonary metastases not amenable to curative local treatment. reviewOptions.label: Systemic treatment planning with the primary left in place
reviewOptions.rationale: The record lacks clinical or radiographic obstruction and other primary-related complications. For incurable metastatic disease in this setting, systemic treatment generally precedes prophylactic primary surgery.

reviewOptions.label: Sigmoid colectomy followed by systemic treatment planning
reviewOptions.rationale: The smaller scope passed, bowel function continues and CT shows no upstream dilation; prophylactic colectomy would delay treatment of the dominant metastatic disease.

reviewOptions.label: Diverting colostomy followed by systemic treatment planning

after.explanation: The adult scope's nonpassage does not alone establish bowel obstruction. Ongoing bowel function, absent obstructive symptoms and no upstream dilation define the present primary-related burden. With incurable metastases and no primary complication, initial systemic treatment planning is generally preferred to prophylactic colectomy or diversion.

after.currentUpdate: The founder reviews the operative decision recorded during his outside admission for a perforated sigmoid primary with unresectable liver and lung metastases. Before admission he requested treatment of reversible acute complications. At the recorded decision point, the perforated sigmoid segment had been resected and the remaining bowel ends were viable. Diffuse fecal contamination had been encountered. Despite fluids, antibiotics and resection, norepinephrine was still required and the bowel was edematous. The operative team judged fascial closure feasible without a planned open abdomen.
after.task: At that outside intraoperative decision point, which reconstruction plan best fits {patientName}'s recorded findings?

reviewOptions.label: Close the rectal stump and create an end colostomy
reviewOptions.rationale: Ongoing vasopressor need with fecal contamination and edematous bowel favors avoiding a new colorectal anastomosis. A concrete Hartmann reconstruction is supported here; no universal rule for every perforation is asserted.

reviewOptions.label: Create a colorectal anastomosis and a diverting loop ileostomy
reviewOptions.rationale: Diversion does not remove an anastomosis or its failure risk. The continuing vasopressor need and adverse local conditions favor not constructing it at this recorded point.
reviewOptions.distractorRationale: Diversion does not remove an anastomosis or its failure risk. The continuing vasopressor need and adverse local conditions favor not constructing it at this recorded point.

reviewOptions.label: Create a colorectal anastomosis without proximal diversion
reviewOptions.rationale: The relevant observations are the current vasopressor need, contamination and edema, not earlier cancer-treatment eligibility.
reviewOptions.distractorRationale: The relevant observations are the current vasopressor need, contamination and edema, not earlier cancer-treatment eligibility.

after.explanation: Review the physiology at the actual reconstruction point. Persistent vasopressor need plus fecal contamination and bowel edema favor avoiding a colorectal anastomosis; closing the stump and forming an end colostomy is a concrete plan. Diversion cannot erase the risk of an anastomosis already constructed. This scoped decision does not prescribe Hartmann reconstruction for every perforated cancer.

distractorRationales.rationale: Diversion does not remove an anastomosis or its failure risk. The continuing vasopressor need and adverse local conditions favor not constructing it at this recorded point.

draftCases.name: Daniel Fraser
draftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 60-year-old man, attends clinic with a removed sigmoid-polyp specimen and operative diagram.

nodes.title: Complete favorable invasive-polyp excision
nodes.objective: Integrate specimen adequacy, depth and adverse-feature assessment before colectomy.
nodes.update: The pedunculated lesion was retrieved intact. Well-formed malignant glands enter 0.5 mm into stalk submucosa, stopping 2 mm above transection. No lymphovascular or perineural invasion or budding is identified.
nodes.task: Which postexcision plan fits {patientName}'s sigmoid-polyp specimen?

choices.label: Colonoscopic surveillance after polypectomy
choices.temptation: Interpret invasion and clearance separately
choices.rationale: The intact shallow favorable specimen supports surveillance.
choices.reasonableWhen: Complete local excision with favorable invasion features.

choices.label: Endoscopic full-thickness scar resection
choices.temptation: Equate stalk invasion with a positive margin
choices.rationale: The represented cut edge is clear; invasion has not reached transection.
choices.reasonableWhen: A specialist-defined unresolved local margin.

choices.label: Oncologic sigmoid colectomy
choices.temptation: Rank all stalk-invasive cancers as adverse
choices.rationale: The represented depth and remaining features do not establish adverse-polyp risk.
choices.reasonableWhen: A transected invasive front or vascular invasion.

nodes.explanation: Shallow stalk invasion and an involved stalk cut edge are different observations. The intact clear specimen and remaining favorable findings support local follow-up.

gate.cueAttack: No Haggitt level or low-risk conclusion is supplied. Three comparable plans avoid treatment caricatures.
steps: Locate the invasive front relative to transection.
Integrate adequacy and adverse-feature absence rather than treating every stalk-invasive lesion as adverse.
gate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: stalk invasion may be confused with invasion below the stalk or transection.
gate.decidingObservation: The invasive front stops above an intact clear cut edge.
gate.consequence: Unnecessary scar treatment or colectomy.
gate.deletionTest: Orientation earns clearance; other findings govern whether local success is sufficient.
gate.counterfactual: Cut invasive glands across the cautery edge: oncologic sigmoid resection becomes best.
gate.sequence: Independent variant, not paired with a favorable-polyp explanation.

draftCases.name: Lydia Barnes
draftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 62-year-old woman, attends clinic after en-bloc sigmoid-polyp excision.

nodes.title: Regional risk despite local clearance
nodes.objective: Distinguish vascular invasion from local clearance when selecting regional treatment.
nodes.update: Malignant glands enter submucosa and occupy endothelial-lined channels away from the main front. None reaches the inked edge. Endoscopy shows a flat scar; CT shows no distant deposits or enlarged nodes. Operative assessment finds no prohibitive risk.
nodes.task: Which treatment plan should be discussed for {patientName}'s sigmoid lesion?

choices.label: Sigmoid colectomy with regional lymphadenectomy
choices.temptation: Separate local clearance from regional risk
choices.rationale: The vascular-channel finding supports regional resection despite a clear edge and normal-sized nodes.
choices.reasonableWhen: An operable patient has an adverse invasive-polyp feature.

choices.label: Full-thickness endoscopic scar excision
choices.temptation: Treat local clearance as the entire oncologic problem
choices.rationale: Local excision does not address the regional risk raised by vascular invasion.
choices.reasonableWhen: A selected local-clearance problem without adverse regional-risk features.

choices.label: Colonoscopic scar surveillance
choices.temptation: Let a healed scar override pathology
choices.rationale: A healed surface cannot erase the adverse feature.
choices.reasonableWhen: An intact fully assessed favorable polyp.

nodes.explanation: Vascular involvement and cut-edge clearance answer different questions. Discuss resection of the involved segment and its draining lymphatic territory.

gate.cueAttack: Lymphovascular invasion is not given as a diagnosis. Clear CT and scar create a real clinical misconception rather than permission for the key.
steps: Recognize malignant glands in endothelial-lined channels.
Determine that local-edge clearance does not settle regional risk.
gate.difficulty: Moderate/hard prediction: reassuring margins and CT can incorrectly dominate invasive histology.
gate.decidingObservation: Malignant glands in endothelial-lined channels despite a clear edge.
gate.consequence: Undertreatment of microscopic regional disease.
gate.deletionTest: Removing the channels changes risk; margin and CT reassurance establish the competing error. Fitness limits surgery ranking.
gate.counterfactual: Remove vascular invasion and supply a completely assessed favorable profile: surveillance becomes best.
gate.sequence: Standalone; the frozen N2 provenance matrix remains exact.

draftCases.name: Owen Parker
draftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 59-year-old man, attends clinic to discuss an outside descending-colon polypectomy.

nodes.title: Regional risk despite local clearance
nodes.objective: Distinguish vascular invasion from local clearance when selecting regional treatment.
nodes.update: Fragments contain moderately differentiated submucosal carcinoma. One ends through invasive glands at a cauterized edge; depth cannot be reconstructed. No vascular invasion is seen in represented sections. The scar looks clear, distant staging is negative and he is fit for resection.
nodes.task: Which treatment plan best addresses {patientName}'s descending-colon pathology?

choices.label: Oncologic descending-colon resection
choices.temptation: Treat an unassessable invasive front as an oncologic issue
choices.rationale: The transected invasive edge and unknown depth do not meet favorable-polyp criteria.
choices.reasonableWhen: An operable patient has a positive or indeterminate invasive margin.

choices.label: Endoscopic full-thickness scar resection
choices.temptation: Convert every uncertainty into a local clearance problem
choices.rationale: Local treatment may not settle the regional question from inadequately assessed invasive cancer.
choices.reasonableWhen: A selected noninvasive residual lesion or specialist-defined local-only issue.

choices.label: Colonoscopic scar surveillance
choices.temptation: Treat no vascular invasion as sufficient for low risk
choices.rationale: A sampled negative does not repair a transected invasive front.
choices.reasonableWhen: An intact completely assessed favorable polyp.

nodes.explanation: The actual cut-edge involvement matters more than the clear-looking scar. Sampled negatives do not turn an incomplete invasive specimen into a fully assessed favorable one.

gate.cueAttack: Removed the margin-naming lead-in. Raw transection and unmeasurable depth require interpretation. Options compare definitive lesion plans.
steps: Identify transected invasive glands and the missing complete front.
Do not extrapolate sampled negatives to global favorable risk.
gate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: sampled negative findings may be overextended to the full specimen.
gate.decidingObservation: Invasive glands are cut across at cautery and depth is unassessable.
gate.consequence: False confidence in local treatment of inadequately staged cancer.
gate.deletionTest: Transected glands change the key; fragment count alone would not prove an adverse invasive edge.
gate.counterfactual: Replace fragments with an intact shallow favorable specimen and clear edges: surveillance becomes best.
gate.sequence: Standalone; no frozen colon-cancer companion is rebound.

draftCases.name: Peter Lawson
draftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 61-year-old man, attends clinic after a sigmoid-polyp pathology report used the word carcinoma.

nodes.title: Mucosal carcinoma versus T1 invasion
nodes.objective: Use represented tissue boundaries rather than a cancer label to select local versus regional care.
nodes.update: The lesion was removed intact. Malignant glands are confined to lamina propria with continuous muscularis mucosae beneath them. Represented submucosa contains no invasive glands; all cut edges are clear.
nodes.task: Which lesion-directed plan fits {patientName}'s represented pathology?

choices.label: Colonoscopic surveillance after local excision
choices.temptation: Apply the actual depth boundary
choices.rationale: The adequately represented mucosal lesion has been excised; submucosal T1 invasion is not shown.
choices.reasonableWhen: Complete local excision of intramucosal disease.

choices.label: Full-thickness endoscopic scar resection
choices.temptation: Treat carcinoma wording as unremoved deeper tissue
choices.rationale: The intact specimen already represents the relevant boundary and clear margins.
choices.reasonableWhen: A selected unresolved local-clearance question.

choices.label: Sigmoid colectomy with regional lymphadenectomy
choices.temptation: Collapse mucosal carcinoma and adverse T1 cancer
choices.rationale: The represented submucosa contains no invasive glands.
choices.reasonableWhen: Submucosal invasion with adverse histology supports regional treatment.

nodes.explanation: Interpret depth and adequacy before acting on terminology. An intact specimen showing mucosal confinement and clear edges supports local treatment with surveillance.

gate.cueAttack: No stage-zero label precedes the answer. Represented submucosa is retained because a superficial negative would not establish the same conclusion.
steps: Interpret the muscularis-mucosae boundary and represented submucosa.
Choose local care rather than regional surgery from the word carcinoma.
gate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: pathology terminology can provoke overtreatment if depth is ignored.
gate.decidingObservation: Glands remain above continuous muscularis mucosae; submucosa is represented.
gate.consequence: Unnecessary regional resection.
gate.deletionTest: Removing represented submucosa destroys confidence in the local conclusion; clear edges establish local completion.
gate.counterfactual: Show glands inside submucosal vascular channels: regional colectomy becomes best.
gate.sequence: Standalone; no histology-label task precedes the applied decision.

draftCases.name: Martha Nolan
draftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 34-year-old woman with established FAP, attends clinic while the founder reviews outside colonoscopy and operative-planning records.

nodes.title: Rectal removal for uncontrolled FAP burden
nodes.objective: Integrate rectal clearance, continence and restorative goals when choosing FAP operative extent.
nodes.update: The colon contains extensive adenomas. In the rectum, confluent adenomatous areas remain between several prior resection scars; two further clearing sessions left visible lesions, including a broad focus with high-grade dysplasia. She has normal continence and wants intestinal continuity after counseling.
nodes.task: Which operative plan should be discussed for {patientName}'s colorectal disease?

choices.label: Proctocolectomy with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis
choices.temptation: Interpret failed rectal control alongside function
choices.rationale: Removing the uncontrolled rectum addresses the disease; preserved continence and informed restorative goals support IPAA.
choices.reasonableWhen: Rectal burden requires removal and pouch function is clinically appropriate.

choices.label: Colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis
choices.temptation: Preserve the rectum despite the actual clearance record
choices.rationale: IRA retains the repeatedly uncleared rectal adenoma field.
choices.reasonableWhen: Relative rectal sparing with endoscopically controllable adenomas.

choices.label: Proctocolectomy with end ileostomy
choices.temptation: Choose rectal removal without using the functional goal
choices.rationale: It removes the field but is less aligned with her stated restorative goal and preserved continence.
choices.reasonableWhen: Poor sphincter function or an informed preference against pouch-related functional effects.

nodes.explanation: Repeated failure to clear the rectal field changes the operation from colon removal to colorectal removal. Continence and the informed functional goal then guide reconstruction.

gate.cueAttack: Removed the conclusion rectal burden not controllable. Actual failed clearing, residual field and dysplasia establish it. Three named operations have similar scope; continence and goals are necessary rather than decorative.
steps: Infer that the repeatedly uncleared dysplastic rectal field cannot safely be retained as in IRA.
Use continence and restorative goals to select IPAA rather than an end stoma.
gate.difficulty: Moderate/hard prediction: a resident may preserve an unsafe rectum to avoid pelvic dissection or remove restoration despite adequate function.
gate.decidingObservation: Repeated visible rectal residual disease with high-grade dysplasia, normal continence.
gate.consequence: Retained high-risk rectal disease or avoidable loss of desired restoration.
gate.deletionTest: Failed clearance establishes extent; continence and goals distinguish two rectum-removing operations.
gate.counterfactual: Change to a sparsely involved rectum with all adenomas removed and a priority to avoid pelvic dissection: IRA becomes reasonable.
gate.sequence: Standalone; genetics testing interpretation is outside the scored topic.

draftCases.name: Nathan Cole
draftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 29-year-old man with established FAP, attends clinic to review prophylactic surgery with the founder.

nodes.title: Rectal-sparing FAP operation
nodes.objective: Assess whether relative rectal sparing permits a colon-only operation under informed functional goals.
nodes.update: Hundreds of colonic adenomas remain after an outside colonoscopy. The rectum contained three small adenomas, all removed intact; the remaining rectum was adequately inspected. Continence is normal. After counseling, he prioritizes avoiding pelvic dissection if the retained rectum can be safely monitored and accepts continuing endoscopy.
nodes.task: Which operative plan best fits {patientName}'s disease distribution and stated priorities?

choices.label: Total colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis
choices.temptation: Use relative rectal sparing under informed priorities
choices.rationale: The documented clearable rectum permits an IRA option, with ongoing surveillance.
choices.reasonableWhen: Relative rectal sparing, clearable lesions and willingness to retain surveillance.

choices.label: Proctocolectomy with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis
choices.temptation: Apply the most extensive restorative operation to every FAP case
choices.rationale: IPAA is a valid broader option, but the supplied relative sparing and functional priority favor IRA here.
choices.reasonableWhen: Rectal burden cannot be controlled or informed goals favor rectal removal.

choices.label: Proctocolectomy with end ileostomy
choices.temptation: Treat all polyposis as incompatible with restoration
choices.rationale: No sphincter problem or preference favors an end stoma in this case.
choices.reasonableWhen: Poor sphincter function or a preference against pouch function.

nodes.explanation: The operation depends on distribution, not a single FAP label. Relative rectal sparing permits IRA when the patient accepts ongoing rectal risk assessment and surveillance.

gate.cueAttack: The preference is necessary because both IRA and IPAA can be valid. It does not by itself establish that the rectum is retainable. All alternatives name complete operations.
steps: Interpret the colon-versus-rectum adenoma distribution and completeness of rectal clearance.
Apply the informed priority only after establishing that rectal retention is a supported option.
gate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: diagnosis-based automatic IPAA competes with inappropriate rectal preservation regardless of burden.
gate.decidingObservation: Three rectal adenomas completely removed versus extensive persistent colonic disease.
gate.consequence: Unnecessary pelvic dissection or, if distribution is misread, unsafe rectal retention.
gate.deletionTest: Without the clearing record, the priority cannot choose IRA; without the informed priority, IPAA remains equally defensible.
gate.counterfactual: Replace relative sparing with repeatedly uncleared rectal high-grade disease: proctocolectomy with IPAA becomes best despite the wish to avoid pelvic dissection.
gate.sequence: First decision; feedback gives no future progression findings.

draftCases.name: Helen Marsh
draftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 48-year-old woman with FAP, attends clinic for review of outside colorectal surgical recommendations.

nodes.title: Reconstruction when continence is poor
nodes.objective: Integrate rectal removal needs with established sphincter dysfunction and informed functional priorities.
nodes.update: The rectal adenoma field includes high-grade dysplasia and has remained after repeated clearing attempts. She has daily leakage of formed stool despite prior continence treatment; examination documents a weak disrupted sphincter. After counseling, she prioritizes reliable evacuation and accepts a permanent stoma.
nodes.task: Which operative plan best fits {patientName}'s disease and functional record?

choices.label: Proctocolectomy with end ileostomy
choices.temptation: Use established poor function when choosing reconstruction
choices.rationale: The rectum needs removal and a pouch would depend on an already poorly functioning outlet; her informed goal supports an end stoma.
choices.reasonableWhen: Rectal removal is needed with poor sphincter function and compatible informed goals.

choices.label: Proctocolectomy with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis
choices.temptation: Apply restoration without checking the outlet
choices.rationale: It removes the field but uses the impaired sphincter and conflicts with her functional priority.
choices.reasonableWhen: Good sphincter function with a restorative goal.

choices.label: Colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis
choices.temptation: Avoid pouch surgery by retaining an unsafe rectum
choices.rationale: IRA leaves the uncleared rectal dysplastic field and does not resolve the outlet dysfunction.
choices.reasonableWhen: Relative rectal sparing and adequate control permit retention.

nodes.explanation: Disease distribution determines what must be removed; sphincter function and informed goals determine whether restoration is appropriate.

gate.cueAttack: The stoma preference is supported by raw formed-stool leakage and structural weakness, not used as an isolated answer label. Three specific operations share grammar.
steps: Identify both uncontrolled rectal disease and a compromised outlet.
Choose rectal removal without a reconstruction relying on that outlet.
gate.difficulty: Moderate/hard prediction: reflex IPAA in a younger patient can override functional evidence.
gate.decidingObservation: Established daily formed-stool leakage and sphincter disruption.
gate.consequence: Poor pouch continence or retention of uncontrolled rectal disease.
gate.deletionTest: Without poor function, restorative IPAA competes strongly; burden still determines the need for rectal removal.
gate.counterfactual: Replace dysfunction with normal continence and an informed restorative goal: IPAA becomes best.
gate.sequence: Standalone; demographic facts do not select the operation.

draftCases.name: Laura Sutton
draftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 54-year-old woman, attends clinic after an outside biopsy identified mid-rectal adenocarcinoma.

nodes.title: Neoadjuvant sequence for locally advanced rectal cancer
nodes.objective: Use local stage and threatened planes to select treatment before definitive surgery.
nodes.update: The outside MRI shows tumor extending through muscle into mesorectal fat, touching the mesorectal fascia, with two irregular heterogeneous mesorectal nodes. The tumor lies below the anterior peritoneal reflection. Mismatch-repair proteins are retained. Distant staging remains negative and she is fit for combined treatment.
nodes.task: Which treatment sequence should be discussed for {patientName}'s rectal cancer?

choices.label: Total neoadjuvant therapy followed by reassessment
choices.temptation: Integrate local and systemic control before surgery
choices.rationale: The locally advanced mid-rectal findings support a neoadjuvant multimodal pathway before definitive surgical planning.
choices.reasonableWhen: Fit patient with stage II/III mid or low rectal disease.

choices.label: Total mesorectal excision followed by adjuvant therapy
choices.temptation: Treat a technically resectable tumor as ready for immediate surgery
choices.rationale: This sequence bypasses the neoadjuvant opportunity in the supplied high-risk local setting.
choices.reasonableWhen: Selected low-risk or upper-rectal disease can favor initial surgery.

choices.label: Transanal excision followed by adjuvant therapy
choices.temptation: Substitute local wall removal for a mesorectal disease strategy
choices.rationale: Local excision does not address the represented extramural and nodal disease.
choices.reasonableWhen: Selected small favorable cT1N0 lesions can be locally excised.

nodes.explanation: Interpret the extramural, nodal and fascia findings before selecting the sequence. Total neoadjuvant treatment is a supported pathway for this fit patient before definitive resection planning.

gate.cueAttack: No cT3N-positive or locally advanced label supplies the staging inference. Three options are named treatment sequences of comparable length.
steps: Infer extramural/regional disease and a threatened local surgical plane from MRI observations.
Select preoperative multimodal treatment rather than immediate or local surgery.
gate.difficulty: Moderate/hard prediction: technically resectable and colon-like surgery-first reasoning can override rectal local-control needs.
gate.decidingObservation: Extramural tumor touching fascia, irregular nodes and position below the reflection.
gate.consequence: Loss of a supported neoadjuvant local/systemic treatment opportunity.
gate.deletionTest: The MRI changes the plan; mismatch repair narrows modern treatment context without testing germline interpretation.
gate.counterfactual: Move the tumor entirely above the reflection with clear local planes and no high-risk extension: initial resection becomes a reasonable offered sequence.
gate.sequence: First explanation names staging scope, not neoadjuvant treatment. MRI findings appear only after that answer.

draftCases.name: Samuel Price
draftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 57-year-old man, attends clinic for review of a small outside rectal-cancer workup.

nodes.title: Completion treatment after unexpected T2 disease
nodes.objective: Use depth found after local excision to address untreated regional risk despite clear margins.
nodes.update: At a later clinic visit, the founder reviews the outside full-thickness excision. Cancer infiltrates the muscularis propria but stops before perirectal fat. All specimen edges are clear. Pelvic restaging shows no enlarged nodes or distant disease; he is fit for radical resection and has not received radiation.
nodes.task: Which next treatment plan should be discussed for {patientName}'s rectal cancer?

choices.label: Completion rectal resection with total mesorectal excision
choices.temptation: Address disease outside the scope of local excision
choices.rationale: Muscularis-propria invasion places the lesion beyond the favorable T1 local-excision group; clear wall edges do not stage mesorectal nodes.
choices.reasonableWhen: An operable patient has T2 disease after local excision.

choices.label: Repeat full-thickness transanal scar excision
choices.temptation: Use more local clearance to solve regional risk
choices.rationale: The local edges are already clear; another scar specimen does not remove the regional nodal basin.
choices.reasonableWhen: A selected local-margin problem without a need for radical regional treatment.

choices.label: Endoscopic rectal scar surveillance
choices.temptation: Treat a clear margin and negative imaging as node-negative proof
choices.rationale: Local clearance and imaging cannot settle microscopic mesorectal disease.
choices.reasonableWhen: A favorable adequately assessed T1 lesion treated completely locally.

nodes.explanation: The new pathology changes the relevant treatment scope. Clear local margins do not make a muscle-invasive rectal cancer adequately treated by local excision in a fit patient.

gate.cueAttack: No T2 label is supplied. The raw muscle boundary must be interpreted. Options compare three postexcision plans rather than information gathering against premature therapy.
steps: Infer muscularis-propria invasion from the specimen.
Address regional mesorectal risk that local excision cannot stage or treat.
gate.difficulty: Moderate/hard prediction: a clear local edge and CT-sized nodes may be mistaken for completed oncologic treatment.
gate.decidingObservation: Cancer infiltrates muscularis propria despite clear specimen edges.
gate.consequence: Inadequate regional treatment.
gate.deletionTest: Delete muscle invasion and favorable T1 surveillance may follow; the update therefore earns a new decision.
gate.counterfactual: Change to a fully assessed favorable T1 lesion with clear edges: surveillance becomes best.
gate.sequence: Prior EUS feedback identifies a staging question but gives no final-depth result or completion operation.

draftCases.name: Amelia Grant
draftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 57-year-old woman, attends clinic after outside neoadjuvant treatment for a previously node-positive low rectal adenocarcinoma.

nodes.title: Select a rectal organ-preservation pathway
nodes.objective: Distinguish adequate clinical response from persistent tumor before offering watch-and-wait.
nodes.update: Treatment ended in July. In September, a firm mural nodule was palpable beneath intact mucosa; on a later October assessment it was larger. MRI shows a corresponding intermediate-T2 focus with diffusion restriction. Superficial biopsies contain scar and inflammation. Distant restaging is negative. She is fit for resection and remains interested in organ preservation.
nodes.task: Which treatment plan best fits {patientName}'s current rectal findings?

choices.label: Oncologic rectal resection with total mesorectal excision
choices.temptation: Do not equate negative surface biopsy with wall eradication
choices.rationale: Progressive concordant mural abnormalities are not a complete response; regional oncologic resection assessment is supported.
choices.reasonableWhen: Persistent rectal tumor is present in an operable patient.

choices.label: Full-thickness transanal excision of the treated site
choices.temptation: Use a local specimen to avoid regional treatment
choices.rationale: The prior regional disease and persistent mural findings do not establish a favorable local-only treatment group.
choices.reasonableWhen: Selected small favorable early tumors may be treated locally.

choices.label: Protocolized watch-and-wait surveillance
choices.temptation: Let preference and superficial histology overrule the response record
choices.rationale: Interest in organ preservation does not convert progressive palpable/MRI disease into a complete clinical response.
choices.reasonableWhen: Concordant clinical complete response after informed counseling in an experienced program.

nodes.explanation: The biopsy describes the surface specimen. Progressive concordant mural findings defeat a complete-response conclusion despite that negative sample and her organ-preservation goal.

gate.cueAttack: No residual-tumor or incomplete-response label is supplied. The organ-preservation preference cannot select the key and is deliberately overruled by actual progression. No fixed timing threshold is taught.
steps: Reconcile superficial negative tissue with an enlarging palpable and diffusion-restricting wall focus.
Decline the complete-response watch-and-wait pathway and address persistent oncologic disease.
gate.difficulty: Hard prediction: false-negative biopsy reassurance and preference anchoring compete with progression.
gate.decidingObservation: The palpable nodule enlarges and corresponds to a persistent restricting wall focus.
gate.consequence: Observation of persistent tumor rather than timely oncologic treatment.
gate.deletionTest: Without progression the owner-held near-complete boundary could recur; it is deliberately excluded. Surface provenance explains the negative biopsy.
gate.counterfactual: Replace the mural findings with concordant smooth flat scar, no restricting focus and no suspicious nodes: informed protocolized watch-and-wait becomes a supported option.
gate.sequence: Standalone. This is not the held shrinking equivocal ulcer at eight weeks; that version and clinical question remain held.

draftCases.name: Robert Hayes
draftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 65-year-old man, attends clinic while the founder reviews outside surveillance after a prior clinical complete response managed by watch-and-wait.

nodes.title: Salvage assessment after rectal regrowth
nodes.objective: Use proven localized regrowth and depth to plan salvage rather than continue the old response pathway.
nodes.update: New endoscopy shows a nodule at the treated site; biopsy contains adenocarcinoma. MRI shows growth through the muscularis propria, with an achievable surgical plane. Chest and abdominal staging show no distant disease. He is fit for surgery after prior completed neoadjuvant therapy.
nodes.task: Which treatment plan should now be discussed for {patientName}'s rectal lesion?

choices.label: Salvage rectal resection with total mesorectal excision
choices.temptation: Update the plan from current proven disease
choices.rationale: Localized operable regrowth with deep-wall involvement warrants oncologic salvage assessment.
choices.reasonableWhen: Resectable regrowth is established after watch-and-wait.

choices.label: Transanal full-thickness nodule excision
choices.temptation: Treat all small-looking luminal regrowth as local-only disease
choices.rationale: The MRI demonstrates depth beyond a favorable early local-excision group.
choices.reasonableWhen: Selected superficial favorable local lesions may permit a local approach.

choices.label: Continue protocolized watch-and-wait surveillance
choices.temptation: Carry the old complete-response conclusion forward
choices.rationale: Biopsy-proven regrowth is not continued clinical complete response.
choices.reasonableWhen: Current evaluation still demonstrates complete response without suspicious recurrence.

nodes.explanation: A prior complete response is historical evidence, not permanent clearance. Proven localized regrowth changes the treatment objective to salvage.

gate.cueAttack: Known biopsy diagnosis is legitimate because the task is treatment. Raw depth and completed staging distinguish salvage scope; no invented recurrence probability appears.
gate.stage: Three treatment plans for current localized regrowth.
steps: Recognize that current pathology overrides the older complete response.
Use depth and negative distant staging to choose regional oncologic salvage assessment.
gate.difficulty: Moderate/hard prediction: prior organ-preservation success and a small luminal nodule can favor insufficient local treatment.
gate.decidingObservation: Biopsy-proven regrowth extends through muscularis propria without distant disease.
gate.consequence: Delayed or inadequate salvage treatment.
gate.deletionTest: Without depth, local salvage possibilities compete; without distant staging, the curative local plan is less secure.
gate.counterfactual: Replace current nodule/biopsy/MRI findings with unchanged complete-response assessments: continued protocol surveillance becomes appropriate.
gate.sequence: Independent case; no earlier newly authored explanation supplies salvage selection.

draftCases.name: Irene Wells
draftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 67-year-old woman, attends clinic after an outside sigmoid colectomy.

nodes.title: Postoperative planning with a tumor deposit
nodes.objective: Recognize regional disease from a confirmed tumor deposit despite negative recovered nodes.
nodes.update: Additional pathology finds a total of 15 negative nodes. A separate pericolic nodule contains discontinuous adenocarcinoma; the pathologist confirms a tumor deposit rather than residual lymph-node, vessel or nerve tissue. Margins remain clear, distant staging is negative, mismatch-repair proteins are retained and she has recovered sufficiently for adjuvant treatment assessment.
nodes.task: Which postoperative plan should be discussed for {patientName}'s updated pathology?

choices.label: Adjuvant FOLFOX planning with medical oncology
choices.temptation: Classify the regional deposit before selecting intent
choices.rationale: A confirmed pericolic deposit can establish regional N1c disease despite negative nodes, supporting adjuvant systemic treatment assessment.
choices.reasonableWhen: Completely resected nonmetastatic colon cancer has regional disease.

choices.label: Surveillance after node-negative colectomy
choices.temptation: Count negative nodes and ignore the separate deposit
choices.rationale: The adequate negative-node count does not erase deposit-defined regional involvement.
choices.reasonableWhen: A completely resected lower-risk node-negative tumor may enter surveillance.

choices.label: Adjuvant pelvic chemoradiation planning
choices.temptation: Apply a rectal local-control pathway to a colon deposit
choices.rationale: This is a sigmoid-colon regional pathology problem, not an indication for routine pelvic radiation.
choices.reasonableWhen: Selected rectal-cancer local-control pathways can include pelvic chemoradiation.

nodes.explanation: A confirmed tumor deposit is not canceled by an adequate set of negative nodes. Interpret it as regional disease before discussing adjuvant systemic treatment; regimen details remain individualized.

gate.cueAttack: No stage III label appears. The pathologist-confirmed tissue category is legitimate data because treatment is scored; no invented nodule classification is inferred by the author. Options are postoperative treatment strategies.
steps: Interpret a discontinuous confirmed pericolic deposit despite negative nodes.
Apply the regional-disease treatment pathway rather than a node-count-only conclusion.
gate.difficulty: Hard prediction: an adequate negative-node count can distract from N1c disease.
gate.decidingObservation: Confirmed discontinuous pericolic tumor deposit with no distant disease.
gate.consequence: Omission of an indicated adjuvant treatment discussion.
gate.deletionTest: The deposit changes treatment; without it the new adequate node-negative report could support surveillance depending on other risks.
gate.counterfactual: Remove the deposit and all high-risk features from an adequately staged completely resected tumor: surveillance becomes a reasonable offered plan.
gate.sequence: Earlier feedback requests an adequate node search but does not state deposit classification or adjuvant therapy.

draftCases.name: Joan Miller
draftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 63-year-old woman, attends clinic to reconcile an outside colonoscopy report and pathology fragment count.

nodes.title: Count adenomas by lesions rather than fragments
nodes.objective: Use the actual number of removed lesions and the assessed histology to select surveillance.
nodes.update: The complete, adequately prepared procedure log records two polyps, 6 mm and 8 mm, each removed completely and placed together in one container. The laboratory describes four tissue fragments of tubular adenoma without advanced features. No other lesions, previous neoplasia, hereditary syndrome or relevant family history are recorded.
nodes.task: Under USMSTF guidance, when should {patientName}'s surveillance colonoscopy be planned?

choices.label: Colonoscopy in seven to ten years
choices.temptation: Reconcile the procedure count with specimen fragmentation
choices.rationale: Two small completely removed nonadvanced adenomas remain two lesions despite four laboratory fragments.
choices.reasonableWhen: One or two small nonadvanced tubular adenomas at a high-quality baseline.

choices.label: Colonoscopy in three to five years
choices.temptation: Count tissue fragments as separate adenomas
choices.rationale: The procedure documented two lesions; four fragments do not establish four adenomas.
choices.reasonableWhen: Three or four small tubular adenomas were actually removed.

choices.label: Colonoscopy in three years
choices.temptation: Treat any multiple-fragment adenoma jar as high-burden disease
choices.rationale: Neither five-to-ten actual adenomas nor an advanced feature is established.
choices.reasonableWhen: Five to ten small adenomas or an advanced adenoma is found.

nodes.explanation: Use lesion-level procedural provenance rather than fragment count. The two small nonadvanced adenomas support the USMSTF seven-to-ten-year interval.

gate.cueAttack: No low-risk-count label is supplied. Procedure sites and laboratory fragments must be reconciled. Three parallel interval options carry identical colonoscopy preview scope.
steps: Infer that four fragments from one jar do not establish four removed lesions.
Apply the actual two-lesion count and nonadvanced histology to the surveillance interval.
gate.difficulty: Hard prediction: fragment counting produces a specifically plausible three-to-five-year error.
gate.decidingObservation: Two documented lesions versus four fragments in the shared pathology container.
gate.consequence: Unnecessary surveillance from a falsely inflated adenoma count.
gate.deletionTest: Without the procedure count the jar cannot establish lesion number; size and histology keep the low-count rule applicable.
gate.counterfactual: Replace the procedure log with four separate completely removed small adenomas: three-to-five years becomes best.
gate.sequence: Standalone; this is a provenance-to-management decision, not a cosmetic size variant.

draftCases.name: Henry Wallace
draftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 58-year-old man, attends clinic to reconcile outside colorectal screening results.

nodes.title: Complete abnormal stool screening
nodes.objective: Select diagnostic colonoscopy after an abnormal FIT despite a later negative repeat.
nodes.update: The August screening FIT was positive and a September repeat was negative. An October colonoscopy reached the cecum and found no lesion. Its withdrawal record describes adherent stool covering much of the ascending and transverse mucosa after irrigation and suction; the distal mucosa was visible. The summary calls the colonoscopy negative.
nodes.task: Which next colorectal investigation should be arranged for {patientName} after these outside results?

choices.label: Repeat colonoscopy with a revised preparation plan
choices.temptation: Accept the latest label only after checking what was actually examined.
choices.rationale: The proximal mucosa was not adequately evaluated. The positive FIT still needs a complete diagnostic colonoscopy despite the repeat FIT and negative summary.
choices.reasonableWhen: A positive stool screen is followed by a colonoscopy whose mucosal visualization remains inadequate.

choices.label: CT colonography with a colonic preparation plan
choices.temptation: Use an alternative complete-colon investigation after an incomplete report.
choices.rationale: The record describes a preparation problem, not an anatomic barrier or contraindication to repeating colonoscopy; colonoscopy can also sample or remove a lesion.
choices.reasonableWhen: A distal cancer prevents complete colonoscopy and proximal-colon assessment is needed.

choices.label: Repeat fecal immunochemical screening next year
choices.temptation: Let a negative repeat screen and a negative summary end the workup.
choices.rationale: Neither the repeat stool test nor the poorly visualized proximal colon establishes completed positive-FIT evaluation.
choices.reasonableWhen: Routine stool screening is being chosen before any abnormal screening result.

nodes.explanation: Read the withdrawal observations before accepting the negative summary. Cecal reach did not establish adequate proximal inspection, so the positive FIT remains incompletely evaluated. Repeat prepared colonoscopy addresses that deficit; repeating FIT does not.

gate.cueAttack: Removed the permission that colonoscopy is clinically appropriate and the announcement that no examination followed. The competing negative report must be reconciled with its raw withdrawal observations. Options are concrete next investigation plans; CT colonography is a credible completion alternative rather than an already completed distal examination.
gate.stage: One next-investigation decision after discordant screening and colonoscopy records.
steps: Infer from the final withdrawal observations that the negative colonoscopy summary does not represent a complete mucosal evaluation.
Apply the unresolved positive-FIT pathway to select repeat colonoscopy rather than rescreening or an unnecessary modality substitution.
gate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: anchoring on cecal reach, the negative repeat FIT or the report headline produces a specific wrong completion decision. This is not claimed independently hard.
gate.decidingObservation: The limiting factor is persistent stool after cleansing, with no anatomic completion failure or stated contraindication to repeat colonoscopy.
gate.consequence: Missed proximal pathology or failure to complete abnormal screening.
gate.deletionTest: The FIT results establish the diagnostic pathway; final segment visibility determines whether it was completed. The negative headline creates a real reconciliation task; no availability permission remains.
gate.counterfactual: If an otherwise adequately prepared examination instead stopped at an impassable distal cancer, CT colonography would become an offered method to assess the unexamined proximal colon.
gate.sequence: Standalone; no preceding colonoscopy or biopsy feedback supplies the judgment.

draftCases.name: Grace Bennett
draftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 64-year-old woman, attends clinic to review an outside screening colonoscopy.

nodes.title: Judge the final preparation rather than the insertion view
nodes.objective: Use final mucosal visualization after cleansing to decide whether a normal colonoscopy supports standard screening.
nodes.update: During insertion, stool covered the right-colon mucosa. The cecum was reached. After irrigation and suction, the withdrawal record documents the entire mucosa in every segment as visible, with no obscured area and no polyp or mass. This was her first screening colonoscopy; there is no prior neoplasia, hereditary syndrome or relevant family history.
nodes.task: Under USMSTF guidance, which next colonoscopy plan fits {patientName}'s completed examination?

choices.label: Repeat colonoscopy in ten years
choices.temptation: Use the final examination quality and normal findings.
choices.rationale: Preparation is judged after cleansing. A complete normal examination with adequate final visualization supports the usual ten-year interval in this scoped screening setting.
choices.reasonableWhen: The entire colon is adequately inspected and normal without a history requiring shorter surveillance.

choices.label: Repeat colonoscopy within one year
choices.temptation: Let the initially dirty right colon define the whole examination.
choices.rationale: The final withdrawal record establishes that cleaning resolved the obscuration; an inadequacy-driven early repeat is not supported.
choices.reasonableWhen: Mucosa remains inadequately visualized after cleansing in a screening examination.

choices.label: Repeat colonoscopy in three years
choices.temptation: Compromise between an initially dirty view and a normal final report.
choices.rationale: An intermediate interval does not replace classification of the final examination, and no advanced adenoma was found.
choices.reasonableWhen: A completely removed advanced adenoma establishes a three-year surveillance indication.

nodes.explanation: Insertion quality and final withdrawal quality are different observations. After cleansing, every segment was visible and normal. That final examination supports standard screening timing; an initially dirty view does not independently create an early-repeat indication.

gate.cueAttack: Replaced the editorially signaled bad report and the completed-sigmoidoscopy foil. All options now name colonoscopy timing. The learner must reconcile insertion and withdrawal rather than match the word inadequate to repeat.
gate.stage: Three next-colonoscopy plans for the same completed screening examination.
steps: Determine whether the initial obscuration persisted after endoscopist cleaning.
Use the resulting complete normal examination, rather than insertion appearance, to select standard screening timing.
gate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: an inadequacy heuristic competes with the final visualization record. No unsupported numerical cleanliness score is required.
gate.decidingObservation: Every segment became fully visible on withdrawal after cleaning; the initially dirty view did not persist.
gate.consequence: Unnecessary early invasive testing if insertion quality is mistaken for final adequacy.
gate.deletionTest: Remove the initial view and there is no quality reconciliation; remove the final observations and a standard interval cannot be justified. History excludes a separate surveillance pathway.
gate.counterfactual: If adherent stool still obscured broad proximal areas after all cleansing, the final examination would remain inadequate and the offered within-one-year repeat would replace the ten-year plan in this screening setting.
gate.sequence: Standalone with a normal screening frame; not a second question that inherits an earlier inadequate-preparation answer.

draftCases.name: Grace Bennett
draftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 64-year-old woman, attends clinic to reconcile an outside polypectomy report with the pathology processing record.

nodes.title: Surveillance after an advanced adenoma
nodes.objective: Use the completed baseline and resection details to select USMSTF surveillance.
nodes.update: The complete, adequately prepared colonoscopy documented one 24-mm nonpedunculated adenoma removed by a single en-bloc snare resection. The specimen arrived intact; the laboratory grossing log records that it was divided into four pieces for processing. Final pathology shows tubular adenoma without invasive cancer, and the assessed margins are free of adenoma. No other lesion, prior neoplasia, hereditary syndrome or relevant family history is recorded.
nodes.task: Under USMSTF guidance, when should {patientName}'s first surveillance colonoscopy be planned after this resection?

choices.label: Colonoscopy in three years
choices.temptation: Reconstruct the resection method from procedure and laboratory records.
choices.rationale: The lesion was removed intact in one resection; later laboratory division does not make that procedure piecemeal. Size establishes an advanced adenoma with confident complete removal.
choices.reasonableWhen: An adenoma at least 10 mm is completely removed at a high-quality baseline examination.

choices.label: Colonoscopy in six months
choices.temptation: Treat four laboratory pieces as four resection fragments.
choices.rationale: The early piecemeal scar interval applies to the endoscopic removal method, not subsequent grossing of an intact specimen.
choices.reasonableWhen: An adenoma at least 20 mm was removed piecemeal.

choices.label: Colonoscopy in one year
choices.temptation: Apply another large-polyp follow-up interval without checking which surveillance visit is being scheduled.
choices.rationale: This is the first follow-up after complete en-bloc removal, not the later visit after an initial piecemeal scar check.
choices.reasonableWhen: The first six-month surveillance after a large piecemeal resection has been completed and the next visit is being scheduled.

nodes.explanation: Separate endoscopic resection from laboratory processing. Four grossing pieces from a specimen received intact do not establish piecemeal removal. The completely excised 24-mm adenoma therefore follows the three-year advanced-adenoma pathway.

gate.cueAttack: The procedure and pathology records now create a consequential discrepancy. Removed the prior routine size-only stem. Three equally formatted intervals are credible within post-polypectomy care; no ten-year foil remains.
steps: Infer that fragmentation occurred in laboratory processing, not during resection.
Apply the size-defined advanced-adenoma interval rather than the large-piecemeal scar interval.
gate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: conflating laboratory fragments with resection pieces changes the correct interval; size recall alone no longer solves the record.
gate.decidingObservation: The specimen was received intact after one en-bloc resection, then divided by the laboratory.
gate.consequence: Unnecessary early scar surveillance from misclassifying the resection method.
gate.deletionTest: The laboratory division is the competing signal; intact receipt and procedure technique resolve it. Size and complete assessed margins set the interval boundary.
gate.counterfactual: If the procedure instead removed this 24-mm adenoma in overlapping pieces before retrieval, the offered six-month first surveillance would become appropriate.
gate.sequence: Standalone; no preparation or resection feedback has already classified this specimen.

draftCases.name: Victor Ellis
draftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 67-year-old man, attends clinic with outside endoscopy records for a cecal lesion.

nodes.title: Advanced resection before colectomy
nodes.objective: Choose expert endoscopic assessment for a large lesion without demonstrated deep invasion.
nodes.update: The 28-mm laterally spreading cecal lesion has a uniform granular surface without a depressed or ulcerated focus on documented image-enhanced inspection. A small superficial sample contains adenoma; submucosa is not represented. The first operator stopped before resection because of size.
nodes.task: Which referral should guide {patientName}'s next lesion-removal plan?

choices.label: Advanced-endoscopy referral for endoscopic resection planning
choices.temptation: Distinguish technical size from observed deep invasion.
choices.rationale: Large nonpedunculated lesions without deep invasive features merit advanced-resection expertise; the superficial biopsy does not itself prove the whole lesion benign.
choices.reasonableWhen: A large lesion lacks overt deep invasive features and has not yet undergone an expert resection assessment.

choices.label: Colorectal-surgery referral for oncologic resection planning
choices.temptation: Treat lesion size or unassessed submucosa as sufficient evidence for colectomy.
choices.rationale: Neither size alone nor an unrepresented layer establishes deep invasion that rules out endoscopic treatment.
choices.reasonableWhen: Deep invasive features or an expert assessment establishes a lesion unsuitable for curative endoscopic removal.

choices.label: Diagnostic-endoscopy referral for repeat biopsy planning
choices.temptation: Require a more reassuring biopsy before any resection referral.
choices.rationale: Repeating a small sample may still miss the relevant invasive focus and does not address the expertise required for definitive removal.
choices.reasonableWhen: A suspicious lesion needs histologic confirmation for a nonendoscopic treatment pathway and the initial sample was unrepresentative.

nodes.explanation: Interpret the optical morphology separately from the limited superficial sample. The absent submucosa prevents the biopsy from excluding invasion, but size alone does not establish an indication for colectomy. Advanced endoscopic resection planning is the appropriate referral at this stage.

gate.cueAttack: All options now commit to a referral for a specified planning objective. Removed the key-only cautious assessment wording, committed colectomy contrast and serial partial-resection foil. The raw morphology, rather than the biopsy word adenoma, supplies the discriminating evidence.
gate.stage: Three referral plans before definitive lesion treatment.
steps: Interpret the optical appearance and sampling depth without treating superficial adenoma as proof of absent invasion.
Select advanced endoscopic resection expertise rather than size-driven oncologic planning or another limited biopsy.
gate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: colectomy for size and repeated biopsy for unrepresented submucosa are credible competing errors; no independent hard label is asserted.
gate.decidingObservation: Uniform granular morphology without a depressed or ulcerated focus, with size as the first operator's reason for stopping.
gate.consequence: Avoidable colectomy or repeated sampling that delays definitive assessment.
gate.deletionTest: Size establishes the expertise requirement; morphology separates the endoscopic route from an invasion-driven surgical route. Sampling depth prevents a false benign-biopsy inference.
gate.counterfactual: If image-enhanced inspection instead showed a deeply depressed ulcerated focus with a deep invasive pattern, oncologic resection planning would become the best offered referral.
gate.sequence: Standalone; the later piecemeal-surveillance candidate is not assembled as a companion while awaiting review.

draftCases.name: Victor Ellis
draftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 67-year-old man, attends clinic with an outside polypectomy procedure log and pathology report.

nodes.title: Early surveillance after piecemeal EMR
nodes.objective: Select early scar assessment after large piecemeal adenoma resection.
nodes.update: The outside procedure log describes removal of a 28-mm ascending-colon adenoma with four overlapping snare captures. All retrieved portions were placed in one container. Pathology calls it one aggregate of tubular adenoma without invasive cancer and notes a free cut edge on one fragment. Endoscopic inspection found no visible remnant. The rest of the colon was completely examined with adequate preparation.
nodes.task: Under USMSTF guidance, when should {patientName}'s first surveillance colonoscopy be planned after this procedure?

choices.label: Colonoscopy in six months
choices.temptation: Use the actual removal method rather than the specimen-container label.
choices.rationale: Four overlapping captures establish piecemeal removal of an adenoma at least 20 mm. A free edge on one fragment cannot establish a single complete perimeter.
choices.reasonableWhen: A large adenoma was removed piecemeal and the first scar check is due.

choices.label: Colonoscopy in three years
choices.temptation: Treat one aggregate or a free fragment edge as proof of complete en-bloc removal.
choices.rationale: Routine advanced-adenoma timing does not replace the early scar check after large piecemeal removal.
choices.reasonableWhen: A size-defined advanced adenoma was completely removed en bloc.

choices.label: Colonoscopy in one year
choices.temptation: Apply a later large-piecemeal surveillance visit as the first visit.
choices.rationale: The one-year subsequent interval follows the initial six-month surveillance; this patient has not had that first check.
choices.reasonableWhen: The first surveillance after the large piecemeal resection has already been completed.

nodes.explanation: One container is not one resection. The procedure shows piecemeal removal, and the assessed edge of one fragment cannot establish the whole lesion's perimeter. The first large-piecemeal surveillance visit is about six months after resection.
