gate.cueAttack: Removed the supplied margin-management conclusion and the remote ten-year option. Procedure captures, container count and fragment-edge wording must now be reconciled; all three options are plausible surveillance intervals.
gate.stage: Three first-surveillance colonoscopy intervals after removal.
steps: Infer the actual piecemeal method from four overlapping captures despite the single aggregate and fragment-edge report.
Apply the early large-piecemeal scar interval instead of routine advanced-adenoma or subsequent-surveillance timing.
gate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: a reassuring pathology label or single-container heuristic points to a different interval. The author does not claim the timing rule itself is hard.
gate.decidingObservation: Four overlapping endoscopic captures, not the number of containers or the margin of one fragment.
gate.consequence: Delay in detecting residual adenoma at a large piecemeal resection site.
gate.deletionTest: The procedure and laboratory observations are both required to resolve the apparent completeness; size establishes the relevant piecemeal threshold. The rest-of-colon quality excludes a separate completion problem.
gate.counterfactual: If the 28-mm adenoma had instead been removed in one intact oriented specimen with all margins assessed clear, the offered three-year interval would become appropriate.
gate.sequence: Standalone; no earlier resection explanation identifies the method or surveillance pathway.

draftCases.name: Susan Mercer
draftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 55-year-old woman, attends clinic after removal of an ascending-colon lesion.

nodes.title: Complete favorable invasive-polyp excision
nodes.objective: Integrate specimen adequacy, depth and adverse-feature assessment before colectomy.
nodes.update: The nonpedunculated ascending-colon lesion was removed completely and retrieved in one oriented piece. Moderately differentiated glands extend 0.6 mm into submucosa; the invasive front is 2 mm from the deep cut edge. Both lateral mucosal edges were identified histologically and are free of adenoma and carcinoma. No lymphovascular or perineural invasion is found; budding is low. No lesion remained endoscopically.
nodes.task: Which lesion-directed plan should be discussed for {patientName}'s resected ascending-colon lesion?

choices.label: Colonoscopic surveillance of the excision site
choices.temptation: Use the complete specimen rather than the cancer label
choices.rationale: The intact assessment and favorable features support endoscopic treatment with surveillance.
choices.reasonableWhen: A fully assessed invasive polyp has favorable features and clear edges.

choices.label: Endoscopic full-thickness scar excision
choices.temptation: Treat all submucosal cancer as local residual
choices.rationale: No outstanding local margin question is established.
choices.reasonableWhen: A specialist-defined unresolved local-clearance problem.

choices.label: Oncologic ascending-colon resection
choices.temptation: Treat invasion as automatic colectomy
choices.rationale: No adverse feature puts this fully assessed lesion in the regional resection group.
choices.reasonableWhen: Adverse histology or an involved invasive margin.

nodes.explanation: Assess the whole intact specimen, including lateral and deep clearance, depth, grade, vascular/neural invasion and budding. These findings support a favorable fully excised submucosally invasive lesion for which endoscopic treatment with surveillance can be discussed; a visually clear scar alone would not establish that conclusion.

gate.cueAttack: Added explicit nonpedunculated morphology, complete excision and histologically assessed clear lateral margins. No visual-to-histologic margin substitution remains. Retained the concrete surveillance, local scar excision and regional resection alternatives.
steps: Integrate depth and adverse-feature observations with complete deep and lateral histologic clearance.
Choose surveillance rather than another local excision or regional oncologic resection in this fully assessed favorable specimen.
gate.difficulty: Fair moderate: the independent review found the intended favorable-risk reasoning reasonable once lateral clearance and morphology were supplied. No extra difficulty is manufactured.
gate.decidingObservation: An intact nonpedunculated specimen with clear assessed deep and lateral margins, superficial submucosal depth, low budding and no lymphovascular invasion.
gate.consequence: Unnecessary colectomy or reverse undertreatment of adverse disease.
gate.deletionTest: Every pathology feature establishes a relevant favorable-risk or completeness criterion. Visual clearance is corroborative and does not substitute for the added histologic lateral assessment.
gate.counterfactual: If lymphovascular invasion were identified while all margins remained clear, regional oncologic resection would become the best offered lesion-directed plan for a surgically suitable patient.
gate.sequence: Standalone. No preserved PASS malignant-polyp variant is edited or used as teaching feedback.

draftCases.name: Elaine Porter
draftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 66-year-old woman, attends clinic after partial cecal-polyp removal at an outside center.

nodes.title: Advanced resection before colectomy
nodes.objective: Choose expert endoscopic assessment for a large lesion without demonstrated deep invasion.
nodes.update: The original 26-mm lesion had a uniform granular surface. Cautery removed one part; carbon tattoo was injected beneath the remainder. On repeat inspection, residual tissue fails to lift at that site. Removed tissue contains adenoma. No ulcerated or depressed focus is described.
nodes.task: Which referral should guide {patientName}'s next treatment plan?

choices.label: Advanced-endoscopy referral for completion-resection planning
choices.temptation: Recognize a treatment-related confounder of the lift sign.
choices.rationale: Prior cautery and tattoo beneath the residual lesion can produce fibrosis. Expert completion planning is warranted; nonlifting alone does not prove deep invasion.
choices.reasonableWhen: A scarred residual lesion without documented deep invasive features requires advanced assessment.

choices.label: Colorectal-surgery referral for oncologic resection planning
choices.temptation: Treat the nonlifting sign as sufficient proof of invasive cancer.
choices.rationale: This lift test was performed after interventions that can scar the submucosa; the original granular morphology and lack of an invasive focus matter.
choices.reasonableWhen: Optical deep invasion or expert assessment establishes a lesion unsuitable for curative endoscopic treatment.

choices.label: Diagnostic-endoscopy referral for repeat biopsy planning
choices.temptation: Try to settle the lift finding with another small tissue sample.
choices.rationale: Another limited sample may miss invasion and does not solve the scarred completion-resection problem.
choices.reasonableWhen: Representative tissue confirmation is needed to direct an established nonendoscopic treatment pathway.

nodes.explanation: Interpret a lift test in its procedural history. Tattoo and cautery beneath a residual lesion can cause fibrosis, so this nonlift does not independently establish deep invasion. Advanced completion-resection planning addresses the actual problem without assuming either cancer or easy routine snare removal.

gate.cueAttack: Converted all three answers to parallel referral plans. Removed standard repeat snaring and the cautious assessment versus committed operation contrast. The temporal relation between injury, tattoo and nonlift remains raw evidence.
gate.stage: Three referral plans for the residual lesion before definitive treatment.
steps: Interpret nonlifting after cautery and sublesional tattoo as a confounded finding, not proof of deep invasion.
Use the residual lesion's complexity and available original morphology to choose expert completion-resection planning.
gate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: anchoring on a later nonlift despite its procedural cause competes with expert endoscopic referral.
gate.decidingObservation: The lift failure arose at a site already treated with cautery and tattoo beneath the lesion.
gate.consequence: Unnecessary regional resection or repeated superficial sampling rather than definitive expert planning.
gate.deletionTest: Original morphology and prior interventions determine how to interpret nonlift; residual tissue establishes a completion problem. The adenoma sample cannot exclude an unsampled invasive focus.
gate.counterfactual: If the untreated lesion had a depressed ulcerated invasive focus before any injection, biopsy or cautery, oncologic resection planning would become the best offered referral.
gate.sequence: Standalone; the large-polyp referral draft cannot supply this answer as prior feedback.

draftCases.name: Nathan Cole
draftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 35-year-old man with FAP and a prior ileorectal anastomosis, attends clinic to review outside rectal surveillance records.

nodes.title: Rectal removal for uncontrolled FAP burden
nodes.objective: Integrate rectal clearance, continence and restorative goals when choosing FAP operative extent.
nodes.update: Years after colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis for FAP, the retained rectum now contains a confluent adenoma field left after repeated endoscopic clearing attempts. Submitted fragments contain high-grade dysplasia; no invasive carcinoma is present in those fragments. Pelvic MRI shows no extrarectal extension or suspicious regional nodes. Continence is normal. After counseling about further surgery, he prioritizes maintaining intestinal continuity over a permanent end ileostomy.
nodes.task: Which next operative plan should be discussed for {patientName}'s retained rectum?

choices.label: Completion proctectomy with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis
choices.temptation: Update operative extent from current rather than prior burden
choices.rationale: The earlier rectal-sparing premise no longer holds; removing the uncontrolled rectum addresses the new disease while permitting restoration.
choices.reasonableWhen: A retained rectum develops disease no longer manageable endoscopically.

choices.label: Continue IRA with repeated endoscopic clearing
choices.temptation: Carry forward an earlier appropriate choice unchanged
choices.rationale: Repeated residual high-grade field disease defeats the original rectal-retention premise.
choices.reasonableWhen: A limited rectal burden remains endoscopically clearable.

choices.label: Completion proctectomy with end ileostomy
choices.temptation: Remove the rectum without using the preserved function
choices.rationale: This is an option, but the supplied function and restorative goal favor pouch planning.
choices.reasonableWhen: Poor continence or a preference to avoid pouch-related function.

nodes.explanation: Failure of endoscopic control requires reconsideration of the retained rectum. Fragment histology and MRI do not exclude microscopic invasion throughout the field. Completion proctectomy with IPAA can address the rectal burden while respecting preserved function and the stated continuity goal; final pathology still matters.

gate.cueAttack: Removed the claim that MRI shows no invasive cancer and the ambiguous desire for restoration in a patient who already has IRA. Separate fragment histology from extrarectal MRI observations; the preference now concerns future continuity versus end ileostomy.
gate.stage: Three plans for the retained rectum after IRA surveillance failure.
steps: Infer from persistent confluent dysplasia after repeated clearing that rectal preservation is no longer endoscopically controlled.
Combine the need for rectal removal with preserved continence and the stated future functional goal to choose restorative completion surgery.
gate.difficulty: Fair moderate: two clinical constraints determine extent and reconstruction. The revised case does not imply imaging excludes microscopic invasive disease.
gate.decidingObservation: The retained field persists after repeated clearing and contains high-grade dysplasia in submitted tissue.
gate.consequence: Continued uncontrolled rectal neoplasia or a reconstruction inconsistent with function and goals.
gate.deletionTest: Prior IRA identifies the retained organ; failed clearing and dysplasia establish its problem; continence and future continuity distinguish reconstruction. MRI is limited to its observed extrarectal scope.
gate.counterfactual: If the retained rectal adenomas were sparse, fully clearable and without high-grade dysplasia, continued IRA with endoscopic clearing and surveillance would become the best offered plan.
gate.sequence: New standalone post-IRA visit. The exact PASS prophylactic-IRA question and its original header remain unchanged in their own case.

draftCases.name: Felix Turner
draftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 68-year-old man, attends clinic after an outside diagnostic laparoscopy was stopped to arrange colorectal and urologic surgery.

nodes.title: Plan en-bloc resection while preserving uninvolved bladder
nodes.objective: Use the location and extent of an adherent colon cancer to plan en-bloc bladder resection without automatically sacrificing the whole bladder.
nodes.update: Biopsy confirms sigmoid adenocarcinoma and distant staging is negative. The outside exploration record describes a firm focal attachment to the bladder dome, with the neck, trigone and ureteric entries separate from the tumor. The remainder of the bladder wall is uninvolved and would retain a substantial reservoir after dome removal. No peritoneal deposits were found. The patient is being considered for curative surgery, and the attachment has not been divided.
nodes.task: Which operative plan best fits {patientName}'s recorded anatomy, subject to confirmation of clear margins at surgery?

choices.label: Sigmoid colectomy with en-bloc partial cystectomy
choices.temptation: Match the organ extent to the involved dome while preserving the tumor interface.
choices.rationale: A focal dome attachment can be removed en bloc with a bladder portion while retaining uninvolved neck, trigone and reservoir; the plan still requires an achievable clear margin.
choices.reasonableWhen: The attached bladder portion can be removed with negative margins and useful remaining bladder.

choices.label: Sigmoid colectomy with en-bloc total cystectomy
choices.temptation: Equate any bladder adherence with a need to remove the whole bladder.
choices.rationale: The represented attachment is focal at the dome; the record does not show neck/trigone involvement or loss of a usable remaining bladder requiring total removal.
choices.reasonableWhen: Extent or location prevents clear-margin partial resection with a usable bladder.

choices.label: Sigmoid colectomy with separation of the bladder attachment
choices.temptation: Assume focal attachment can be peeled away to preserve bladder.
choices.rationale: An adherent cancer interface should not be divided to decide whether the adhesion is malignant; partial bladder resection preserves an en-bloc specimen.
choices.reasonableWhen: No true tumor-organ attachment exists and an uninvolved plane is established without dividing an adherent cancer interface.

nodes.explanation: First preserve the adherent tumor-organ interface. Then use the involved anatomy to choose the planned bladder extent: a focal dome attachment with separate neck/trigone and a usable remnant supports en-bloc partial cystectomy, provided a clear margin is achievable. Adherence does not itself establish histologic invasion, and total cystectomy is not automatic.

gate.cueAttack: Replaced two attachment-division near-duplicates with three distinct operative extents. The task is a conditional surgical plan, not a guarantee of final margin status. No endoscopic mucosal-negative claim is used to exclude outer-wall involvement.
gate.stage: Three combined colorectal/bladder operative plans at the same planning stage.
steps: Infer that the firm cancer-bladder interface must remain en bloc regardless of whether pathology later shows invasion.
Use dome-limited attachment, separate neck/trigone and a usable remnant to distinguish partial from total cystectomy planning.
gate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: either preserving all bladder by interface division or overextending en-bloc surgery to total cystectomy is a credible resident error.
gate.decidingObservation: The attachment is confined to the dome, with uninvolved neck/trigone and substantial uninvolved bladder remaining.
gate.consequence: Tumor-plane violation or unnecessary loss of the bladder.
gate.deletionTest: Attachment establishes the en-bloc requirement; its location and remaining reservoir determine partial versus total extent. Curative intent and negative distant staging define the operative goal.
gate.counterfactual: If the attachment instead involved the bladder neck and trigone such that no clear-margin partial resection could retain a usable bladder, the offered en-bloc total cystectomy plan would become appropriate.
gate.sequence: Standalone. The meaning now includes bladder extent, so the prior concept version is retained without FSRS migration.

draftCases.name: Thomas Hale
draftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 66-year-old man, attends clinic after outside resections of synchronous right-colon and sigmoid cancers.

nodes.title: Reassess a low node yield
nodes.objective: Distinguish negative sampled nodes from an adequate pathologic regional assessment.
nodes.update: Two synchronous colon cancers were removed in separately labeled right-colon and sigmoid specimens. The right-colon report lists 17 negative regional nodes. The sigmoid report lists five negative regional nodes; that tumor extends through muscularis propria into pericolic fat with clear margins. No metastases were found on preoperative staging. Both submitted mesenteric specimens remain available to pathology.
nodes.task: Which pathology plan should next improve {patientName}'s regional-stage assessment for these two resections?

choices.label: Request an additional node search in the sigmoid specimen
choices.temptation: Keep each primary linked to its own submitted regional specimen.
choices.rationale: The sigmoid basin has only five assessed nodes. The 17 nodes assigned to the other primary do not repair that specimen-specific deficit.
choices.reasonableWhen: Fewer than 12 nodes are reported in the specimen for the cancer being staged.

choices.label: Request an additional node search in the right-colon specimen
choices.temptation: Focus on the larger node-bearing specimen while overlooking which basin is undersampled.
choices.rationale: The right-colon specimen already has 17 reported nodes; the identified low count belongs to the sigmoid specimen.
choices.reasonableWhen: The right-colon specimen rather than the sigmoid specimen has fewer than 12 assessed nodes.

choices.label: Accept the combined 22-node assessment for both primaries
choices.temptation: Pool all negative nodes from the operation.
choices.rationale: Separate primary tumors require their own regional specimen provenance; a pooled total does not establish adequate assessment for the five-node sigmoid basin.
choices.reasonableWhen: Each primary has an adequate separately assigned regional-node assessment and no additional pathology deficit is identified.

nodes.explanation: Assign nodes to the primary and specimen from which they came before assessing the count. Seventeen right-colon nodes cannot be transferred to the sigmoid basin. Additional pathology evaluation should target the sigmoid specimen with five assessed nodes; this does not itself prove nodal metastasis or require repeat colectomy.

gate.cueAttack: Replaced PET and anatomically awkward mesenteric MRI with three pathology-disposition plans. A pooled adequate-looking count now competes with a genuinely inadequate specimen-specific count; retained tissue is background feasibility for either targeted search rather than a uniquely named key action.
gate.stage: Three pathology plans for regional staging after completed resection.
steps: Separate nodes by the two labeled primaries rather than pool the operation's total.
Identify the five-node sigmoid specimen as needing additional pathology retrieval before relying on its node-negative assessment.
gate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: counting 22 negative nodes across two specimens obscures the undersampled cancer's own basin.
gate.decidingObservation: The five sigmoid nodes and 17 right-colon nodes were assigned to separate primary-specific specimens.
gate.consequence: Overconfidence in an inadequately assessed sigmoid regional stage.
gate.deletionTest: Two primaries and specimen labels create the provenance problem; both node counts distinguish the proper search from the competing plans. Submitted-tissue availability makes either pathology request possible.
gate.counterfactual: If the counts were reversed, with five right-colon nodes and 17 sigmoid nodes, the offered additional search in the right-colon specimen would become best.
gate.sequence: Standalone with a distinct patient; the exact PASS tumor-deposit question retains its original patient and wording.

draftCases.name: Martin Shaw
draftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 70-year-old man, attends clinic while the founder reviews outside multidisciplinary records for sigmoid adenocarcinoma with metastases.

nodes.title: Initial treatment of an asymptomatic metastatic primary
nodes.objective: Distinguish symptom control from prophylactic primary resection when distant disease is not curatively resectable.
nodes.update: The outside multidisciplinary team records diffuse bilobar liver and pulmonary metastases not amenable to curative local treatment. At colonoscopy an adult instrument could not pass the sigmoid tumor, but a pediatric instrument passed it. He reports daily formed stools without pain, vomiting, bleeding or transfusion need. CT shows no upstream colonic dilation.
nodes.task: Which initial treatment sequence best fits {patientName}'s current metastatic-primary record?

choices.label: Systemic treatment planning with the primary left in place
choices.temptation: Distinguish a narrow endoscopic lumen from a clinically obstructing primary.
choices.rationale: The record lacks clinical or radiographic obstruction and other primary-related complications. For incurable metastatic disease in this setting, systemic treatment generally precedes prophylactic primary surgery.
choices.reasonableWhen: Metastatic disease is incurable and the primary is not causing obstruction, significant bleeding or perforation.

choices.label: Sigmoid colectomy followed by systemic treatment planning
choices.temptation: Treat failure of the adult scope to pass as a surgical obstruction indication.
choices.rationale: The smaller scope passed, bowel function continues and CT shows no upstream dilation; prophylactic colectomy would delay treatment of the dominant metastatic disease.
choices.reasonableWhen: Primary-related perforation or another surgically managed complication requires resection before systemic treatment.

choices.label: Diverting colostomy followed by systemic treatment planning
choices.temptation: Decompress preemptively because the adult scope did not pass.
choices.rationale: No symptomatic or radiographic obstruction requiring diversion is established.
choices.reasonableWhen: A clinically obstructing unresectable primary requires decompression and diversion is the selected feasible route.

nodes.explanation: The adult scope's nonpassage does not alone establish bowel obstruction. Ongoing bowel function, absent obstructive symptoms and no upstream dilation define the present primary-related burden. With incurable metastases and no primary complication, initial systemic treatment planning is generally preferred to prophylactic colectomy or diversion.

gate.cueAttack: Removed the fitness endorsement and patent-lumen interpretation. Replaced stenting with a parallel diversion-first sequence. Endoscope caliber now creates a credible concern that must be interpreted against bowel function and CT.
gate.stage: Three initial treatment sequences for incurable metastatic colon cancer.
steps: Determine whether the instrument-level narrowing represents a clinical obstruction in the current record.
Choose the systemic-first sequence for the uncomplicated primary rather than a prophylactic resection or diversion-first sequence.
gate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: instrument nonpassage can be mistaken for a mandatory local intervention despite contrary functional and radiographic observations.
gate.decidingObservation: A pediatric instrument passed, stools continue, and CT shows no proximal dilation or other primary complication.
gate.consequence: Unnecessary local intervention and delayed metastatic treatment, or failure to respond if a true complication develops.
gate.deletionTest: Metastatic resectability establishes treatment intent; scope caliber creates the competing concern; symptoms and dilation establish whether that concern is currently a complication. No affirmative treatment-fitness sentence supplies the answer.
gate.counterfactual: If the primary perforated with generalized contamination, a local resection-first sequence would supersede systemic-first planning among these choices.
gate.sequence: Standalone; the revised reconstruction question uses a distinct retrospective admission case and does not inherit this explanation.

draftCases.name: Martin Shaw
draftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 70-year-old man, attends clinic after an outside admission; the founder reviews the recorded operation for his metastatic sigmoid cancer.

nodes.title: Choose reconstruction after emergency sigmoid resection
nodes.objective: Use the intraoperative physiology and contamination to choose a concrete reconstruction strategy after resection of a perforated sigmoid cancer.
nodes.update: The founder reviews the operative decision recorded during his outside admission for a perforated sigmoid primary with unresectable liver and lung metastases. Before admission he requested treatment of reversible acute complications. At the recorded decision point, the perforated sigmoid segment had been resected and the remaining bowel ends were viable. Diffuse fecal contamination had been encountered. Despite fluids, antibiotics and resection, norepinephrine was still required and the bowel was edematous. The operative team judged fascial closure feasible without a planned open abdomen.
nodes.task: At that outside intraoperative decision point, which reconstruction plan best fits {patientName}'s recorded findings?

choices.label: Close the rectal stump and create an end colostomy
choices.temptation: Interpret continuing circulatory support and contamination when deciding whether to create an anastomosis.
choices.rationale: Ongoing vasopressor need with fecal contamination and edematous bowel favors avoiding a new colorectal anastomosis. A concrete Hartmann reconstruction is supported here; no universal rule for every perforation is asserted.
choices.reasonableWhen: After left-sided perforation resection, current physiology and local conditions make primary anastomosis inappropriate and the abdomen can be closed.

choices.label: Create a colorectal anastomosis and a diverting loop ileostomy
choices.temptation: Assume proximal diversion makes a high-risk anastomosis acceptable regardless of current physiology.
choices.rationale: Diversion does not remove an anastomosis or its failure risk. The continuing vasopressor need and adverse local conditions favor not constructing it at this recorded point.
choices.reasonableWhen: Resuscitation has restored stable physiology and local bowel conditions support a primary anastomosis, with diversion selected for the residual risk.

choices.label: Create a colorectal anastomosis without proximal diversion
choices.temptation: Transfer preadmission fitness into a septic operative decision.
choices.rationale: The relevant observations are the current vasopressor need, contamination and edema, not earlier cancer-treatment eligibility.
choices.reasonableWhen: Physiology, perfusion, contamination and anastomotic conditions are favorable enough for primary anastomosis without diversion.

nodes.explanation: Review the physiology at the actual reconstruction point. Persistent vasopressor need plus fecal contamination and bowel edema favor avoiding a colorectal anastomosis; closing the stump and forming an end colostomy is a concrete plan. Diversion cannot erase the risk of an anastomosis already constructed. This scoped decision does not prescribe Hartmann reconstruction for every perforated cancer.

gate.cueAttack: Rebuilt the failed item at one past intraoperative moment after resection. All answers are specific reconstruction operations; no stent, delayed source control, vague staged plan or supplied definitive-source-control cue remains.
gate.stage: Three concrete reconstruction plans after the same completed sigmoid resection.
steps: Interpret ongoing norepinephrine need after resuscitation together with fecal contamination and bowel edema as adverse conditions for a new anastomosis.
Choose stump closure and end colostomy rather than assume that proximal diversion or earlier cancer-treatment fitness makes an anastomosis suitable.
gate.difficulty: Fair moderate: protected anastomosis is the nearest real competitor. No invented pressor-dose, lactate or timeline threshold is used, and prior systemic-treatment fitness supplies no inference.
gate.decidingObservation: At the reconstruction point vasopressor support remained necessary and bowel edema with diffuse fecal contamination was documented.
gate.consequence: Anastomotic failure risk from constructing an anastomosis under unfavorable current conditions.
gate.deletionTest: Metastatic context and the stated goals establish why the acute complication was treated; viable ends establish that reconstruction is the decision. Current physiology and local findings distinguish the operations, while feasible closure excludes an unstated open-abdomen stoma-delay question.
gate.counterfactual: If resuscitation instead restored stable physiology without vasopressors and the viable bowel was well perfused without edema or diffuse contamination, a colorectal anastomosis with selected protective diversion would become a reasonable offered reconstruction rather than a mandatory end colostomy. That counterfactual permits the alternative; it does not claim diversion is universally required.
gate.sequence: Standalone retrospective clinic chart review. No uncomplicated-primary question or its feedback precedes the reconstruction decision.

draftCases.name: George Sutton
draftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 68-year-old man, attends clinic with records from two outside colonoscopies.

nodes.title: Integrate baseline and first surveillance
nodes.objective: Choose USMSTF second-surveillance timing from both the baseline adenoma and the first follow-up.
nodes.update: At baseline, a 14-mm tubular adenoma was completely removed in one piece during a high-quality examination. The first surveillance colonoscopy, performed three years later, was also complete and adequately prepared and found no adenoma or serrated lesion. He has no prior cancer, hereditary syndrome or relevant family history.
nodes.task: Under USMSTF guidance, when should {patientName}'s next colonoscopy be planned after this normal first surveillance examination?

choices.label: Colonoscopy in five years
choices.temptation: Combine the baseline and first-surveillance findings
choices.rationale: A normal first surveillance examination after an advanced baseline adenoma supports a five-year next interval.
choices.reasonableWhen: Advanced adenoma at baseline followed by a normal high-quality first surveillance.

choices.label: Colonoscopy in three years
choices.temptation: Repeat the baseline advanced-adenoma interval unchanged
choices.rationale: The normal first surveillance modifies the next interval.
choices.reasonableWhen: Advanced adenoma or another corresponding higher-risk finding persists at first surveillance.

choices.label: Colonoscopy in ten years
choices.temptation: Erase baseline risk after one normal follow-up
choices.rationale: The advanced baseline finding continues to matter when selecting the next interval.
choices.reasonableWhen: A low-risk baseline followed by normal first surveillance can support a longer interval.

nodes.explanation: Second-surveillance planning uses two examinations. A normal first follow-up modifies, but does not erase, the advanced baseline adenoma history.

gate.cueAttack: Added the missing three-year baseline-to-first-surveillance interval. Retained the reviewed two-examination decision and three parallel timing choices without introducing extraneous chronology.
steps: Classify the size-defined baseline adenoma and verify that the normal first surveillance occurred at its appropriate interval.
Apply the serial-surveillance recommendation rather than reuse either the baseline-only or latest-examination-only interval.
gate.difficulty: Fair moderate, consistent with independent review: interpreting both examinations is consequential; the newly stated first interval removes ambiguity rather than manufacturing difficulty.
gate.decidingObservation: A completely removed 14-mm baseline adenoma followed three years later by a normal high-quality first surveillance examination.
gate.consequence: Over- or under-surveillance from ignoring one examination.
gate.deletionTest: Each examination determines a different part of the serial-surveillance recommendation, and the added interval establishes that this is the appropriate first surveillance rather than an arbitrary early examination.
gate.counterfactual: Replace the first surveillance result with a new advanced adenoma: three years becomes the appropriate offered interval.
gate.sequence: Standalone; exact PASS count/provenance surveillance item remains untouched.

caseDraft.name: Andrew Holt
caseDraft.presentation: {patientName}, a 63-year-old man, attends clinic while the founder reviews an outside endoscopist's proposed sigmoid-polyp removal.

nodes.title: Stalk protection before polyp removal
nodes.objective: Assess head and stalk independently when planning preventive hemostasis.
nodes.update: An 18-mm head hangs from a distinct mobile stalk 12 mm thick. The adjacent wall is separate from the stalk. Removal has not occurred.
nodes.task: Which resection sequence best fits {patientName}'s documented polyp?

choices.label: Stalk ligation followed by hot-snare transection
choices.temptation: Assess stalk independently of head size
choices.rationale: Protection precedes transection for this thick stalk; hot snare fits the pedunculated lesion.
choices.reasonableWhen: Large head or thick stalk meets preventive criteria.

choices.label: Hot-snare transection followed by rescue clipping
choices.temptation: Use rescue instead of prevention
choices.rationale: Waiting for bleeding omits preventive stalk treatment.
choices.reasonableWhen: A narrower-stalk lesion below preventive criteria.

choices.label: Cold-snare transection followed by specimen retrieval
choices.temptation: Generalize small-flat-polyp removal
choices.rationale: The substantial true stalk changes method and sequence.
choices.reasonableWhen: A small nonpedunculated lesion without invasive features.

nodes.explanation: The smaller head does not negate the thick stalk. Plan mechanical stalk protection before hot-snare transection; clips and loops are alternatives.

gate.cueAttack: No availability or medication permission. Head is below one trigger but stalk exceeds an independently sourced trigger; all procedure estimates have equal scope.
steps: Recognize true pedunculation and assess the stalk separately.
Choose prevention before transection rather than rescue or a flat-polyp technique.
gate.difficulty: Moderate/hard prediction: head-size anchoring competes with stalk risk.
gate.decidingObservation: 12-mm stalk despite an 18-mm head.
gate.consequence: Preventable postpolypectomy bleeding.
gate.deletionTest: Head creates the near-miss; stalk changes sequence; separate wall establishes pedunculation.
gate.counterfactual: Change stalk to 3 mm with the same head: hot snare with rescue available becomes reasonable.
gate.sequence: Standalone clinic adaptation; retained n4r2 definition is untouched.

authorWithdrawnAttempts.reason: The earlier n4 review2 explicitly rejected supplied head/stalk measurements followed by the prophylaxis rule as easy one-step recall. The attempted clinic adaptation repeated that defect. No new keyed version is offered; clinical correctness is distinct from author-gate difficulty.
authorWithdrawnAttempts.nextAction: Manager decides whether to seek an explicit basic-purpose exception or commission a permitted-source technical comparison that actually changes the sequence.

questions.stem: Which postexcision plan fits {patientName}'s sigmoid-polyp specimen?
questions.explanation: Shallow stalk invasion and an involved stalk cut edge are different observations. The intact clear specimen and remaining favorable findings support local follow-up.

answerChoices.label: Colonoscopic surveillance after polypectomy
answerChoices.rationale: The intact shallow favorable specimen supports surveillance.

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic full-thickness scar resection
answerChoices.rationale: The represented cut edge is clear; invasion has not reached transection.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The represented cut edge is clear; invasion has not reached transection.

answerChoices.label: Oncologic sigmoid colectomy
answerChoices.rationale: The represented depth and remaining features do not establish adverse-polyp risk.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The represented depth and remaining features do not establish adverse-polyp risk.

questions.stem: Which treatment plan should be discussed for {patientName}'s sigmoid lesion?
questions.explanation: Vascular involvement and cut-edge clearance answer different questions. Discuss resection of the involved segment and its draining lymphatic territory.

answerChoices.label: Sigmoid colectomy with regional lymphadenectomy
answerChoices.rationale: The vascular-channel finding supports regional resection despite a clear edge and normal-sized nodes.

answerChoices.label: Full-thickness endoscopic scar excision
answerChoices.rationale: Local excision does not address the regional risk raised by vascular invasion.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Local excision does not address the regional risk raised by vascular invasion.

answerChoices.label: Colonoscopic scar surveillance
answerChoices.rationale: A healed surface cannot erase the adverse feature.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A healed surface cannot erase the adverse feature.

questions.stem: Which treatment plan best addresses {patientName}'s descending-colon pathology?
questions.explanation: The actual cut-edge involvement matters more than the clear-looking scar. Sampled negatives do not turn an incomplete invasive specimen into a fully assessed favorable one.

answerChoices.label: Oncologic descending-colon resection
answerChoices.rationale: The transected invasive edge and unknown depth do not meet favorable-polyp criteria.

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic full-thickness scar resection
answerChoices.rationale: Local treatment may not settle the regional question from inadequately assessed invasive cancer.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Local treatment may not settle the regional question from inadequately assessed invasive cancer.

answerChoices.label: Colonoscopic scar surveillance
answerChoices.rationale: A sampled negative does not repair a transected invasive front.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A sampled negative does not repair a transected invasive front.

questions.stem: Which lesion-directed plan fits {patientName}'s represented pathology?
questions.explanation: Interpret depth and adequacy before acting on terminology. An intact specimen showing mucosal confinement and clear edges supports local treatment with surveillance.

answerChoices.label: Colonoscopic surveillance after local excision
answerChoices.rationale: The adequately represented mucosal lesion has been excised; submucosal T1 invasion is not shown.

answerChoices.label: Full-thickness endoscopic scar resection
answerChoices.rationale: The intact specimen already represents the relevant boundary and clear margins.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The intact specimen already represents the relevant boundary and clear margins.

answerChoices.label: Sigmoid colectomy with regional lymphadenectomy
answerChoices.rationale: The represented submucosa contains no invasive glands.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The represented submucosa contains no invasive glands.

questions.stem: Which operative plan should be discussed for {patientName}'s colorectal disease?
questions.explanation: Repeated failure to clear the rectal field changes the operation from colon removal to colorectal removal. Continence and the informed functional goal then guide reconstruction.

answerChoices.label: Proctocolectomy with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis
answerChoices.rationale: Removing the uncontrolled rectum addresses the disease; preserved continence and informed restorative goals support IPAA.

answerChoices.label: Colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis
answerChoices.rationale: IRA retains the repeatedly uncleared rectal adenoma field.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: IRA retains the repeatedly uncleared rectal adenoma field.

answerChoices.label: Proctocolectomy with end ileostomy
answerChoices.rationale: It removes the field but is less aligned with her stated restorative goal and preserved continence.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: It removes the field but is less aligned with her stated restorative goal and preserved continence.

questions.stem: Which operative plan best fits {patientName}'s disease distribution and stated priorities?
questions.explanation: The operation depends on distribution, not a single FAP label. Relative rectal sparing permits IRA when the patient accepts ongoing rectal risk assessment and surveillance.

answerChoices.label: Total colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis
answerChoices.rationale: The documented clearable rectum permits an IRA option, with ongoing surveillance.

answerChoices.label: Proctocolectomy with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis
answerChoices.rationale: IPAA is a valid broader option, but the supplied relative sparing and functional priority favor IRA here.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: IPAA is a valid broader option, but the supplied relative sparing and functional priority favor IRA here.

answerChoices.label: Proctocolectomy with end ileostomy
answerChoices.rationale: No sphincter problem or preference favors an end stoma in this case.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: No sphincter problem or preference favors an end stoma in this case.

questions.stem: Which operative plan best fits {patientName}'s disease and functional record?
questions.explanation: Disease distribution determines what must be removed; sphincter function and informed goals determine whether restoration is appropriate.

answerChoices.label: Proctocolectomy with end ileostomy
answerChoices.rationale: The rectum needs removal and a pouch would depend on an already poorly functioning outlet; her informed goal supports an end stoma.

answerChoices.label: Proctocolectomy with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis
answerChoices.rationale: It removes the field but uses the impaired sphincter and conflicts with her functional priority.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: It removes the field but uses the impaired sphincter and conflicts with her functional priority.

answerChoices.label: Colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis
answerChoices.rationale: IRA leaves the uncleared rectal dysplastic field and does not resolve the outlet dysfunction.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: IRA leaves the uncleared rectal dysplastic field and does not resolve the outlet dysfunction.

questions.stem: Which treatment sequence should be discussed for {patientName}'s rectal cancer?
questions.explanation: Interpret the extramural, nodal and fascia findings before selecting the sequence. Total neoadjuvant treatment is a supported pathway for this fit patient before definitive resection planning.

answerChoices.label: Total neoadjuvant therapy followed by reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: The locally advanced mid-rectal findings support a neoadjuvant multimodal pathway before definitive surgical planning.

answerChoices.label: Total mesorectal excision followed by adjuvant therapy
answerChoices.rationale: This sequence bypasses the neoadjuvant opportunity in the supplied high-risk local setting.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This sequence bypasses the neoadjuvant opportunity in the supplied high-risk local setting.

answerChoices.label: Transanal excision followed by adjuvant therapy
answerChoices.rationale: Local excision does not address the represented extramural and nodal disease.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Local excision does not address the represented extramural and nodal disease.

questions.stem: Which next treatment plan should be discussed for {patientName}'s rectal cancer?
questions.explanation: The new pathology changes the relevant treatment scope. Clear local margins do not make a muscle-invasive rectal cancer adequately treated by local excision in a fit patient.

answerChoices.label: Completion rectal resection with total mesorectal excision
answerChoices.rationale: Muscularis-propria invasion places the lesion beyond the favorable T1 local-excision group; clear wall edges do not stage mesorectal nodes.

answerChoices.label: Repeat full-thickness transanal scar excision
answerChoices.rationale: The local edges are already clear; another scar specimen does not remove the regional nodal basin.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The local edges are already clear; another scar specimen does not remove the regional nodal basin.

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic rectal scar surveillance
answerChoices.rationale: Local clearance and imaging cannot settle microscopic mesorectal disease.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Local clearance and imaging cannot settle microscopic mesorectal disease.

questions.stem: Which treatment plan best fits {patientName}'s current rectal findings?
questions.explanation: The biopsy describes the surface specimen. Progressive concordant mural findings defeat a complete-response conclusion despite that negative sample and her organ-preservation goal.

answerChoices.label: Oncologic rectal resection with total mesorectal excision
answerChoices.rationale: Progressive concordant mural abnormalities are not a complete response; regional oncologic resection assessment is supported.

answerChoices.label: Full-thickness transanal excision of the treated site
answerChoices.rationale: The prior regional disease and persistent mural findings do not establish a favorable local-only treatment group.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The prior regional disease and persistent mural findings do not establish a favorable local-only treatment group.

answerChoices.label: Protocolized watch-and-wait surveillance
answerChoices.rationale: Interest in organ preservation does not convert progressive palpable/MRI disease into a complete clinical response.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Interest in organ preservation does not convert progressive palpable/MRI disease into a complete clinical response.

questions.stem: Which treatment plan should now be discussed for {patientName}'s rectal lesion?
questions.explanation: A prior complete response is historical evidence, not permanent clearance. Proven localized regrowth changes the treatment objective to salvage.

answerChoices.label: Salvage rectal resection with total mesorectal excision
answerChoices.rationale: Localized operable regrowth with deep-wall involvement warrants oncologic salvage assessment.

answerChoices.label: Transanal full-thickness nodule excision
answerChoices.rationale: The MRI demonstrates depth beyond a favorable early local-excision group.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The MRI demonstrates depth beyond a favorable early local-excision group.

answerChoices.label: Continue protocolized watch-and-wait surveillance
answerChoices.rationale: Biopsy-proven regrowth is not continued clinical complete response.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Biopsy-proven regrowth is not continued clinical complete response.

questions.stem: Which postoperative plan should be discussed for {patientName}'s updated pathology?
questions.explanation: A confirmed tumor deposit is not canceled by an adequate set of negative nodes. Interpret it as regional disease before discussing adjuvant systemic treatment; regimen details remain individualized.

answerChoices.label: Adjuvant FOLFOX planning with medical oncology
answerChoices.rationale: A confirmed pericolic deposit can establish regional N1c disease despite negative nodes, supporting adjuvant systemic treatment assessment.

answerChoices.label: Surveillance after node-negative colectomy
answerChoices.rationale: The adequate negative-node count does not erase deposit-defined regional involvement.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The adequate negative-node count does not erase deposit-defined regional involvement.

answerChoices.label: Adjuvant pelvic chemoradiation planning
answerChoices.rationale: This is a sigmoid-colon regional pathology problem, not an indication for routine pelvic radiation.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This is a sigmoid-colon regional pathology problem, not an indication for routine pelvic radiation.

questions.stem: Under USMSTF guidance, when should {patientName}'s surveillance colonoscopy be planned?
questions.explanation: Use lesion-level procedural provenance rather than fragment count. The two small nonadvanced adenomas support the USMSTF seven-to-ten-year interval.

answerChoices.label: Colonoscopy in seven to ten years
answerChoices.rationale: Two small completely removed nonadvanced adenomas remain two lesions despite four laboratory fragments.

answerChoices.label: Colonoscopy in three to five years
answerChoices.rationale: The procedure documented two lesions; four fragments do not establish four adenomas.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The procedure documented two lesions; four fragments do not establish four adenomas.

answerChoices.label: Colonoscopy in three years
answerChoices.rationale: Neither five-to-ten actual adenomas nor an advanced feature is established.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Neither five-to-ten actual adenomas nor an advanced feature is established.

questions.stem: Which next colorectal investigation should be arranged for {patientName} after these outside results?
questions.explanation: Read the withdrawal observations before accepting the negative summary. Cecal reach did not establish adequate proximal inspection, so the positive FIT remains incompletely evaluated. Repeat prepared colonoscopy addresses that deficit; repeating FIT does not.

answerChoices.label: Repeat colonoscopy with a revised preparation plan
answerChoices.rationale: The proximal mucosa was not adequately evaluated. The positive FIT still needs a complete diagnostic colonoscopy despite the repeat FIT and negative summary.

answerChoices.label: CT colonography with a colonic preparation plan
answerChoices.rationale: The record describes a preparation problem, not an anatomic barrier or contraindication to repeating colonoscopy; colonoscopy can also sample or remove a lesion.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The record describes a preparation problem, not an anatomic barrier or contraindication to repeating colonoscopy; colonoscopy can also sample or remove a lesion.

answerChoices.label: Repeat fecal immunochemical screening next year
answerChoices.rationale: Neither the repeat stool test nor the poorly visualized proximal colon establishes completed positive-FIT evaluation.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Neither the repeat stool test nor the poorly visualized proximal colon establishes completed positive-FIT evaluation.

questions.stem: Under USMSTF guidance, which next colonoscopy plan fits {patientName}'s completed examination?
questions.explanation: Insertion quality and final withdrawal quality are different observations. After cleansing, every segment was visible and normal. That final examination supports standard screening timing; an initially dirty view does not independently create an early-repeat indication.

answerChoices.label: Repeat colonoscopy in ten years
answerChoices.rationale: Preparation is judged after cleansing. A complete normal examination with adequate final visualization supports the usual ten-year interval in this scoped screening setting.

answerChoices.label: Repeat colonoscopy within one year
answerChoices.rationale: The final withdrawal record establishes that cleaning resolved the obscuration; an inadequacy-driven early repeat is not supported.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The final withdrawal record establishes that cleaning resolved the obscuration; an inadequacy-driven early repeat is not supported.

answerChoices.label: Repeat colonoscopy in three years
answerChoices.rationale: An intermediate interval does not replace classification of the final examination, and no advanced adenoma was found.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: An intermediate interval does not replace classification of the final examination, and no advanced adenoma was found.

questions.stem: Under USMSTF guidance, when should {patientName}'s first surveillance colonoscopy be planned after this resection?
questions.explanation: Separate endoscopic resection from laboratory processing. Four grossing pieces from a specimen received intact do not establish piecemeal removal. The completely excised 24-mm adenoma therefore follows the three-year advanced-adenoma pathway.

answerChoices.label: Colonoscopy in three years
answerChoices.rationale: The lesion was removed intact in one resection; later laboratory division does not make that procedure piecemeal. Size establishes an advanced adenoma with confident complete removal.

answerChoices.label: Colonoscopy in six months
answerChoices.rationale: The early piecemeal scar interval applies to the endoscopic removal method, not subsequent grossing of an intact specimen.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The early piecemeal scar interval applies to the endoscopic removal method, not subsequent grossing of an intact specimen.

answerChoices.label: Colonoscopy in one year
answerChoices.rationale: This is the first follow-up after complete en-bloc removal, not the later visit after an initial piecemeal scar check.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This is the first follow-up after complete en-bloc removal, not the later visit after an initial piecemeal scar check.

questions.stem: Which referral should guide {patientName}'s next lesion-removal plan?
questions.explanation: Interpret the optical morphology separately from the limited superficial sample. The absent submucosa prevents the biopsy from excluding invasion, but size alone does not establish an indication for colectomy. Advanced endoscopic resection planning is the appropriate referral at this stage.

answerChoices.label: Advanced-endoscopy referral for endoscopic resection planning
answerChoices.rationale: Large nonpedunculated lesions without deep invasive features merit advanced-resection expertise; the superficial biopsy does not itself prove the whole lesion benign.

answerChoices.label: Colorectal-surgery referral for oncologic resection planning
answerChoices.rationale: Neither size alone nor an unrepresented layer establishes deep invasion that rules out endoscopic treatment.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Neither size alone nor an unrepresented layer establishes deep invasion that rules out endoscopic treatment.

answerChoices.label: Diagnostic-endoscopy referral for repeat biopsy planning
answerChoices.rationale: Repeating a small sample may still miss the relevant invasive focus and does not address the expertise required for definitive removal.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Repeating a small sample may still miss the relevant invasive focus and does not address the expertise required for definitive removal.

questions.stem: Under USMSTF guidance, when should {patientName}'s first surveillance colonoscopy be planned after this procedure?
questions.explanation: One container is not one resection. The procedure shows piecemeal removal, and the assessed edge of one fragment cannot establish the whole lesion's perimeter. The first large-piecemeal surveillance visit is about six months after resection.

answerChoices.label: Colonoscopy in six months
answerChoices.rationale: Four overlapping captures establish piecemeal removal of an adenoma at least 20 mm. A free edge on one fragment cannot establish a single complete perimeter.

answerChoices.label: Colonoscopy in three years
answerChoices.rationale: Routine advanced-adenoma timing does not replace the early scar check after large piecemeal removal.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Routine advanced-adenoma timing does not replace the early scar check after large piecemeal removal.

answerChoices.label: Colonoscopy in one year
answerChoices.rationale: The one-year subsequent interval follows the initial six-month surveillance; this patient has not had that first check.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The one-year subsequent interval follows the initial six-month surveillance; this patient has not had that first check.

questions.stem: Which lesion-directed plan should be discussed for {patientName}'s resected ascending-colon lesion?
questions.explanation: Assess the whole intact specimen, including lateral and deep clearance, depth, grade, vascular/neural invasion and budding. These findings support a favorable fully excised submucosally invasive lesion for which endoscopic treatment with surveillance can be discussed; a visually clear scar alone would not establish that conclusion.

answerChoices.label: Colonoscopic surveillance of the excision site
answerChoices.rationale: The intact assessment and favorable features support endoscopic treatment with surveillance.

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic full-thickness scar excision
answerChoices.rationale: No outstanding local margin question is established.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: No outstanding local margin question is established.

answerChoices.label: Oncologic ascending-colon resection
answerChoices.rationale: No adverse feature puts this fully assessed lesion in the regional resection group.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: No adverse feature puts this fully assessed lesion in the regional resection group.

questions.stem: Which referral should guide {patientName}'s next treatment plan?
questions.explanation: Interpret a lift test in its procedural history. Tattoo and cautery beneath a residual lesion can cause fibrosis, so this nonlift does not independently establish deep invasion. Advanced completion-resection planning addresses the actual problem without assuming either cancer or easy routine snare removal.

answerChoices.label: Advanced-endoscopy referral for completion-resection planning
answerChoices.rationale: Prior cautery and tattoo beneath the residual lesion can produce fibrosis. Expert completion planning is warranted; nonlifting alone does not prove deep invasion.

answerChoices.label: Colorectal-surgery referral for oncologic resection planning
answerChoices.rationale: This lift test was performed after interventions that can scar the submucosa; the original granular morphology and lack of an invasive focus matter.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This lift test was performed after interventions that can scar the submucosa; the original granular morphology and lack of an invasive focus matter.

answerChoices.label: Diagnostic-endoscopy referral for repeat biopsy planning
answerChoices.rationale: Another limited sample may miss invasion and does not solve the scarred completion-resection problem.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Another limited sample may miss invasion and does not solve the scarred completion-resection problem.

questions.stem: Which next operative plan should be discussed for {patientName}'s retained rectum?
questions.explanation: Failure of endoscopic control requires reconsideration of the retained rectum. Fragment histology and MRI do not exclude microscopic invasion throughout the field. Completion proctectomy with IPAA can address the rectal burden while respecting preserved function and the stated continuity goal; final pathology still matters.

answerChoices.label: Completion proctectomy with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis
answerChoices.rationale: The earlier rectal-sparing premise no longer holds; removing the uncontrolled rectum addresses the new disease while permitting restoration.

answerChoices.label: Continue IRA with repeated endoscopic clearing
answerChoices.rationale: Repeated residual high-grade field disease defeats the original rectal-retention premise.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Repeated residual high-grade field disease defeats the original rectal-retention premise.

answerChoices.label: Completion proctectomy with end ileostomy
answerChoices.rationale: This is an option, but the supplied function and restorative goal favor pouch planning.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This is an option, but the supplied function and restorative goal favor pouch planning.

questions.stem: Which operative plan best fits {patientName}'s recorded anatomy, subject to confirmation of clear margins at surgery?
questions.explanation: First preserve the adherent tumor-organ interface. Then use the involved anatomy to choose the planned bladder extent: a focal dome attachment with separate neck/trigone and a usable remnant supports en-bloc partial cystectomy, provided a clear margin is achievable. Adherence does not itself establish histologic invasion, and total cystectomy is not automatic.

answerChoices.label: Sigmoid colectomy with en-bloc partial cystectomy
answerChoices.rationale: A focal dome attachment can be removed en bloc with a bladder portion while retaining uninvolved neck, trigone and reservoir; the plan still requires an achievable clear margin.

answerChoices.label: Sigmoid colectomy with en-bloc total cystectomy
answerChoices.rationale: The represented attachment is focal at the dome; the record does not show neck/trigone involvement or loss of a usable remaining bladder requiring total removal.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The represented attachment is focal at the dome; the record does not show neck/trigone involvement or loss of a usable remaining bladder requiring total removal.

answerChoices.label: Sigmoid colectomy with separation of the bladder attachment
answerChoices.rationale: An adherent cancer interface should not be divided to decide whether the adhesion is malignant; partial bladder resection preserves an en-bloc specimen.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: An adherent cancer interface should not be divided to decide whether the adhesion is malignant; partial bladder resection preserves an en-bloc specimen.

questions.stem: Which pathology plan should next improve {patientName}'s regional-stage assessment for these two resections?
questions.explanation: Assign nodes to the primary and specimen from which they came before assessing the count. Seventeen right-colon nodes cannot be transferred to the sigmoid basin. Additional pathology evaluation should target the sigmoid specimen with five assessed nodes; this does not itself prove nodal metastasis or require repeat colectomy.

answerChoices.label: Request an additional node search in the sigmoid specimen
answerChoices.rationale: The sigmoid basin has only five assessed nodes. The 17 nodes assigned to the other primary do not repair that specimen-specific deficit.

answerChoices.label: Request an additional node search in the right-colon specimen
answerChoices.rationale: The right-colon specimen already has 17 reported nodes; the identified low count belongs to the sigmoid specimen.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The right-colon specimen already has 17 reported nodes; the identified low count belongs to the sigmoid specimen.

answerChoices.label: Accept the combined 22-node assessment for both primaries
answerChoices.rationale: Separate primary tumors require their own regional specimen provenance; a pooled total does not establish adequate assessment for the five-node sigmoid basin.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Separate primary tumors require their own regional specimen provenance; a pooled total does not establish adequate assessment for the five-node sigmoid basin.

questions.stem: Which initial treatment sequence best fits {patientName}'s current metastatic-primary record?
questions.explanation: The adult scope's nonpassage does not alone establish bowel obstruction. Ongoing bowel function, absent obstructive symptoms and no upstream dilation define the present primary-related burden. With incurable metastases and no primary complication, initial systemic treatment planning is generally preferred to prophylactic colectomy or diversion.

answerChoices.label: Systemic treatment planning with the primary left in place
answerChoices.rationale: The record lacks clinical or radiographic obstruction and other primary-related complications. For incurable metastatic disease in this setting, systemic treatment generally precedes prophylactic primary surgery.

answerChoices.label: Sigmoid colectomy followed by systemic treatment planning
answerChoices.rationale: The smaller scope passed, bowel function continues and CT shows no upstream dilation; prophylactic colectomy would delay treatment of the dominant metastatic disease.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The smaller scope passed, bowel function continues and CT shows no upstream dilation; prophylactic colectomy would delay treatment of the dominant metastatic disease.

answerChoices.label: Diverting colostomy followed by systemic treatment planning
answerChoices.rationale: No symptomatic or radiographic obstruction requiring diversion is established.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: No symptomatic or radiographic obstruction requiring diversion is established.

questions.stem: At that outside intraoperative decision point, which reconstruction plan best fits {patientName}'s recorded findings?
questions.explanation: Review the physiology at the actual reconstruction point. Persistent vasopressor need plus fecal contamination and bowel edema favor avoiding a colorectal anastomosis; closing the stump and forming an end colostomy is a concrete plan. Diversion cannot erase the risk of an anastomosis already constructed. This scoped decision does not prescribe Hartmann reconstruction for every perforated cancer.

answerChoices.label: Close the rectal stump and create an end colostomy
answerChoices.rationale: Ongoing vasopressor need with fecal contamination and edematous bowel favors avoiding a new colorectal anastomosis. A concrete Hartmann reconstruction is supported here; no universal rule for every perforation is asserted.

answerChoices.label: Create a colorectal anastomosis and a diverting loop ileostomy
answerChoices.rationale: Diversion does not remove an anastomosis or its failure risk. The continuing vasopressor need and adverse local conditions favor not constructing it at this recorded point.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Diversion does not remove an anastomosis or its failure risk. The continuing vasopressor need and adverse local conditions favor not constructing it at this recorded point.

answerChoices.label: Create a colorectal anastomosis without proximal diversion
answerChoices.rationale: The relevant observations are the current vasopressor need, contamination and edema, not earlier cancer-treatment eligibility.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The relevant observations are the current vasopressor need, contamination and edema, not earlier cancer-treatment eligibility.

questions.stem: Under USMSTF guidance, when should {patientName}'s next colonoscopy be planned after this normal first surveillance examination?
questions.explanation: Second-surveillance planning uses two examinations. A normal first follow-up modifies, but does not erase, the advanced baseline adenoma history.

answerChoices.label: Colonoscopy in five years
answerChoices.rationale: A normal first surveillance examination after an advanced baseline adenoma supports a five-year next interval.

answerChoices.label: Colonoscopy in three years
answerChoices.rationale: The normal first surveillance modifies the next interval.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The normal first surveillance modifies the next interval.

answerChoices.label: Colonoscopy in ten years
answerChoices.rationale: The advanced baseline finding continues to matter when selecting the next interval.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The advanced baseline finding continues to matter when selecting the next interval.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: The nonpedunculated ascending-colon lesion was removed completely and retrieved in one oriented piece. Moderately differentiated glands extend 0.6 mm into submucosa; the invasive front is 2 mm from the deep cut edge. Both lateral mucosal edges were identified histologically and are free of adenoma and carcinoma. No lymphovascular or perineural invasion is found; budding is low. No lesion remained endoscopically.
decisionNodes.stem: Which lesion-directed plan should be discussed for {patientName}'s resected ascending-colon lesion?

answerChoices.label: Colonoscopic surveillance of the excision site
answerChoices.rationale: The intact assessment and favorable features support endoscopic treatment with surveillance.

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic full-thickness scar excision
answerChoices.rationale: No outstanding local margin question is established.

answerChoices.label: Oncologic ascending-colon resection
answerChoices.rationale: No adverse feature puts this fully assessed lesion in the regional resection group.

decisionNodes.explanation: Assess the whole intact specimen, including lateral and deep clearance, depth, grade, vascular/neural invasion and budding. These findings support a favorable fully excised submucosally invasive lesion for which endoscopic treatment with surveillance can be discussed; a visually clear scar alone would not establish that conclusion.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: The original 26-mm lesion had a uniform granular surface. Cautery removed one part; carbon tattoo was injected beneath the remainder. On repeat inspection, residual tissue fails to lift at that site. Removed tissue contains adenoma. No ulcerated or depressed focus is described.
decisionNodes.stem: Which referral should guide {patientName}'s next treatment plan?

answerChoices.label: Advanced-endoscopy referral for completion-resection planning
answerChoices.rationale: Prior cautery and tattoo beneath the residual lesion can produce fibrosis. Expert completion planning is warranted; nonlifting alone does not prove deep invasion.

answerChoices.label: Colorectal-surgery referral for oncologic resection planning
answerChoices.rationale: This lift test was performed after interventions that can scar the submucosa; the original granular morphology and lack of an invasive focus matter.

answerChoices.label: Diagnostic-endoscopy referral for repeat biopsy planning
answerChoices.rationale: Another limited sample may miss invasion and does not solve the scarred completion-resection problem.

decisionNodes.explanation: Interpret a lift test in its procedural history. Tattoo and cautery beneath a residual lesion can cause fibrosis, so this nonlift does not independently establish deep invasion. Advanced completion-resection planning addresses the actual problem without assuming either cancer or easy routine snare removal.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Years after colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis for FAP, the retained rectum now contains a confluent adenoma field left after repeated endoscopic clearing attempts. Submitted fragments contain high-grade dysplasia; no invasive carcinoma is present in those fragments. Pelvic MRI shows no extrarectal extension or suspicious regional nodes. Continence is normal. After counseling about further surgery, he prioritizes maintaining intestinal continuity over a permanent end ileostomy.
decisionNodes.stem: Which next operative plan should be discussed for {patientName}'s retained rectum?

answerChoices.label: Completion proctectomy with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis
answerChoices.rationale: The earlier rectal-sparing premise no longer holds; removing the uncontrolled rectum addresses the new disease while permitting restoration.

answerChoices.label: Continue IRA with repeated endoscopic clearing
answerChoices.rationale: Repeated residual high-grade field disease defeats the original rectal-retention premise.

answerChoices.label: Completion proctectomy with end ileostomy
answerChoices.rationale: This is an option, but the supplied function and restorative goal favor pouch planning.

decisionNodes.explanation: Failure of endoscopic control requires reconsideration of the retained rectum. Fragment histology and MRI do not exclude microscopic invasion throughout the field. Completion proctectomy with IPAA can address the rectal burden while respecting preserved function and the stated continuity goal; final pathology still matters.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Biopsy confirms sigmoid adenocarcinoma and distant staging is negative. The outside exploration record describes a firm focal attachment to the bladder dome, with the neck, trigone and ureteric entries separate from the tumor. The remainder of the bladder wall is uninvolved and would retain a substantial reservoir after dome removal. No peritoneal deposits were found. The patient is being considered for curative surgery, and the attachment has not been divided.
decisionNodes.stem: Which operative plan best fits {patientName}'s recorded anatomy, subject to confirmation of clear margins at surgery?

answerChoices.label: Sigmoid colectomy with en-bloc partial cystectomy
answerChoices.rationale: A focal dome attachment can be removed en bloc with a bladder portion while retaining uninvolved neck, trigone and reservoir; the plan still requires an achievable clear margin.

answerChoices.label: Sigmoid colectomy with en-bloc total cystectomy
answerChoices.rationale: The represented attachment is focal at the dome; the record does not show neck/trigone involvement or loss of a usable remaining bladder requiring total removal.

answerChoices.label: Sigmoid colectomy with separation of the bladder attachment
answerChoices.rationale: An adherent cancer interface should not be divided to decide whether the adhesion is malignant; partial bladder resection preserves an en-bloc specimen.

decisionNodes.explanation: First preserve the adherent tumor-organ interface. Then use the involved anatomy to choose the planned bladder extent: a focal dome attachment with separate neck/trigone and a usable remnant supports en-bloc partial cystectomy, provided a clear margin is achievable. Adherence does not itself establish histologic invasion, and total cystectomy is not automatic.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Two synchronous colon cancers were removed in separately labeled right-colon and sigmoid specimens. The right-colon report lists 17 negative regional nodes. The sigmoid report lists five negative regional nodes; that tumor extends through muscularis propria into pericolic fat with clear margins. No metastases were found on preoperative staging. Both submitted mesenteric specimens remain available to pathology.
decisionNodes.stem: Which pathology plan should next improve {patientName}'s regional-stage assessment for these two resections?

answerChoices.label: Request an additional node search in the sigmoid specimen
answerChoices.rationale: The sigmoid basin has only five assessed nodes. The 17 nodes assigned to the other primary do not repair that specimen-specific deficit.

answerChoices.label: Request an additional node search in the right-colon specimen
answerChoices.rationale: The right-colon specimen already has 17 reported nodes; the identified low count belongs to the sigmoid specimen.

answerChoices.label: Accept the combined 22-node assessment for both primaries
answerChoices.rationale: Separate primary tumors require their own regional specimen provenance; a pooled total does not establish adequate assessment for the five-node sigmoid basin.

decisionNodes.explanation: Assign nodes to the primary and specimen from which they came before assessing the count. Seventeen right-colon nodes cannot be transferred to the sigmoid basin. Additional pathology evaluation should target the sigmoid specimen with five assessed nodes; this does not itself prove nodal metastasis or require repeat colectomy.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: The outside multidisciplinary team records diffuse bilobar liver and pulmonary metastases not amenable to curative local treatment. At colonoscopy an adult instrument could not pass the sigmoid tumor, but a pediatric instrument passed it. He reports daily formed stools without pain, vomiting, bleeding or transfusion need. CT shows no upstream colonic dilation.
decisionNodes.stem: Which initial treatment sequence best fits {patientName}'s current metastatic-primary record?

answerChoices.label: Systemic treatment planning with the primary left in place
answerChoices.rationale: The record lacks clinical or radiographic obstruction and other primary-related complications. For incurable metastatic disease in this setting, systemic treatment generally precedes prophylactic primary surgery.

answerChoices.label: Sigmoid colectomy followed by systemic treatment planning
answerChoices.rationale: The smaller scope passed, bowel function continues and CT shows no upstream dilation; prophylactic colectomy would delay treatment of the dominant metastatic disease.

answerChoices.label: Diverting colostomy followed by systemic treatment planning
answerChoices.rationale: No symptomatic or radiographic obstruction requiring diversion is established.

decisionNodes.explanation: The adult scope's nonpassage does not alone establish bowel obstruction. Ongoing bowel function, absent obstructive symptoms and no upstream dilation define the present primary-related burden. With incurable metastases and no primary complication, initial systemic treatment planning is generally preferred to prophylactic colectomy or diversion.
sourceLabels: ASCRS Management of Colon Cancer (2022)
