optionAudit.temptation: Combine the baseline and first-surveillance findings
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: A normal first surveillance examination after an advanced baseline adenoma supports a five-year next interval.
optionAudit.reasonableWhen: Advanced adenoma at baseline followed by a normal high-quality first surveillance.

optionAudit.temptation: Repeat the baseline advanced-adenoma interval unchanged
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: The normal first surveillance modifies the next interval.
optionAudit.reasonableWhen: Advanced adenoma or another corresponding higher-risk finding persists at first surveillance.

optionAudit.temptation: Erase baseline risk after one normal follow-up
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: The advanced baseline finding continues to matter when selecting the next interval.
optionAudit.reasonableWhen: A low-risk baseline followed by normal first surveillance can support a longer interval.

steps: Infer that four fragments from one jar do not establish four removed lesions.

selfChecks.consequence: Unnecessary surveillance from a falsely inflated adenoma count.
selfChecks.deletionTest: Without the procedure count the jar cannot establish lesion number; size and histology keep the low-count rule applicable.
selfChecks.counterfactual: Replace the procedure log with four separate completely removed small adenomas: three-to-five years becomes best.

optionAudit.whyRankedHere: Two small completely removed nonadvanced adenomas remain two lesions despite four laboratory fragments.

optionAudit.temptation: Count tissue fragments as separate adenomas
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: The procedure documented two lesions; four fragments do not establish four adenomas.
optionAudit.reasonableWhen: Three or four small tubular adenomas were actually removed.

optionAudit.temptation: Treat any multiple-fragment adenoma jar as high-burden disease
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: Neither five-to-ten actual adenomas nor an advanced feature is established.
optionAudit.reasonableWhen: Five to ten small adenomas or an advanced adenoma is found.

optionAudit.reasonableWhen: A separate unresolved systemic target may justify PET.

reviewedDraftCases.name: Henry Wallace
reviewedDraftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 58-year-old man, attends clinic to reconcile outside colorectal screening results.

nodes.title: Complete abnormal stool screening
nodes.objective: Select diagnostic colonoscopy after an abnormal FIT despite a later negative repeat.
nodes.update: The August screening FIT was positive. A second kit from another office in September was negative. No colon examination has followed; colonoscopy is clinically appropriate.
nodes.task: Which investigation should complete {patientName}'s evaluation of these screening records?

choices.label: Diagnostic colonoscopy
choices.temptation: Let the screening indication determine diagnostic completion
choices.rationale: An earlier positive screen still requires colonoscopy; a later negative screen does not complete its evaluation.
choices.reasonableWhen: An abnormal stool screen remains unresolved and colonoscopy is appropriate.

choices.label: Another fecal immunochemical test
choices.temptation: Let the newest screen cancel the older result
choices.rationale: Another screening result does not resolve the first abnormal result.
choices.reasonableWhen: Routine eligible screening without an outstanding abnormal result.

choices.label: CT colonography
choices.temptation: Prefer a whole-colon image over direct examination
choices.rationale: No barrier to diagnostic colonoscopy is supplied; tissue sampling may be needed.
choices.reasonableWhen: An incomplete or contraindicated colonoscopy could change the completion pathway.

nodes.explanation: A negative repeat screen cannot cancel the diagnostic evaluation required by an earlier positive FIT.

gate.cueAttack: Neither complaint nor task names the keyed instrument. All three tests have estimates. Removed ready-for-recommended-workup wording.
gate.stage: Three diagnostic investigations after abnormal screening.
steps: Recognize a negative repeat as another screen rather than diagnostic completion.
Choose a colon examination rather than further screening.
gate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: recency bias can overwrite the unresolved earlier result.
gate.decidingObservation: Initial positive FIT without a completed colon examination.
gate.consequence: Delayed diagnostic evaluation.
gate.deletionTest: Both results create the discordance; colonoscopy suitability limits the offered alternatives.
gate.counterfactual: Replace both results with a single negative FIT in routine screening: scheduled repeat FIT becomes reasonable.
gate.sequence: First node; its explanation gives no tissue-provenance rule.

nodes.title: Resolve unrepresentative colon sampling
nodes.objective: Arrange lesion-directed tissue acquisition when a benign submitted specimen came from outside a persistent lesion.
nodes.update: At a later visit, the founder reviews the completed outside colonoscopy. An irregular sigmoid mucosal lesion remains in place. The procedure diagram maps the submitted bites to adjacent mucosa; histology contains intact crypts and lamina propria. Lesion-directed endoscopic sampling is feasible.
nodes.task: Which tissue-assessment plan should be arranged for {patientName}'s sigmoid lesion?

choices.label: Repeat endoscopic sampling of the lesion
choices.temptation: Match submitted tissue to the target
choices.rationale: Benign adjacent mucosa does not establish the separate lesion diagnosis.
choices.reasonableWhen: A suspicious lesion remains unsampled and can be sampled safely.

choices.label: Obtain deeper levels from the existing block
choices.temptation: Treat a provenance problem as a processing problem
choices.rationale: Further levels cannot turn adjacent tissue into the persistent lesion.
choices.reasonableWhen: A correctly targeted specimen has an incompletely sectioned diagnostic focus.

choices.label: Repeat endoscopy at a surveillance visit
choices.temptation: Accept benign tissue as a resolved baseline
choices.rationale: The actual lesion remains histologically unresolved.
choices.reasonableWhen: A completely removed concordantly benign lesion can enter surveillance.

nodes.explanation: Map the specimen before trusting its scope. The submitted mucosa does not represent the persistent lesion; arrange targeted tissue assessment.

gate.cueAttack: The record does not label sampling inadequate. The map and constituents require interpretation; all assessment options carry estimates.
gate.stage: Three tissue-assessment plans for an unresolved diagnosis.
steps: Identify that the submitted specimen comes from adjacent surface mucosa.
Acquire the actual lesion rather than reprocess off-target tissue or assume clearance.
gate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: a reassuring pathology label may obscure target mismatch.
gate.decidingObservation: Procedure map places the bites outside the lesion.
gate.consequence: False reassurance from an unrepresentative specimen.
gate.deletionTest: Deleting the map makes deeper levels a more credible first action; persistent lesion and feasibility delimit the decision.
gate.counterfactual: Move the bites into the lesion and add a pathologist request for additional levels to resolve a partially sectioned focus: block review becomes appropriate.
gate.sequence: Earlier FIT feedback supplies no specimen-location inference.

reviewedDraftCases.name: Grace Bennett
reviewedDraftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 64-year-old woman, attends clinic to review an outside colonoscopy after a positive FIT.

nodes.title: Complete an inadequately prepared examination
nodes.objective: Distinguish cecal intubation from adequate proximal mucosal assessment.
nodes.update: The scope reached the cecum. After washing, adherent stool still obscured broad areas of the ascending and transverse colon. The left colon was well seen; the report nevertheless assigned a routine screening interval.
nodes.task: Which investigation should complete {patientName}'s positive-FIT evaluation?

choices.label: Repeat colonoscopy with revised preparation
choices.temptation: Judge visualization separately from scope reach
choices.rationale: Obscured proximal mucosa remains unresolved despite cecal intubation.
choices.reasonableWhen: A required diagnostic colon examination remains inadequate.

choices.label: Flexible sigmoidoscopy with standard preparation
choices.temptation: Focus on the adequately seen distal colon
choices.rationale: A distal repeat leaves the poorly seen proximal colon unexamined.
choices.reasonableWhen: An isolated distal question after adequate proximal evaluation.

choices.label: Repeat fecal immunochemical screening
choices.temptation: Treat cecal reach as a completed negative scope
choices.rationale: A repeat screen cannot complete the unresolved diagnostic examination.
choices.reasonableWhen: Routine screening after an appropriately resolved prior evaluation.

nodes.explanation: Reaching the cecum does not establish adequate mucosal inspection. Complete the poorly visualized colon with an adequately prepared repeat; no universal repeat deadline is specified.

gate.cueAttack: Removed interpretive cannot-support-screening wording. Raw regional visibility competes with the cecal landmark. All tests have previews.
steps: Recognize the mismatch between anatomic reach and mucosal assessment.
Complete the unresolved positive-FIT evaluation rather than accept a routine interval.
gate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: residents may trust the cecal endpoint or a reassuring distal examination.
gate.decidingObservation: Proximal mucosa remains obscured after washing.
gate.consequence: Missed proximal neoplasia and an unjustified interval.
gate.deletionTest: Cecal reach creates the error; regional obscuration defeats it. Positive FIT establishes the diagnostic phase.
gate.counterfactual: If the whole colon were adequately inspected with no neoplasia, returning to an appropriate screening pathway becomes reasonable.
gate.sequence: No later pathology or surveillance rule is exposed.

nodes.title: Surveillance after an advanced adenoma
nodes.objective: Use the completed baseline and resection details to select USMSTF surveillance.
nodes.update: The repeat examination had adequate visualization throughout. A 12-mm tubular adenoma was removed in one intact specimen with complete excision documented and no invasive cancer. There were no other polyps, prior neoplasia, hereditary syndrome or relevant family history.
nodes.task: Under USMSTF guidance, when should {patientName}'s next colonoscopy be planned?

choices.label: Colonoscopy in three years
choices.temptation: Combine adenoma size with complete intact removal
choices.rationale: An adenoma at least 10 mm warrants three-year surveillance after a high-quality baseline.
choices.reasonableWhen: An advanced adenoma has been confidently completely removed.

choices.label: Colonoscopy in six months
choices.temptation: Apply a large-piecemeal scar-check rule
choices.rationale: This smaller lesion was removed intact, so the early piecemeal pathway does not apply.
choices.reasonableWhen: An adenoma at least 20 mm was removed piecemeal.

choices.label: Colonoscopy in ten years
choices.temptation: Let corrected preparation reset the case to normal screening
choices.rationale: The adequate examination still found a size-defined advanced adenoma.
choices.reasonableWhen: A normal high-quality examination in an average-risk patient.

nodes.explanation: The adequate repeat becomes the baseline. The adenoma size supports three years, while intact complete removal distinguishes this from an early piecemeal scar check.

gate.cueAttack: Identical investigation labels differ only by supported interval. US framework is stated because intervals are guideline-specific.
steps: Interpret the now-adequate baseline, specimen size and intact removal.
Select advanced-adenoma surveillance rather than a scar check or normal-screen interval.
gate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: the earlier incomplete examination or adenoma size may provoke an unnecessary early repeat.
gate.decidingObservation: 12-mm adenoma, intact complete excision and adequate whole-colon examination.
gate.consequence: Over-surveillance or delayed surveillance.
gate.deletionTest: Size and removal mode independently change the category; exclusions delimit guideline applicability.
gate.counterfactual: Change to a 25-mm adenoma removed piecemeal: six-month surveillance becomes best.
gate.sequence: The prior explanation addresses adequacy, not adenoma surveillance.

reviewedDraftCases.name: Victor Ellis
reviewedDraftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 67-year-old man, attends clinic with outside endoscopy records for a cecal lesion.

nodes.title: Advanced resection before colectomy
nodes.objective: Choose expert endoscopic assessment for a large lesion without demonstrated deep invasion.
nodes.update: The lesion spans 28 mm and spreads laterally with a uniform granular surface. Documented image-enhanced inspection shows no depressed or ulcerated focus. A superficial sample contains adenoma. The first operator stopped before attempting resection because of size.
nodes.task: Which referral should guide {patientName}'s next lesion-removal plan?

choices.label: Advanced endoscopist for resection assessment
choices.temptation: Separate technical complexity from an oncologic indication
choices.rationale: Size supports advanced expertise; neither the appearance nor the superficial sample establishes mandatory colectomy.
choices.reasonableWhen: A large nonpedunculated lesion lacks overt deep-invasive features.

choices.label: Colorectal surgeon for segmental colectomy
choices.temptation: Interpret size as proof that endoscopy cannot be definitive
choices.rationale: A technically difficult adenoma can still be removable by an expert.
choices.reasonableWhen: Deep invasion or expert-confirmed inability to achieve safe complete endoscopic removal.

choices.label: Referring endoscopist for serial partial resections
choices.temptation: Convert a large lesion into several routine removals
choices.rationale: Repeated incomplete attempts can complicate definitive resection.
choices.reasonableWhen: A readily removable small lesion can be completely excised by the routine operator.

nodes.explanation: Separate size-related difficulty from established deep cancer. Expert assessment can define a complete endoscopic removal plan before colectomy is chosen for technical complexity.

gate.cueAttack: No statement calls the lesion benign or curable. The reason the operator stopped is observed chronology, not a promise that an expert can succeed.
steps: Interpret morphology, superficial-biopsy scope and why the first procedure stopped.
Seek appropriate resection expertise before equating technical difficulty with mandatory colectomy.
gate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: size and incomplete removal can trigger premature surgery.
gate.decidingObservation: No deep-invasive morphology; size stopped an unattempted resection.
gate.consequence: Unnecessary colectomy or repeated scarring partial attempts.
gate.deletionTest: Morphology prevents a cancer-first assumption; superficial sampling remains explicitly limited.
gate.counterfactual: Confirm deep submucosal invasion and replace the surface with an ulcerated invasive focus: surgical evaluation becomes best.
gate.sequence: No previous scored finding; the later EMR method is not yet visible.

nodes.title: Early surveillance after piecemeal EMR
nodes.objective: Select early scar assessment after large piecemeal adenoma resection.
nodes.update: At the next clinic visit, the founder reviews expert EMR records. The 28-mm lesion was removed in several pieces. No residual tissue was visible; fragments contain adenoma without invasive cancer, but cannot establish a continuous lateral margin. The remaining colon was adequately examined.
nodes.task: Under USMSTF guidance, when should {patientName}'s first postresection colonoscopy be planned?

choices.label: Colonoscopy at about six months
choices.temptation: Match follow-up to removal mode
choices.rationale: Large piecemeal EMR needs early recurrence assessment despite apparent visual clearance.
choices.reasonableWhen: An adenoma at least 20 mm was removed piecemeal.

choices.label: Colonoscopy at three years
choices.temptation: Use the ordinary advanced-adenoma interval
choices.rationale: That interval omits the separate early scar check for this resection.
choices.reasonableWhen: A smaller advanced adenoma was confidently removed intact.

choices.label: Colonoscopy at ten years
choices.temptation: Treat visual clearance as a normal baseline
choices.rationale: A large piecemeal-resected adenoma is not a normal screening examination.
choices.reasonableWhen: A high-quality colonoscopy finds no neoplasia.

nodes.explanation: Visual clearance and intact margin assessment are different. Large size plus piecemeal removal supports the early scar-surveillance pathway.

gate.cueAttack: All options are the same examination at different intervals. Removed a complete-clearance conclusion; method and specimen architecture determine follow-up.
steps: Distinguish clear-looking surface from confidently assessed continuous margins.
Apply early piecemeal surveillance rather than routine advanced-adenoma follow-up.
gate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: noninvasive fragments and visual clearance may falsely reassure into a three-year interval.
gate.decidingObservation: 28-mm lesion removed piecemeal despite a clear final surface.
gate.consequence: Delayed detection of residual or recurrent adenoma.
gate.deletionTest: Removal mode and size are necessary; no invasion keeps this separate from adverse malignant-polyp surgery.
gate.counterfactual: Change to an intact completely excised 12-mm adenoma: three-year surveillance becomes best.
gate.sequence: The first referral explanation gives no surveillance interval or future removal method.

reviewedDraftCases.name: Susan Mercer
reviewedDraftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 55-year-old woman, attends clinic after removal of an ascending-colon lesion.

nodes.title: Complete favorable invasive-polyp excision
nodes.objective: Integrate specimen adequacy, depth and adverse-feature assessment before colectomy.
nodes.update: The lesion was retrieved in one oriented piece. Moderately differentiated glands extend 0.6 mm into submucosa and remain 2 mm from the deep cut edge. No lymphovascular or perineural invasion is found; budding is low. No lesion remained endoscopically.
nodes.task: Which lesion-directed plan should be discussed for {patientName}'s resected ascending-colon lesion?

choices.label: Colonoscopic surveillance of the excision site
choices.temptation: Use the complete specimen rather than the cancer label
choices.rationale: The intact assessment and favorable features support endoscopic treatment with surveillance.
choices.reasonableWhen: A fully assessed invasive polyp has favorable features and clear edges.

choices.label: Endoscopic full-thickness scar excision
choices.temptation: Treat all submucosal cancer as local residual
choices.rationale: No outstanding local margin question is established.
choices.reasonableWhen: A specialist-defined unresolved local-clearance problem.

choices.label: Oncologic ascending-colon resection
choices.temptation: Treat invasion as automatic colectomy
choices.rationale: No adverse feature puts this fully assessed lesion in the regional resection group.
choices.reasonableWhen: Adverse histology or an involved invasive margin.

nodes.explanation: The intact specimen can establish depth and clearance. Its favorable represented features support surveillance after endoscopic treatment.

gate.cueAttack: Neither task nor presentation says low-risk. Removed chemotherapy and radiation foils; individual pathology components must be integrated.
steps: Establish that the intact specimen supports depth and margin assessment.
Combine grade, budding and vascular/neural findings to distinguish local follow-up from regional treatment.
gate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: over-treating a cancer label and underweighting specimen adequacy are credible errors.
gate.decidingObservation: Intact shallow specimen, clear 2-mm edge and no adverse findings.
gate.consequence: Unnecessary colectomy or reverse undertreatment of adverse disease.
gate.deletionTest: Architecture earns negative-margin confidence; adverse-feature assessment is necessary.
gate.counterfactual: Add malignant glands in vascular channels: regional resection becomes best despite the clear edge.
gate.sequence: Standalone; no preceding favorable-profile feedback.

reviewedDraftCases.name: Daniel Fraser
reviewedDraftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 60-year-old man, attends clinic with a removed sigmoid-polyp specimen and operative diagram.

nodes.title: Complete favorable invasive-polyp excision
nodes.objective: Integrate specimen adequacy, depth and adverse-feature assessment before colectomy.
nodes.update: The pedunculated lesion was retrieved intact. Well-formed malignant glands enter 0.5 mm into stalk submucosa, stopping 2 mm above transection. No lymphovascular or perineural invasion or budding is identified.
nodes.task: Which postexcision plan fits {patientName}'s sigmoid-polyp specimen?

choices.label: Colonoscopic surveillance after polypectomy
choices.temptation: Interpret invasion and clearance separately
choices.rationale: The intact shallow favorable specimen supports surveillance.
choices.reasonableWhen: Complete local excision with favorable invasion features.

choices.label: Endoscopic full-thickness scar resection
choices.temptation: Equate stalk invasion with a positive margin
choices.rationale: The represented cut edge is clear; invasion has not reached transection.
choices.reasonableWhen: A specialist-defined unresolved local margin.

choices.label: Oncologic sigmoid colectomy
choices.temptation: Rank all stalk-invasive cancers as adverse
choices.rationale: The represented depth and remaining features do not establish adverse-polyp risk.
choices.reasonableWhen: A transected invasive front or vascular invasion.

nodes.explanation: Shallow stalk invasion and an involved stalk cut edge are different observations. The intact clear specimen and remaining favorable findings support local follow-up.

gate.cueAttack: No Haggitt level or low-risk conclusion is supplied. Three comparable plans avoid treatment caricatures.
steps: Locate the invasive front relative to transection.
Integrate adequacy and adverse-feature absence rather than treating every stalk-invasive lesion as adverse.
gate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: stalk invasion may be confused with invasion below the stalk or transection.
gate.decidingObservation: The invasive front stops above an intact clear cut edge.
gate.consequence: Unnecessary scar treatment or colectomy.
gate.deletionTest: Orientation earns clearance; other findings govern whether local success is sufficient.
gate.counterfactual: Cut invasive glands across the cautery edge: oncologic sigmoid resection becomes best.
gate.sequence: Independent variant, not paired with a favorable-polyp explanation.

reviewedDraftCases.name: Lydia Barnes
reviewedDraftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 62-year-old woman, attends clinic after en-bloc sigmoid-polyp excision.

nodes.title: Regional risk despite local clearance
nodes.objective: Distinguish vascular invasion from local clearance when selecting regional treatment.
nodes.update: Malignant glands enter submucosa and occupy endothelial-lined channels away from the main front. None reaches the inked edge. Endoscopy shows a flat scar; CT shows no distant deposits or enlarged nodes. Operative assessment finds no prohibitive risk.
nodes.task: Which treatment plan should be discussed for {patientName}'s sigmoid lesion?

choices.label: Sigmoid colectomy with regional lymphadenectomy
choices.temptation: Separate local clearance from regional risk
choices.rationale: The vascular-channel finding supports regional resection despite a clear edge and normal-sized nodes.
choices.reasonableWhen: An operable patient has an adverse invasive-polyp feature.

choices.label: Full-thickness endoscopic scar excision
choices.temptation: Treat local clearance as the entire oncologic problem
choices.rationale: Local excision does not address the regional risk raised by vascular invasion.
choices.reasonableWhen: A selected local-clearance problem without adverse regional-risk features.

choices.label: Colonoscopic scar surveillance
choices.temptation: Let a healed scar override pathology
choices.rationale: A healed surface cannot erase the adverse feature.
choices.reasonableWhen: An intact fully assessed favorable polyp.

nodes.explanation: Vascular involvement and cut-edge clearance answer different questions. Discuss resection of the involved segment and its draining lymphatic territory.

gate.cueAttack: Lymphovascular invasion is not given as a diagnosis. Clear CT and scar create a real clinical misconception rather than permission for the key.
steps: Recognize malignant glands in endothelial-lined channels.
Determine that local-edge clearance does not settle regional risk.
gate.difficulty: Moderate/hard prediction: reassuring margins and CT can incorrectly dominate invasive histology.
gate.decidingObservation: Malignant glands in endothelial-lined channels despite a clear edge.
gate.consequence: Undertreatment of microscopic regional disease.
gate.deletionTest: Removing the channels changes risk; margin and CT reassurance establish the competing error. Fitness limits surgery ranking.
gate.counterfactual: Remove vascular invasion and supply a completely assessed favorable profile: surveillance becomes best.
gate.sequence: Standalone; the frozen N2 provenance matrix remains exact.

reviewedDraftCases.name: Owen Parker
reviewedDraftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 59-year-old man, attends clinic to discuss an outside descending-colon polypectomy.

nodes.title: Regional risk despite local clearance
nodes.objective: Distinguish vascular invasion from local clearance when selecting regional treatment.
nodes.update: Fragments contain moderately differentiated submucosal carcinoma. One ends through invasive glands at a cauterized edge; depth cannot be reconstructed. No vascular invasion is seen in represented sections. The scar looks clear, distant staging is negative and he is fit for resection.
nodes.task: Which treatment plan best addresses {patientName}'s descending-colon pathology?

choices.label: Oncologic descending-colon resection
choices.temptation: Treat an unassessable invasive front as an oncologic issue
choices.rationale: The transected invasive edge and unknown depth do not meet favorable-polyp criteria.
choices.reasonableWhen: An operable patient has a positive or indeterminate invasive margin.

choices.label: Endoscopic full-thickness scar resection
choices.temptation: Convert every uncertainty into a local clearance problem
choices.rationale: Local treatment may not settle the regional question from inadequately assessed invasive cancer.
choices.reasonableWhen: A selected noninvasive residual lesion or specialist-defined local-only issue.

choices.label: Colonoscopic scar surveillance
choices.temptation: Treat no vascular invasion as sufficient for low risk
choices.rationale: A sampled negative does not repair a transected invasive front.
choices.reasonableWhen: An intact completely assessed favorable polyp.

nodes.explanation: The actual cut-edge involvement matters more than the clear-looking scar. Sampled negatives do not turn an incomplete invasive specimen into a fully assessed favorable one.

gate.cueAttack: Removed the margin-naming lead-in. Raw transection and unmeasurable depth require interpretation. Options compare definitive lesion plans.
steps: Identify transected invasive glands and the missing complete front.
Do not extrapolate sampled negatives to global favorable risk.
gate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: sampled negative findings may be overextended to the full specimen.
gate.decidingObservation: Invasive glands are cut across at cautery and depth is unassessable.
gate.consequence: False confidence in local treatment of inadequately staged cancer.
gate.deletionTest: Transected glands change the key; fragment count alone would not prove an adverse invasive edge.
gate.counterfactual: Replace fragments with an intact shallow favorable specimen and clear edges: surveillance becomes best.
gate.sequence: Standalone; no frozen colon-cancer companion is rebound.

reviewedDraftCases.name: Elaine Porter
reviewedDraftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 66-year-old woman, attends clinic after partial cecal-polyp removal at an outside center.

nodes.title: Advanced resection before colectomy
nodes.objective: Choose expert endoscopic assessment for a large lesion without demonstrated deep invasion.
nodes.update: The original 26-mm lesion had a uniform granular surface. Cautery removed one part; carbon tattoo was injected beneath the remainder. On repeat inspection, residual tissue fails to lift at that site. Removed tissue contains adenoma. No ulcerated or depressed focus is described.
nodes.task: Which referral should guide {patientName}'s next treatment plan?

choices.label: Advanced endoscopist for scarred-lesion assessment
choices.temptation: Interpret nonlifting in its chronology
choices.rationale: Prior cautery and tattoo can cause fibrosis; expert assessment can determine whether endoscopic completion is appropriate.
choices.reasonableWhen: Nonlifting residual tissue follows intervention without established deep invasion.

choices.label: Colorectal surgeon for oncologic colectomy
choices.temptation: Equate all nonlifting with deep invasion
choices.rationale: Prior intervention supplies a competing cause; nonlifting alone does not establish an oncologic operation.
choices.reasonableWhen: Confirmed deep cancer or expert determination that safe endoscopic completion is unsuitable.

choices.label: Referring endoscopist for repeat standard snaring
choices.temptation: Treat possible fibrosis as proof routine removal is safe
choices.rationale: Nonlifting residual tissue remains technically complex despite the alternative explanation.
choices.reasonableWhen: Small readily lifting residual tissue can be removed routinely.

nodes.explanation: Prior cautery and tattoo change the meaning of nonlifting. They do not guarantee benignity or safe routine removal; obtain expert completion assessment.

gate.cueAttack: The record does not diagnose fibrosis or declare benignity. Chronology changes the nonlift interpretation. No uniquely cautious key competes with unqualified immediate treatment; each choice is a referral/removal pathway.
gate.stage: Three pathways for definitive residual-lesion management.
steps: Recognize a procedure-related cause competing with deep invasion.
Choose advanced assessment instead of automatic colectomy or another routine attempt.
gate.difficulty: Hard prediction: both overcalling invasion and underestimating fibrosis are credible errors.
gate.decidingObservation: Nonlifting is localized to the cauterized and tattooed bed.
gate.consequence: Unnecessary colectomy or hazardous incomplete repeat resection.
gate.deletionTest: Without prior intervention, the nonlift has a different meaning; partial adenoma cannot clear unsampled tissue.
gate.counterfactual: Add targeted histology proving deep invasion: oncologic colectomy assessment becomes best.
gate.sequence: Separate variant of advanced-resection meaning; no extra concept solely for tattoo history.

reviewedDraftCases.name: Peter Lawson
reviewedDraftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 61-year-old man, attends clinic after a sigmoid-polyp pathology report used the word carcinoma.

nodes.title: Mucosal carcinoma versus T1 invasion
nodes.objective: Use represented tissue boundaries rather than a cancer label to select local versus regional care.
nodes.update: The lesion was removed intact. Malignant glands are confined to lamina propria with continuous muscularis mucosae beneath them. Represented submucosa contains no invasive glands; all cut edges are clear.
nodes.task: Which lesion-directed plan fits {patientName}'s represented pathology?

choices.label: Colonoscopic surveillance after local excision
choices.temptation: Apply the actual depth boundary
choices.rationale: The adequately represented mucosal lesion has been excised; submucosal T1 invasion is not shown.
choices.reasonableWhen: Complete local excision of intramucosal disease.

choices.label: Full-thickness endoscopic scar resection
choices.temptation: Treat carcinoma wording as unremoved deeper tissue
choices.rationale: The intact specimen already represents the relevant boundary and clear margins.
choices.reasonableWhen: A selected unresolved local-clearance question.

choices.label: Sigmoid colectomy with regional lymphadenectomy
choices.temptation: Collapse mucosal carcinoma and adverse T1 cancer
choices.rationale: The represented submucosa contains no invasive glands.
choices.reasonableWhen: Submucosal invasion with adverse histology supports regional treatment.

nodes.explanation: Interpret depth and adequacy before acting on terminology. An intact specimen showing mucosal confinement and clear edges supports local treatment with surveillance.

gate.cueAttack: No stage-zero label precedes the answer. Represented submucosa is retained because a superficial negative would not establish the same conclusion.
steps: Interpret the muscularis-mucosae boundary and represented submucosa.
Choose local care rather than regional surgery from the word carcinoma.
gate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: pathology terminology can provoke overtreatment if depth is ignored.
gate.decidingObservation: Glands remain above continuous muscularis mucosae; submucosa is represented.
gate.consequence: Unnecessary regional resection.
gate.deletionTest: Removing represented submucosa destroys confidence in the local conclusion; clear edges establish local completion.
gate.counterfactual: Show glands inside submucosal vascular channels: regional colectomy becomes best.
gate.sequence: Standalone; no histology-label task precedes the applied decision.

reviewedDraftCases.name: Martha Nolan
reviewedDraftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 34-year-old woman with established FAP, attends clinic while the founder reviews outside colonoscopy and operative-planning records.

nodes.title: Rectal removal for uncontrolled FAP burden
nodes.objective: Integrate rectal clearance, continence and restorative goals when choosing FAP operative extent.
nodes.update: The colon contains extensive adenomas. In the rectum, confluent adenomatous areas remain between several prior resection scars; two further clearing sessions left visible lesions, including a broad focus with high-grade dysplasia. She has normal continence and wants intestinal continuity after counseling.
nodes.task: Which operative plan should be discussed for {patientName}'s colorectal disease?

choices.label: Proctocolectomy with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis
choices.temptation: Interpret failed rectal control alongside function
choices.rationale: Removing the uncontrolled rectum addresses the disease; preserved continence and informed restorative goals support IPAA.
choices.reasonableWhen: Rectal burden requires removal and pouch function is clinically appropriate.

choices.label: Colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis
choices.temptation: Preserve the rectum despite the actual clearance record
choices.rationale: IRA retains the repeatedly uncleared rectal adenoma field.
choices.reasonableWhen: Relative rectal sparing with endoscopically controllable adenomas.

choices.label: Proctocolectomy with end ileostomy
choices.temptation: Choose rectal removal without using the functional goal
choices.rationale: It removes the field but is less aligned with her stated restorative goal and preserved continence.
choices.reasonableWhen: Poor sphincter function or an informed preference against pouch-related functional effects.

nodes.explanation: Repeated failure to clear the rectal field changes the operation from colon removal to colorectal removal. Continence and the informed functional goal then guide reconstruction.

gate.cueAttack: Removed the conclusion rectal burden not controllable. Actual failed clearing, residual field and dysplasia establish it. Three named operations have similar scope; continence and goals are necessary rather than decorative.
steps: Infer that the repeatedly uncleared dysplastic rectal field cannot safely be retained as in IRA.
Use continence and restorative goals to select IPAA rather than an end stoma.
gate.difficulty: Moderate/hard prediction: a resident may preserve an unsafe rectum to avoid pelvic dissection or remove restoration despite adequate function.
gate.decidingObservation: Repeated visible rectal residual disease with high-grade dysplasia, normal continence.
gate.consequence: Retained high-risk rectal disease or avoidable loss of desired restoration.
gate.deletionTest: Failed clearance establishes extent; continence and goals distinguish two rectum-removing operations.
gate.counterfactual: Change to a sparsely involved rectum with all adenomas removed and a priority to avoid pelvic dissection: IRA becomes reasonable.
gate.sequence: Standalone; genetics testing interpretation is outside the scored topic.

reviewedDraftCases.name: Nathan Cole
reviewedDraftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 29-year-old man with established FAP, attends clinic to review prophylactic surgery with the founder.

nodes.title: Rectal-sparing FAP operation
nodes.objective: Assess whether relative rectal sparing permits a colon-only operation under informed functional goals.
nodes.update: Hundreds of colonic adenomas remain after an outside colonoscopy. The rectum contained three small adenomas, all removed intact; the remaining rectum was adequately inspected. Continence is normal. After counseling, he prioritizes avoiding pelvic dissection if the retained rectum can be safely monitored and accepts continuing endoscopy.
nodes.task: Which operative plan best fits {patientName}'s disease distribution and stated priorities?

choices.label: Total colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis
choices.temptation: Use relative rectal sparing under informed priorities
choices.rationale: The documented clearable rectum permits an IRA option, with ongoing surveillance.
choices.reasonableWhen: Relative rectal sparing, clearable lesions and willingness to retain surveillance.

choices.label: Proctocolectomy with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis
choices.temptation: Apply the most extensive restorative operation to every FAP case
choices.rationale: IPAA is a valid broader option, but the supplied relative sparing and functional priority favor IRA here.
choices.reasonableWhen: Rectal burden cannot be controlled or informed goals favor rectal removal.

choices.label: Proctocolectomy with end ileostomy
choices.temptation: Treat all polyposis as incompatible with restoration
choices.rationale: No sphincter problem or preference favors an end stoma in this case.
choices.reasonableWhen: Poor sphincter function or a preference against pouch function.

nodes.explanation: The operation depends on distribution, not a single FAP label. Relative rectal sparing permits IRA when the patient accepts ongoing rectal risk assessment and surveillance.

gate.cueAttack: The preference is necessary because both IRA and IPAA can be valid. It does not by itself establish that the rectum is retainable. All alternatives name complete operations.
steps: Interpret the colon-versus-rectum adenoma distribution and completeness of rectal clearance.
Apply the informed priority only after establishing that rectal retention is a supported option.
gate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: diagnosis-based automatic IPAA competes with inappropriate rectal preservation regardless of burden.
gate.decidingObservation: Three rectal adenomas completely removed versus extensive persistent colonic disease.
gate.consequence: Unnecessary pelvic dissection or, if distribution is misread, unsafe rectal retention.
gate.deletionTest: Without the clearing record, the priority cannot choose IRA; without the informed priority, IPAA remains equally defensible.
gate.counterfactual: Replace relative sparing with repeatedly uncleared rectal high-grade disease: proctocolectomy with IPAA becomes best despite the wish to avoid pelvic dissection.
gate.sequence: First decision; feedback gives no future progression findings.

nodes.title: Rectal removal for uncontrolled FAP burden
nodes.objective: Integrate rectal clearance, continence and restorative goals when choosing FAP operative extent.
nodes.update: At a subsequent clinic visit after colectomy with IRA, the founder reviews new surveillance records. The retained rectum now contains a confluent adenoma field with high-grade dysplasia that remained after repeated clearing attempts. Pelvic staging shows no invasive cancer. Continence remains normal and he wants restoration.
nodes.task: Which next operative plan should be discussed for {patientName}'s retained rectum?

choices.label: Completion proctectomy with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis
choices.temptation: Update operative extent from current rather than prior burden
choices.rationale: The earlier rectal-sparing premise no longer holds; removing the uncontrolled rectum addresses the new disease while permitting restoration.
choices.reasonableWhen: A retained rectum develops disease no longer manageable endoscopically.

choices.label: Continue IRA with repeated endoscopic clearing
choices.temptation: Carry forward an earlier appropriate choice unchanged
choices.rationale: Repeated residual high-grade field disease defeats the original rectal-retention premise.
choices.reasonableWhen: A limited rectal burden remains endoscopically clearable.

choices.label: Completion proctectomy with end ileostomy
choices.temptation: Remove the rectum without using the preserved function
choices.rationale: This is an option, but the supplied function and restorative goal favor pouch planning.
choices.reasonableWhen: Poor continence or a preference to avoid pouch-related function.

nodes.explanation: A previously appropriate IRA does not remain appropriate under every later rectal phenotype. Reassess current disease control and function before planning completion surgery.

gate.cueAttack: The prior plan is not called wrong. New observed failed clearance and dysplasia must override its earlier premise. Options are same-stage definitive strategies.
gate.stage: Three plans for the currently retained rectum.
steps: Recognize that new residual dysplastic disease invalidates the earlier clearable-rectum premise.
Select completion rectal removal and restoration using current continence and goals.
gate.difficulty: Hard prediction: anchoring to a previously correct IRA may delay necessary completion proctectomy.
gate.decidingObservation: Persistent high-grade rectal field after repeated clearing.
gate.consequence: Retaining an uncontrolled neoplastic field.
gate.deletionTest: Deleting the update leaves the original IRA appropriate, so the update earns a new decision. Continence distinguishes reconstruction choices.
gate.counterfactual: Return the rectum to a few completely removable adenomas: continued IRA with surveillance becomes best.
gate.sequence: Prior explanation permits IRA only under clearability. It does not reveal the later failure or dictate a reconstruction.

reviewedDraftCases.name: Helen Marsh
reviewedDraftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 48-year-old woman with FAP, attends clinic for review of outside colorectal surgical recommendations.

nodes.title: Reconstruction when continence is poor
nodes.objective: Integrate rectal removal needs with established sphincter dysfunction and informed functional priorities.
nodes.update: The rectal adenoma field includes high-grade dysplasia and has remained after repeated clearing attempts. She has daily leakage of formed stool despite prior continence treatment; examination documents a weak disrupted sphincter. After counseling, she prioritizes reliable evacuation and accepts a permanent stoma.
nodes.task: Which operative plan best fits {patientName}'s disease and functional record?

choices.label: Proctocolectomy with end ileostomy
choices.temptation: Use established poor function when choosing reconstruction
choices.rationale: The rectum needs removal and a pouch would depend on an already poorly functioning outlet; her informed goal supports an end stoma.
choices.reasonableWhen: Rectal removal is needed with poor sphincter function and compatible informed goals.

choices.label: Proctocolectomy with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis
choices.temptation: Apply restoration without checking the outlet
choices.rationale: It removes the field but uses the impaired sphincter and conflicts with her functional priority.
choices.reasonableWhen: Good sphincter function with a restorative goal.

choices.label: Colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis
choices.temptation: Avoid pouch surgery by retaining an unsafe rectum
choices.rationale: IRA leaves the uncleared rectal dysplastic field and does not resolve the outlet dysfunction.
choices.reasonableWhen: Relative rectal sparing and adequate control permit retention.

nodes.explanation: Disease distribution determines what must be removed; sphincter function and informed goals determine whether restoration is appropriate.

gate.cueAttack: The stoma preference is supported by raw formed-stool leakage and structural weakness, not used as an isolated answer label. Three specific operations share grammar.
steps: Identify both uncontrolled rectal disease and a compromised outlet.
Choose rectal removal without a reconstruction relying on that outlet.
gate.difficulty: Moderate/hard prediction: reflex IPAA in a younger patient can override functional evidence.
gate.decidingObservation: Established daily formed-stool leakage and sphincter disruption.
gate.consequence: Poor pouch continence or retention of uncontrolled rectal disease.
gate.deletionTest: Without poor function, restorative IPAA competes strongly; burden still determines the need for rectal removal.
gate.counterfactual: Replace dysfunction with normal continence and an informed restorative goal: IPAA becomes best.
gate.sequence: Standalone; demographic facts do not select the operation.

reviewedDraftCases.name: Laura Sutton
reviewedDraftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 54-year-old woman, attends clinic after an outside biopsy identified mid-rectal adenocarcinoma.

nodes.title: Local rectal staging before treatment
nodes.objective: Choose local staging that evaluates the tumor and mesorectal surgical plane after adequate distant staging.
nodes.update: Colonoscopy identifies a broad lesion 7 cm from the anal verge. Chest and contrast abdominal/pelvic CT show no metastases but do not resolve the tumor edge against the mesorectal fascia. Examination is compatible with a resectable pelvic tumor.
nodes.task: Which examination should complete {patientName}'s local pretreatment assessment?

choices.label: Rectal-protocol pelvic MRI
choices.temptation: Separate local surgical-plane staging from distant staging
choices.rationale: MRI assesses tumor depth, regional disease and relationship to the mesorectal fascia.
choices.reasonableWhen: A rectal tumor needs locoregional planning.

choices.label: Endorectal ultrasound
choices.temptation: Use early wall-layer resolution for all rectal staging
choices.rationale: EUS can help early T-stage distinctions but does not replace the broad mesorectal-plane assessment needed here.
choices.reasonableWhen: A small early lesion needs T1-versus-T2 clarification.

choices.label: Whole-body FDG PET-CT
choices.temptation: Treat another distant study as local planning
choices.rationale: No unresolved systemic target makes PET the local staging examination.
choices.reasonableWhen: Selected unresolved systemic disease can justify PET after appropriate review.

nodes.explanation: Completed distant staging does not establish the local surgical plane. Rectal-protocol MRI addresses the tumor, mesorectum and fascia relationship.

gate.cueAttack: The task names the clinical stage, not an imaging property unique to the key. All imaging options have previews; no statement promises MRI availability.
steps: Identify that existing CT completed distant assessment but not the local mesorectal-plane question.
Select the modality suited to that remaining planning decision.
gate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: confusion between systemic staging, early wall-layer staging and mesorectal-plane mapping.
gate.decidingObservation: The mesorectal-fascia relationship remains unresolved in a broad rectal lesion.
gate.consequence: Treatment planned without the relevant local extent.
gate.deletionTest: Completed distant staging excludes a gratuitous repeat; unresolved fascia relation defines the need.
gate.counterfactual: Change to an otherwise staged small early lesion whose only unresolved issue is T1 versus T2: EUS becomes reasonable.
gate.sequence: First node. Feedback gives no treatment sequence for the still-unseen MRI.

nodes.title: Neoadjuvant sequence for locally advanced rectal cancer
nodes.objective: Use local stage and threatened planes to select treatment before definitive surgery.
nodes.update: The outside MRI shows tumor extending through muscle into mesorectal fat, touching the mesorectal fascia, with two irregular heterogeneous mesorectal nodes. The tumor lies below the anterior peritoneal reflection. Mismatch-repair proteins are retained. Distant staging remains negative and she is fit for combined treatment.
nodes.task: Which treatment sequence should be discussed for {patientName}'s rectal cancer?

choices.label: Total neoadjuvant therapy followed by reassessment
choices.temptation: Integrate local and systemic control before surgery
choices.rationale: The locally advanced mid-rectal findings support a neoadjuvant multimodal pathway before definitive surgical planning.
choices.reasonableWhen: Fit patient with stage II/III mid or low rectal disease.

choices.label: Total mesorectal excision followed by adjuvant therapy
choices.temptation: Treat a technically resectable tumor as ready for immediate surgery
choices.rationale: This sequence bypasses the neoadjuvant opportunity in the supplied high-risk local setting.
choices.reasonableWhen: Selected low-risk or upper-rectal disease can favor initial surgery.

choices.label: Transanal excision followed by adjuvant therapy
choices.temptation: Substitute local wall removal for a mesorectal disease strategy
choices.rationale: Local excision does not address the represented extramural and nodal disease.
choices.reasonableWhen: Selected small favorable cT1N0 lesions can be locally excised.

nodes.explanation: Interpret the extramural, nodal and fascia findings before selecting the sequence. Total neoadjuvant treatment is a supported pathway for this fit patient before definitive resection planning.

gate.cueAttack: No cT3N-positive or locally advanced label supplies the staging inference. Three options are named treatment sequences of comparable length.
steps: Infer extramural/regional disease and a threatened local surgical plane from MRI observations.
Select preoperative multimodal treatment rather than immediate or local surgery.
gate.difficulty: Moderate/hard prediction: technically resectable and colon-like surgery-first reasoning can override rectal local-control needs.
gate.decidingObservation: Extramural tumor touching fascia, irregular nodes and position below the reflection.
gate.consequence: Loss of a supported neoadjuvant local/systemic treatment opportunity.
gate.deletionTest: The MRI changes the plan; mismatch repair narrows modern treatment context without testing germline interpretation.
gate.counterfactual: Move the tumor entirely above the reflection with clear local planes and no high-risk extension: initial resection becomes a reasonable offered sequence.
gate.sequence: First explanation names staging scope, not neoadjuvant treatment. MRI findings appear only after that answer.

reviewedDraftCases.name: Samuel Price
reviewedDraftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 57-year-old man, attends clinic for review of a small outside rectal-cancer workup.

nodes.title: Clarify early rectal wall invasion
nodes.objective: Select complementary EUS when an early depth distinction changes local-excision eligibility.
nodes.update: The lesion is 2 cm across and occupies less than one quarter of the rectal circumference. Biopsy shows well-differentiated adenocarcinoma without represented vascular invasion or budding. MRI shows no suspicious nodes but cannot distinguish submucosal from muscularis-propria involvement. The lesion is accessible transanally; distant staging is negative.
nodes.task: Which examination would best clarify {patientName}'s remaining local-treatment eligibility question?

choices.label: Endorectal ultrasound of the lesion
choices.temptation: Use an early wall-layer question
choices.rationale: EUS complements MRI for the unresolved submucosa-versus-muscularis distinction relevant to local excision.
choices.reasonableWhen: Early T1-versus-T2 distinction remains consequential.

choices.label: Repeat pelvic MRI with the same protocol
choices.temptation: Repeat a completed broad study without changing the limitation
choices.rationale: No correctable acquisition error is given; the remaining problem is early layer discrimination.
choices.reasonableWhen: An inadequate or incorrectly acquired first MRI may need replacement.

choices.label: Whole-body FDG PET-CT
choices.temptation: Treat metabolic staging as wall-layer definition
choices.rationale: PET does not resolve the early wall-layer distinction needed here.
choices.reasonableWhen: A separate indeterminate systemic target could justify PET.

nodes.explanation: The remaining question is early wall depth rather than missing distant or mesorectal staging. Complementary EUS can help resolve eligibility for local treatment.

gate.cueAttack: No meets-local-excision label is supplied. Actual dimensions, morphology, biopsy and imaging limits establish why the unresolved layer matters; all tests carry estimates.
gate.stage: Three examinations before choosing local treatment.
steps: Recognize that favorable size and histology still leave a consequential depth uncertainty.
Use complementary wall-layer imaging rather than repeating the same limitation or systemic staging.
gate.difficulty: Moderate/hard prediction: normal nodes and a small lesion can lead to premature local excision, or repeat-MRI reflex.
gate.decidingObservation: MRI cannot separate submucosal from muscularis involvement in a small otherwise favorable lesion.
gate.consequence: Premature local treatment or redundant staging.
gate.deletionTest: Size, histology and access establish why local treatment is plausible; the unresolved layer changes it.
gate.counterfactual: Document motion-degraded MRI with no diagnostic pelvic acquisition: a properly repeated MRI becomes appropriate.
gate.sequence: First node; feedback does not reveal final excision pathology.

nodes.title: Completion treatment after unexpected T2 disease
nodes.objective: Use depth found after local excision to address untreated regional risk despite clear margins.
nodes.update: At a later clinic visit, the founder reviews the outside full-thickness excision. Cancer infiltrates the muscularis propria but stops before perirectal fat. All specimen edges are clear. Pelvic restaging shows no enlarged nodes or distant disease; he is fit for radical resection and has not received radiation.
nodes.task: Which next treatment plan should be discussed for {patientName}'s rectal cancer?

choices.label: Completion rectal resection with total mesorectal excision
choices.temptation: Address disease outside the scope of local excision
choices.rationale: Muscularis-propria invasion places the lesion beyond the favorable T1 local-excision group; clear wall edges do not stage mesorectal nodes.
choices.reasonableWhen: An operable patient has T2 disease after local excision.

choices.label: Repeat full-thickness transanal scar excision
choices.temptation: Use more local clearance to solve regional risk
choices.rationale: The local edges are already clear; another scar specimen does not remove the regional nodal basin.
choices.reasonableWhen: A selected local-margin problem without a need for radical regional treatment.

choices.label: Endoscopic rectal scar surveillance
choices.temptation: Treat a clear margin and negative imaging as node-negative proof
choices.rationale: Local clearance and imaging cannot settle microscopic mesorectal disease.
choices.reasonableWhen: A favorable adequately assessed T1 lesion treated completely locally.

nodes.explanation: The new pathology changes the relevant treatment scope. Clear local margins do not make a muscle-invasive rectal cancer adequately treated by local excision in a fit patient.

gate.cueAttack: No T2 label is supplied. The raw muscle boundary must be interpreted. Options compare three postexcision plans rather than information gathering against premature therapy.
steps: Infer muscularis-propria invasion from the specimen.
Address regional mesorectal risk that local excision cannot stage or treat.
gate.difficulty: Moderate/hard prediction: a clear local edge and CT-sized nodes may be mistaken for completed oncologic treatment.
gate.decidingObservation: Cancer infiltrates muscularis propria despite clear specimen edges.
gate.consequence: Inadequate regional treatment.
gate.deletionTest: Delete muscle invasion and favorable T1 surveillance may follow; the update therefore earns a new decision.
gate.counterfactual: Change to a fully assessed favorable T1 lesion with clear edges: surveillance becomes best.
gate.sequence: Prior EUS feedback identifies a staging question but gives no final-depth result or completion operation.

reviewedDraftCases.name: Clara Morgan
reviewedDraftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 62-year-old woman, attends clinic after outside neoadjuvant treatment for rectal adenocarcinoma.

nodes.title: Current multimodal rectal response assessment
nodes.objective: Reconcile the date and scope of response records before treatment decisions.
nodes.update: Treatment finished in July. September examination records a smooth flat scar without a nodule; September endoscopy shows a pale scar without ulceration. The attached rectal MRI is dated March and depicts the original tumor. September systemic staging shows no distant disease.
nodes.task: Which examination should complete {patientName}'s local post-treatment assessment?

choices.label: Current rectal-protocol pelvic MRI
choices.temptation: Reconcile chronology across modalities
choices.rationale: The attached local image is pretreatment and cannot establish current wall or nodal response.
choices.reasonableWhen: Current rectal MRI has not been performed.

choices.label: Repeat endoscopy with scar biopsy
choices.temptation: Let a visible luminal scar substitute for wall assessment
choices.rationale: Recent luminal assessment does not supply the missing post-treatment deep-wall and regional evaluation; negative biopsy would not establish eradication.
choices.reasonableWhen: A new suspicious luminal focus may need tissue assessment.

choices.label: Whole-body FDG PET-CT
choices.temptation: Repeat systemic staging to complete a local question
choices.rationale: Distant restaging is current; PET does not replace the standard local combination.
choices.reasonableWhen: A selected unresolved systemic target may justify PET.

nodes.explanation: The dates matter. Current surface and examination findings cannot convert an old MRI into a post-treatment local assessment.

gate.cueAttack: Removed hopes-to-avoid-surgery and planned-response-visit assurances. All dates are constructed chronology, not a treatment-timing recommendation. Three tests have estimates.
gate.stage: Three examinations to complete current local response assessment.
steps: Identify that the packet mixes current surface findings with a pretreatment local image.
Obtain the missing current local component instead of duplicating recent surface or systemic work.
gate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: a complete-looking transferred packet may be accepted without reading dates.
gate.decidingObservation: March local MRI predates July treatment completion.
gate.consequence: Incorrect response classification from stale imaging.
gate.deletionTest: Delete dates and the local adequacy problem cannot be solved; current systemic and luminal records delimit the remaining question.
gate.counterfactual: Make the MRI current but show a new ulcerated mucosal focus not previously sampled: targeted endoscopic assessment becomes appropriate.
gate.sequence: Standalone variant. No complete-response or watch-and-wait management is supplied.

reviewedDraftCases.name: Julia Reeves
reviewedDraftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 59-year-old woman, attends clinic while the founder reconciles a transferred rectal-cancer response packet.

nodes.title: Current multimodal rectal response assessment
nodes.objective: Reconcile the date and scope of response records before treatment decisions.
nodes.update: Examination and endoscopy after treatment show a flat smooth scar. The exported image viewer opens an older MRI. The outside acquisition log and final report document a later post-treatment rectal study with T2 and diffusion series; its images remain in the original hospital archive. The current report and surface assessments disagree about whether a small wall focus persists.
nodes.task: Which imaging plan should resolve {patientName}'s current response-record discrepancy first?

choices.label: Retrieve and review the completed post-treatment MRI
choices.temptation: Distinguish absent export from absent acquisition
choices.rationale: The appropriate current study was performed; reviewing its actual images addresses the discrepancy before repeating acquisition.
choices.reasonableWhen: A suitable completed study is retrievable but absent from the transfer.

choices.label: Repeat rectal-protocol pelvic MRI
choices.temptation: Treat a missing exported series as an unperformed study
choices.rationale: No acquisition inadequacy is yet established; the completed current images should be reviewed first.
choices.reasonableWhen: Current imaging is genuinely absent, inadequate or unavailable.

choices.label: Obtain endorectal ultrasound
choices.temptation: Replace a transfer problem with a different local modality
choices.rationale: EUS does not resolve what the documented current rectal MRI actually showed.
choices.reasonableWhen: An early primary T1-versus-T2 question may benefit from complementary EUS.

nodes.explanation: A missing exported study is different from an unperformed study. Review the documented current acquisition before deciding that a new examination is needed.

gate.cueAttack: No statement says imaging is adequate; protocol and performed acquisition are factual records. Retrieval is not keyed by a named omission alone: current report/surface discordance makes review consequential. No wait estimate is assigned to existing-record retrieval.
gate.stage: Three imaging-completion plans at the same discrepancy stage.
steps: Distinguish the old exported image from the newer performed protocol study.
Retrieve the actual current evidence before ordering duplicate or non-equivalent tests.
gate.difficulty: Moderate/hard prediction: missing-export and unperformed-acquisition errors recur in transferred oncology care.
gate.decidingObservation: A current T2/diffusion study was performed and is archived despite an older exported viewer.
gate.consequence: Redundant acquisition or a treatment decision based on the wrong study.
gate.deletionTest: The log changes repeat versus retrieval; the response disagreement supplies a reason images matter rather than administrative trivia.
gate.counterfactual: Remove the later acquisition from the log and confirm only pretreatment imaging exists: repeat current rectal MRI becomes best.
gate.sequence: Standalone; no treatment plan or eventual image interpretation is exposed.

reviewedDraftCases.name: Amelia Grant
reviewedDraftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 57-year-old woman, attends clinic after outside neoadjuvant treatment for a previously node-positive low rectal adenocarcinoma.

nodes.title: Select a rectal organ-preservation pathway
nodes.objective: Distinguish adequate clinical response from persistent tumor before offering watch-and-wait.
nodes.update: Treatment ended in July. In September, a firm mural nodule was palpable beneath intact mucosa; on a later October assessment it was larger. MRI shows a corresponding intermediate-T2 focus with diffusion restriction. Superficial biopsies contain scar and inflammation. Distant restaging is negative. She is fit for resection and remains interested in organ preservation.
nodes.task: Which treatment plan best fits {patientName}'s current rectal findings?

choices.label: Oncologic rectal resection with total mesorectal excision
choices.temptation: Do not equate negative surface biopsy with wall eradication
choices.rationale: Progressive concordant mural abnormalities are not a complete response; regional oncologic resection assessment is supported.
choices.reasonableWhen: Persistent rectal tumor is present in an operable patient.

choices.label: Full-thickness transanal excision of the treated site
choices.temptation: Use a local specimen to avoid regional treatment
choices.rationale: The prior regional disease and persistent mural findings do not establish a favorable local-only treatment group.
choices.reasonableWhen: Selected small favorable early tumors may be treated locally.

choices.label: Protocolized watch-and-wait surveillance
choices.temptation: Let preference and superficial histology overrule the response record
choices.rationale: Interest in organ preservation does not convert progressive palpable/MRI disease into a complete clinical response.
choices.reasonableWhen: Concordant clinical complete response after informed counseling in an experienced program.

nodes.explanation: The biopsy describes the surface specimen. Progressive concordant mural findings defeat a complete-response conclusion despite that negative sample and her organ-preservation goal.

gate.cueAttack: No residual-tumor or incomplete-response label is supplied. The organ-preservation preference cannot select the key and is deliberately overruled by actual progression. No fixed timing threshold is taught.
steps: Reconcile superficial negative tissue with an enlarging palpable and diffusion-restricting wall focus.
Decline the complete-response watch-and-wait pathway and address persistent oncologic disease.
gate.difficulty: Hard prediction: false-negative biopsy reassurance and preference anchoring compete with progression.
gate.decidingObservation: The palpable nodule enlarges and corresponds to a persistent restricting wall focus.
gate.consequence: Observation of persistent tumor rather than timely oncologic treatment.
gate.deletionTest: Without progression the owner-held near-complete boundary could recur; it is deliberately excluded. Surface provenance explains the negative biopsy.
gate.counterfactual: Replace the mural findings with concordant smooth flat scar, no restricting focus and no suspicious nodes: informed protocolized watch-and-wait becomes a supported option.
gate.sequence: Standalone. This is not the held shrinking equivocal ulcer at eight weeks; that version and clinical question remain held.

reviewedDraftCases.name: Robert Hayes
reviewedDraftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 65-year-old man, attends clinic while the founder reviews outside surveillance after a prior clinical complete response managed by watch-and-wait.

nodes.title: Salvage assessment after rectal regrowth
nodes.objective: Use proven localized regrowth and depth to plan salvage rather than continue the old response pathway.
nodes.update: New endoscopy shows a nodule at the treated site; biopsy contains adenocarcinoma. MRI shows growth through the muscularis propria, with an achievable surgical plane. Chest and abdominal staging show no distant disease. He is fit for surgery after prior completed neoadjuvant therapy.
nodes.task: Which treatment plan should now be discussed for {patientName}'s rectal lesion?

choices.label: Salvage rectal resection with total mesorectal excision
choices.temptation: Update the plan from current proven disease
choices.rationale: Localized operable regrowth with deep-wall involvement warrants oncologic salvage assessment.
choices.reasonableWhen: Resectable regrowth is established after watch-and-wait.

choices.label: Transanal full-thickness nodule excision
choices.temptation: Treat all small-looking luminal regrowth as local-only disease
choices.rationale: The MRI demonstrates depth beyond a favorable early local-excision group.
choices.reasonableWhen: Selected superficial favorable local lesions may permit a local approach.

choices.label: Continue protocolized watch-and-wait surveillance
choices.temptation: Carry the old complete-response conclusion forward
choices.rationale: Biopsy-proven regrowth is not continued clinical complete response.
choices.reasonableWhen: Current evaluation still demonstrates complete response without suspicious recurrence.

nodes.explanation: A prior complete response is historical evidence, not permanent clearance. Proven localized regrowth changes the treatment objective to salvage.

gate.cueAttack: Known biopsy diagnosis is legitimate because the task is treatment. Raw depth and completed staging distinguish salvage scope; no invented recurrence probability appears.
gate.stage: Three treatment plans for current localized regrowth.
steps: Recognize that current pathology overrides the older complete response.
Use depth and negative distant staging to choose regional oncologic salvage assessment.
gate.difficulty: Moderate/hard prediction: prior organ-preservation success and a small luminal nodule can favor insufficient local treatment.
gate.decidingObservation: Biopsy-proven regrowth extends through muscularis propria without distant disease.
gate.consequence: Delayed or inadequate salvage treatment.
gate.deletionTest: Without depth, local salvage possibilities compete; without distant staging, the curative local plan is less secure.
gate.counterfactual: Replace current nodule/biopsy/MRI findings with unchanged complete-response assessments: continued protocol surveillance becomes appropriate.
gate.sequence: Independent case; no earlier newly authored explanation supplies salvage selection.

reviewedDraftCases.name: Diane Foster
reviewedDraftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 63-year-old woman, attends clinic after outside rectal-cancer staging.

nodes.title: Upper-rectal treatment sequence
nodes.objective: Use patient-specific peritoneal-reflection anatomy rather than a fixed endoscopic distance to select sequence.
nodes.update: MRI places the entire tumor above the anterior peritoneal reflection. It extends slightly beyond muscle with a clear surrounding surgical plane, no involved adjacent organ, no suspicious nodes and no extramural vascular invasion. Distant staging is negative, mismatch-repair proteins are retained and she is fit for resection.
nodes.task: Which treatment sequence is most appropriate to discuss for {patientName}'s represented disease?

choices.label: Initial oncologic resection followed by pathology-directed therapy
choices.temptation: Use anatomy and local-risk features together
choices.rationale: The entirely upper-rectal location without the supplied high-risk exceptions supports initial resection rather than routine pelvic radiation.
choices.reasonableWhen: Upper-rectal tumor with clear local planes and no modifying high-risk feature.

choices.label: Total neoadjuvant therapy followed by rectal resection
choices.temptation: Apply a mid/low rectal pathway to every rectal label
choices.rationale: The anatomic relationship and risk record do not establish routine benefit from that sequence here.
choices.reasonableWhen: Stage II/III mid or low rectal disease, especially threatened planes.

choices.label: Transanal local excision followed by surveillance
choices.temptation: Treat absence of suspicious nodes as an early local lesion
choices.rationale: The extramuscular extension excludes favorable T1 local treatment.
choices.reasonableWhen: A small favorable cT1N0 tumor accessible transanally.

nodes.explanation: The anterior peritoneal reflection is patient-specific anatomy. This upper-rectal record supports initial resection; the recommendation is conditional and does not generalize to threatened fascia or adjacent-organ invasion.

gate.cueAttack: No upper-rectal diagnosis or surgery-first phrase supplies the interpretation. Necessary local-risk negatives remain because they delimit the conditional recommendation.
steps: Interpret the tumor relative to the anterior peritoneal reflection and identify the absence of modifying local risks.
Apply the upper-rectal rather than mid/low multimodal pathway.
gate.difficulty: Hard prediction: a generic rectal-cancer label may trigger automatic neoadjuvant radiation despite the anatomy.
gate.decidingObservation: Entire tumor above the reflection with clear planes and no high-risk extension.
gate.consequence: Unnecessary treatment or inappropriate generalization of surgery-first to high-risk disease.
gate.deletionTest: Anatomy changes the pathway; the listed risk observations prevent an unsupported universal rule.
gate.counterfactual: Move the tumor below the reflection and add threatened mesorectal fascia: total neoadjuvant therapy becomes best.
gate.sequence: Standalone; this does not reuse the earlier high-risk case or teach the answer before its decision.

reviewedDraftCases.name: Felix Turner
reviewedDraftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 68-year-old man, attends clinic after an outside diagnostic laparoscopy was stopped to arrange colorectal and urologic surgery.

nodes.title: En-bloc planning for an adherent colon tumor
nodes.objective: Preserve the tumor interface when planning curative resection of a colon cancer adherent to bladder.
nodes.update: Biopsy confirms sigmoid adenocarcinoma. Distant staging is negative. The operative record describes a short firm attachment between tumor and bladder dome, with otherwise separable planes and no peritoneal deposits. He is fit for curative surgery; the attachment was not divided.
nodes.task: Which operative plan should be discussed for {patientName}'s represented anatomy?

choices.label: Sigmoid colectomy with en-bloc involved bladder-dome resection
choices.temptation: Preserve a potentially involved tumor interface
choices.rationale: An adherent interface may contain cancer; en-bloc margin-negative resection avoids separating through it.
choices.reasonableWhen: Resectable colon cancer adheres to an adjacent organ and curative resection is intended.

choices.label: Sigmoid colectomy after separating the bladder attachment
choices.temptation: Assume adhesion is inflammatory until proven otherwise
choices.rationale: Peeling the attachment risks violating a malignant interface.
choices.reasonableWhen: A clearly separate non-tumor plane between organs does not require adjacent-organ resection.

choices.label: Sigmoid colectomy after sampling and dividing the attachment
choices.temptation: Use a small interface sample to authorize separation
choices.rationale: A sampled negative cannot make division of an adherent tumor interface oncologically equivalent to en-bloc removal.
choices.reasonableWhen: A separate suspicious lesion outside the intended curative interface may require diagnostic sampling.

nodes.explanation: Adherence is not pathological proof of bladder invasion, but curative operative planning must preserve the potentially involved interface. The exact bladder extent depends on anatomy.

gate.cueAttack: No T4b diagnosis is supplied. The attachment is an operative observation, not permission to select a named procedure. Three complete operative strategies compare treatment of the same interface.
steps: Recognize that a firm tumor attachment cannot safely be classified as benign by appearance or a small sample.
Plan en-bloc clearance rather than divide a potentially malignant plane.
gate.difficulty: Moderate/hard prediction: tissue-preserving peeling or frozen-section reassurance may tempt an otherwise prepared surgeon.
gate.decidingObservation: Firm tumor-to-bladder attachment with curative resectability and no divided plane.
gate.consequence: Tumor violation or compromised local margins.
gate.deletionTest: Curative intent and attachment determine the plan; no deposits and operative fitness delimit the setting.
gate.counterfactual: Replace the attachment with a documented intact freely separable plane: standard colectomy with bladder preservation becomes reasonable.
gate.sequence: Retrospective clinic planning after stopped outside laparoscopy; no operation occurs in this clinic.

reviewedDraftCases.name: Irene Wells
reviewedDraftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 67-year-old woman, attends clinic after an outside sigmoid colectomy.

nodes.title: Reassess a low node yield
nodes.objective: Distinguish negative sampled nodes from an adequate pathologic regional assessment.
nodes.update: The tumor extends through muscularis propria into pericolic fat; margins are clear. The report lists five negative lymph nodes. Preoperative chest and abdominal/pelvic staging showed no metastases. The remaining mesenteric specimen is retained by pathology.
nodes.task: Which investigation should next improve {patientName}'s postoperative regional-stage assessment?

choices.label: Additional node retrieval from the retained specimen
choices.temptation: Separate observed negatives from staging adequacy
choices.rationale: Request further pathology processing when fewer than 12 nodes were reported before relying on the node-negative assessment.
choices.reasonableWhen: An available colon-resection specimen has an inadequate reported node count.

choices.label: Postoperative FDG PET-CT of regional nodal basins
choices.temptation: Use imaging to replace microscopic staging
choices.rationale: Negative imaging cannot supply the additional regional pathology needed from the submitted specimen.
choices.reasonableWhen: A selected unresolved systemic or recurrent focus can warrant PET review.

choices.label: Pelvic MRI of the remaining mesentery
choices.temptation: Translate rectal local staging into colon specimen staging
choices.rationale: Imaging the remaining pelvis does not improve the sampled microscopic assessment of the removed regional tissue.
choices.reasonableWhen: A rectal primary may need mesorectal-plane assessment.

nodes.explanation: Five observed negative nodes do not provide the same confidence as an adequately examined regional specimen. Request further retrieval from the retained material.

gate.cueAttack: The stem does not say inadequate staging or name the missing action. Three specific investigations have timing metadata. The retained specimen is relevant provenance, not convenience permission.
gate.stage: Three investigations aimed at postoperative regional assessment.
steps: Interpret the low count separately from the negative findings and prior CT.
Use available resection tissue rather than substitute another image for microscopic regional assessment.
