gate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: all nodes negative plus negative CT can falsely settle regional status.
gate.decidingObservation: Only five nodes were examined and mesenteric tissue remains available.
gate.consequence: Understaging and an inadequately informed postoperative plan.
gate.deletionTest: Count creates inadequacy; availability identifies the useful existing specimen rather than an invented reoperation.
gate.counterfactual: Change the record to an adequate node assessment but a newly indeterminate extra-regional focus: a targeted imaging pathway could become appropriate.
gate.sequence: First node; feedback does not reveal what additional pathology will show.

nodes.title: Postoperative planning with a tumor deposit
nodes.objective: Recognize regional disease from a confirmed tumor deposit despite negative recovered nodes.
nodes.update: Additional pathology finds a total of 15 negative nodes. A separate pericolic nodule contains discontinuous adenocarcinoma; the pathologist confirms a tumor deposit rather than residual lymph-node, vessel or nerve tissue. Margins remain clear, distant staging is negative, mismatch-repair proteins are retained and she has recovered sufficiently for adjuvant treatment assessment.
nodes.task: Which postoperative plan should be discussed for {patientName}'s updated pathology?

choices.label: Adjuvant FOLFOX planning with medical oncology
choices.temptation: Classify the regional deposit before selecting intent
choices.rationale: A confirmed pericolic deposit can establish regional N1c disease despite negative nodes, supporting adjuvant systemic treatment assessment.
choices.reasonableWhen: Completely resected nonmetastatic colon cancer has regional disease.

choices.label: Surveillance after node-negative colectomy
choices.temptation: Count negative nodes and ignore the separate deposit
choices.rationale: The adequate negative-node count does not erase deposit-defined regional involvement.
choices.reasonableWhen: A completely resected lower-risk node-negative tumor may enter surveillance.

choices.label: Adjuvant pelvic chemoradiation planning
choices.temptation: Apply a rectal local-control pathway to a colon deposit
choices.rationale: This is a sigmoid-colon regional pathology problem, not an indication for routine pelvic radiation.
choices.reasonableWhen: Selected rectal-cancer local-control pathways can include pelvic chemoradiation.

nodes.explanation: A confirmed tumor deposit is not canceled by an adequate set of negative nodes. Interpret it as regional disease before discussing adjuvant systemic treatment; regimen details remain individualized.

gate.cueAttack: No stage III label appears. The pathologist-confirmed tissue category is legitimate data because treatment is scored; no invented nodule classification is inferred by the author. Options are postoperative treatment strategies.
steps: Interpret a discontinuous confirmed pericolic deposit despite negative nodes.
Apply the regional-disease treatment pathway rather than a node-count-only conclusion.
gate.difficulty: Hard prediction: an adequate negative-node count can distract from N1c disease.
gate.decidingObservation: Confirmed discontinuous pericolic tumor deposit with no distant disease.
gate.consequence: Omission of an indicated adjuvant treatment discussion.
gate.deletionTest: The deposit changes treatment; without it the new adequate node-negative report could support surveillance depending on other risks.
gate.counterfactual: Remove the deposit and all high-risk features from an adequately staged completely resected tumor: surveillance becomes a reasonable offered plan.
gate.sequence: Earlier feedback requests an adequate node search but does not state deposit classification or adjuvant therapy.

reviewedDraftCases.name: Martin Shaw
reviewedDraftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 70-year-old man, attends clinic while the founder reviews outside multidisciplinary records for sigmoid adenocarcinoma with metastases.

nodes.title: Initial treatment of an asymptomatic metastatic primary
nodes.objective: Distinguish symptom control from prophylactic primary resection when distant disease is not curatively resectable.
nodes.update: The outside team documents diffuse bilobar liver and pulmonary metastases not amenable to curative local treatment. The sigmoid lumen remains patent. He is eating and passing stool without bleeding, pain or transfusion need, and is fit for systemic treatment.
nodes.task: Which initial treatment strategy best fits {patientName}'s current record?

choices.label: Medical-oncology systemic treatment planning
choices.temptation: Let metastatic disease determine initial treatment
choices.rationale: An asymptomatic primary with incurable metastatic disease generally favors systemic treatment rather than prophylactic colectomy.
choices.reasonableWhen: Incurable metastatic disease with no primary-related complication.

choices.label: Oncologic sigmoid colectomy before systemic treatment
choices.temptation: Prevent a hypothetical primary complication with immediate surgery
choices.rationale: No current primary symptom establishes a reason to delay systemic treatment for prophylactic resection.
choices.reasonableWhen: A primary-related complication or a curative multimodality strategy can change sequencing.

choices.label: Endoscopic sigmoid stent placement before systemic treatment
choices.temptation: Treat the presence of a luminal tumor as obstruction
choices.rationale: The lumen is patent and there is no obstructive syndrome to palliate.
choices.reasonableWhen: Malignant obstruction without perforation may warrant stenting in a suitable pathway.

nodes.explanation: The primary is not currently causing a complication. Systemic treatment addresses the dominant unresectable disease; prophylactic colectomy or stenting is not established by the diagnosis alone.

gate.cueAttack: No asymptomatic-primary label substitutes for the symptom and patency record. All choices are specific initial strategies. Metastatic unresectability is an outside multidisciplinary conclusion, not a guessed image interpretation.
steps: Recognize incurable distant distribution without a current primary-related complication.
Prioritize systemic treatment instead of prophylactic local intervention.
gate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: resect-the-primary-first is a credible surgical default even when no curative or symptom-control benefit is established.
gate.decidingObservation: Patent lumen, no primary symptoms and incurable metastatic disease.
gate.consequence: Delay or morbidity from unnecessary prophylactic intervention.
gate.deletionTest: Metastatic resectability and symptom status both change the sequence; no irrelevant performance numbers are supplied.
gate.counterfactual: Add a perforation through the primary: local surgical source-control assessment becomes necessary before ordinary systemic sequencing.
gate.sequence: First node; explanation does not describe a later complication.

nodes.title: Source control for a perforated primary
nodes.objective: Use a new outside-hospital complication to revise a previously appropriate systemic-first strategy.
nodes.update: At a later clinic chart-review visit, the founder reviews an intervening outside admission. CT showed free gas and fluid arising from the sigmoid tumor; examination documented diffuse peritoneal tenderness. The hospital team has begun resuscitation and antibiotics and is arranging definitive source control. These events occurred at that hospital, not in the clinic.
nodes.task: Which definitive local plan best fits {patientName}'s outside admission findings?

choices.label: Oncologic tumor resection with a staged reconstruction plan
choices.temptation: Let actual perforation change the immediate objective
choices.rationale: Perforated cancer with peritonitis needs surgical source-control planning; staging of reconstruction depends on physiology and contamination.
choices.reasonableWhen: A perforated colon primary needs operative source control.

choices.label: Endoluminal stenting across the sigmoid tumor
choices.temptation: Carry an obstruction-palliation option into perforation
choices.rationale: Perforation contraindicates endoluminal stenting.
choices.reasonableWhen: An obstructed but nonperforated primary may be considered for stent decompression.

choices.label: Systemic treatment after the initial antibiotic course
choices.temptation: Carry forward the earlier systemic-first strategy
choices.rationale: The former no-complication premise no longer applies; antibiotics do not replace source-control assessment in this record.
choices.reasonableWhen: An asymptomatic incurable primary without perforation or another local complication.

nodes.explanation: The earlier strategy was appropriate to an uncomplicated primary. A new perforation changes the current objective to source control; the clinic reviews the hospital plan rather than delivering emergency surgery.

gate.cueAttack: All options are definitive local/systemic strategies after common resuscitation, rather than resuscitation competing with treatment. Hospital acuity is separate from the stable clinic review.
gate.stage: Three definitive strategies after initial hospital stabilization.
steps: Interpret extraluminal gas/fluid at the primary with peritonitis as perforation.
Override the old asymptomatic-primary pathway and avoid a stent in a perforated setting.
gate.difficulty: Moderate/hard prediction: previously correct systemic-first or obstruction-palliation reasoning can be applied after its premise changes.
gate.decidingObservation: Free gas/fluid from the tumor plus diffuse peritoneal tenderness.
gate.consequence: Failure of source control or inappropriate stenting.
gate.deletionTest: Removing the new findings restores the earlier systemic strategy; this update earns a distinct consequential decision.
gate.counterfactual: Replace free gas/peritonitis with obstruction without perforation: stent palliation becomes a reasonable option after specialist assessment.
gate.sequence: Prior feedback concerns an uncomplicated primary only. The hospital records are a later reveal; no in-clinic admission or emergency execution is implied.

reviewedDraftCases.name: Nora Ellis
reviewedDraftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 56-year-old woman, attends clinic to reconcile outside polypectomy records.

nodes.title: Surveillance after serrated dysplasia
nodes.objective: Use the correct specimen, dysplasia and complete-resection record to select USMSTF surveillance.
nodes.update: The examination was complete and adequately prepared. Container A from a 4-mm sigmoid lesion contains a hyperplastic polyp. Container B from a 9-mm ascending-colon lesion contains a sessile serrated lesion with focal dysplasia. Both were removed intact with complete excision documented. She has no prior colorectal neoplasia, relevant family history or hereditary syndrome.
nodes.task: Under USMSTF guidance, when should {patientName}'s next surveillance colonoscopy be planned?

choices.label: Colonoscopy in three years
choices.temptation: Use the dysplastic serrated specimen rather than the small distal polyp
choices.rationale: Dysplasia changes the surveillance category despite the proximal lesion being smaller than 10 mm.
choices.reasonableWhen: A sessile serrated lesion with dysplasia has been confidently completely removed.

choices.label: Colonoscopy in five to ten years
choices.temptation: Use the interval for a small nondysplastic serrated lesion
choices.rationale: That interval does not incorporate the focal dysplasia in the actual specimen.
choices.reasonableWhen: One or two small sessile serrated lesions without dysplasia after complete high-quality resection.

choices.label: Colonoscopy in six months
choices.temptation: Treat any dysplasia as large-piecemeal residual risk
choices.rationale: The lesions were small and removed intact, not a large piecemeal resection.
choices.reasonableWhen: A lesion at least 20 mm was removed piecemeal.

nodes.explanation: Map each specimen to the correct lesion and integrate dysplasia rather than size alone. The completely removed dysplastic serrated lesion supports the three-year USMSTF interval.

gate.cueAttack: All choices are colonoscopy intervals. The small distal benign specimen creates a provenance error; focal dysplasia is legitimate management data rather than a supplied surveillance conclusion.
steps: Identify the proximal dysplastic serrated lesion as the consequential finding instead of the distal hyperplastic sample.
Use histology and removal completeness to select surveillance rather than size-only or piecemeal rules.
gate.difficulty: Moderate/hard prediction: small size or the first container label may overshadow focal serrated dysplasia.
gate.decidingObservation: Focal dysplasia in the intact 9-mm ascending-colon serrated lesion.
gate.consequence: Delayed surveillance or unnecessary early scar checking.
gate.deletionTest: Both specimen location and dysplasia matter; complete removal excludes an unresolved resection problem.
gate.counterfactual: Remove dysplasia from the single small serrated lesion: five-to-ten-year surveillance becomes the appropriate offered interval.
gate.sequence: Standalone; no prior surveillance explanation supplies the category.

reviewedDraftCases.name: George Sutton
reviewedDraftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 68-year-old man, attends clinic with records from two outside colonoscopies.

nodes.title: Integrate baseline and first surveillance
nodes.objective: Choose USMSTF second-surveillance timing from both the baseline adenoma and the first follow-up.
nodes.update: At baseline, a 14-mm tubular adenoma was completely removed in one piece during a high-quality examination. The first surveillance colonoscopy was also complete and adequately prepared and found no adenoma or serrated lesion. He has no prior cancer, hereditary syndrome or relevant family history.
nodes.task: Under USMSTF guidance, when should {patientName}'s next colonoscopy be planned after this normal first surveillance examination?

choices.label: Colonoscopy in five years
choices.temptation: Combine the baseline and first-surveillance findings
choices.rationale: A normal first surveillance examination after an advanced baseline adenoma supports a five-year next interval.
choices.reasonableWhen: Advanced adenoma at baseline followed by a normal high-quality first surveillance.

choices.label: Colonoscopy in three years
choices.temptation: Repeat the baseline advanced-adenoma interval unchanged
choices.rationale: The normal first surveillance modifies the next interval.
choices.reasonableWhen: Advanced adenoma or another corresponding higher-risk finding persists at first surveillance.

choices.label: Colonoscopy in ten years
choices.temptation: Erase baseline risk after one normal follow-up
choices.rationale: The advanced baseline finding continues to matter when selecting the next interval.
choices.reasonableWhen: A low-risk baseline followed by normal first surveillance can support a longer interval.

nodes.explanation: Second-surveillance planning uses two examinations. A normal first follow-up modifies, but does not erase, the advanced baseline adenoma history.

gate.cueAttack: Neither title nor complaint calls the baseline advanced. All options use identical investigation grammar; the stem asks a specific surveillance stage.
steps: Classify the size-defined baseline adenoma and the quality/normal result of first surveillance.
Apply the serial rather than baseline-only or latest-exam-only recommendation.
gate.difficulty: Hard prediction: each single-examination shortcut points to a different credible wrong interval.
gate.decidingObservation: A 14-mm baseline adenoma followed by normal high-quality first surveillance.
gate.consequence: Over- or under-surveillance from ignoring one examination.
gate.deletionTest: Delete either examination and the five-year serial recommendation is no longer established; no ornamental chronology is added.
gate.counterfactual: Replace the first surveillance result with a new advanced adenoma: three years becomes the appropriate offered interval.
gate.sequence: Standalone; this is not merely another surface variant of the first-surveillance rule.

reviewedDraftCases.name: Joan Miller
reviewedDraftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 63-year-old woman, attends clinic to reconcile an outside colonoscopy report and pathology fragment count.

nodes.title: Count adenomas by lesions rather than fragments
nodes.objective: Use the actual number of removed lesions and the assessed histology to select surveillance.
nodes.update: The complete, adequately prepared procedure log records two polyps, 6 mm and 8 mm, each removed completely and placed together in one container. The laboratory describes four tissue fragments of tubular adenoma without advanced features. No other lesions, previous neoplasia, hereditary syndrome or relevant family history are recorded.
nodes.task: Under USMSTF guidance, when should {patientName}'s surveillance colonoscopy be planned?

choices.label: Colonoscopy in seven to ten years
choices.temptation: Reconcile the procedure count with specimen fragmentation
choices.rationale: Two small completely removed nonadvanced adenomas remain two lesions despite four laboratory fragments.
choices.reasonableWhen: One or two small nonadvanced tubular adenomas at a high-quality baseline.

choices.label: Colonoscopy in three to five years
choices.temptation: Count tissue fragments as separate adenomas
choices.rationale: The procedure documented two lesions; four fragments do not establish four adenomas.
choices.reasonableWhen: Three or four small tubular adenomas were actually removed.

choices.label: Colonoscopy in three years
choices.temptation: Treat any multiple-fragment adenoma jar as high-burden disease
choices.rationale: Neither five-to-ten actual adenomas nor an advanced feature is established.
choices.reasonableWhen: Five to ten small adenomas or an advanced adenoma is found.

nodes.explanation: Use lesion-level procedural provenance rather than fragment count. The two small nonadvanced adenomas support the USMSTF seven-to-ten-year interval.

gate.cueAttack: No low-risk-count label is supplied. Procedure sites and laboratory fragments must be reconciled. Three parallel interval options carry identical colonoscopy preview scope.
steps: Infer that four fragments from one jar do not establish four removed lesions.
Apply the actual two-lesion count and nonadvanced histology to the surveillance interval.
gate.difficulty: Hard prediction: fragment counting produces a specifically plausible three-to-five-year error.
gate.decidingObservation: Two documented lesions versus four fragments in the shared pathology container.
gate.consequence: Unnecessary surveillance from a falsely inflated adenoma count.
gate.deletionTest: Without the procedure count the jar cannot establish lesion number; size and histology keep the low-count rule applicable.
gate.counterfactual: Replace the procedure log with four separate completely removed small adenomas: three-to-five years becomes best.
gate.sequence: Standalone; this is a provenance-to-management decision, not a cosmetic size variant.

reviewedDraftCases.name: Vincent Reed
reviewedDraftCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 60-year-old man, attends clinic after outside neoadjuvant rectal-cancer treatment.

nodes.title: Current multimodal rectal response assessment
nodes.objective: Reconcile the date and scope of response records before treatment decisions.
nodes.update: Current examination and endoscopy describe a smooth flat scar without a nodule. T2 MRI images show a dark scar, but the post-treatment diffusion series is distorted at the tumor bed by artifact and is reported as nondiagnostic there. The transferred summary labels the overall response complete. No diagnostic diffusion series exists in the archive and distant restaging is negative.
nodes.task: Which local imaging plan should resolve {patientName}'s remaining response-assessment limitation?

choices.label: Repeat rectal MRI with diagnostic T2 and diffusion acquisition
choices.temptation: Separate a reassuring component from an incomplete protocol
choices.rationale: The current diffusion component cannot assess the treated bed; repeat an adequate local protocol before relying on the summary.
choices.reasonableWhen: A necessary current MRI component is genuinely nondiagnostic and cannot be retrieved.

choices.label: Retrieve the archived diffusion series for review
choices.temptation: Treat all transfer limitations as missing exports
choices.rationale: The archive has no diagnostic diffusion acquisition; retrieval cannot improve a series that was nondiagnostic when performed.
choices.reasonableWhen: A suitable performed study exists but was not exported.

choices.label: Obtain whole-body FDG PET-CT for response assessment
choices.temptation: Replace a deficient local protocol with metabolic imaging
choices.rationale: PET does not supply the standard local combination or repair the artifact-limited MRI component.
choices.reasonableWhen: A separate unresolved systemic target may justify PET.

nodes.explanation: A complete-response summary does not override an artifact-limited acquisition. Distinguish missing exports from genuinely nondiagnostic imaging before choosing retrieval or repeat acquisition.

gate.cueAttack: The report uses the actual artifact and diagnostic-scope observations rather than an author-authored eligibility label. The complete-response summary is a competing conclusion, not the answer. Test previews cover repeat MRI and PET; record retrieval is not a new test.
steps: Determine that a dark T2 scar does not establish the missing diffusion observation and that this is an acquisition limitation.
Repeat a diagnostic local protocol instead of retrieving nonexistent adequate images or substituting systemic imaging.
gate.difficulty: Hard prediction: a reassuring summary or a learned retrieve-before-repeat rule can override actual acquisition quality.
gate.decidingObservation: The diffusion series is nondiagnostic at the tumor bed and no adequate acquired series exists.
gate.consequence: Incorrect response classification or futile retrieval.
gate.deletionTest: The actual acquisition limitation distinguishes this from the earlier missing-export variant; T2 and surface findings create real reassurance.
gate.counterfactual: Change the log to a diagnostic completed diffusion series omitted from the transfer: retrieving it becomes best.
gate.sequence: Separate variant of the stable multimodal-response concept. It is not paired with the missing-export variant, so that feedback cannot dictate this choice.

choices.reasonableWhen: A size-defined advanced adenoma was completely removed en bloc.

choices.label: Colonoscopy in one year
choices.temptation: Apply a later large-piecemeal surveillance visit as the first visit.
choices.rationale: The one-year subsequent interval follows the initial six-month surveillance; this patient has not had that first check.
choices.reasonableWhen: The first surveillance after the large piecemeal resection has already been completed.

nodes.explanation: One container is not one resection. The procedure shows piecemeal removal, and the assessed edge of one fragment cannot establish the whole lesion's perimeter. The first large-piecemeal surveillance visit is about six months after resection.

gate.cueAttack: Removed the supplied margin-management conclusion and the remote ten-year option. Procedure captures, container count and fragment-edge wording must now be reconciled; all three options are plausible surveillance intervals.
gate.stage: Three first-surveillance colonoscopy intervals after removal.
steps: Infer the actual piecemeal method from four overlapping captures despite the single aggregate and fragment-edge report.
Apply the early large-piecemeal scar interval instead of routine advanced-adenoma or subsequent-surveillance timing.
gate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: a reassuring pathology label or single-container heuristic points to a different interval. The author does not claim the timing rule itself is hard.
gate.decidingObservation: Four overlapping endoscopic captures, not the number of containers or the margin of one fragment.
gate.consequence: Delay in detecting residual adenoma at a large piecemeal resection site.
gate.deletionTest: The procedure and laboratory observations are both required to resolve the apparent completeness; size establishes the relevant piecemeal threshold. The rest-of-colon quality excludes a separate completion problem.
gate.counterfactual: If the 28-mm adenoma had instead been removed in one intact oriented specimen with all margins assessed clear, the offered three-year interval would become appropriate.
gate.sequence: Standalone; no earlier resection explanation identifies the method or surveillance pathway.

revisedCases.name: Susan Mercer
revisedCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 55-year-old woman, attends clinic after removal of an ascending-colon lesion.

nodes.title: Complete favorable invasive-polyp excision
nodes.objective: Integrate specimen adequacy, depth and adverse-feature assessment before colectomy.
nodes.update: The nonpedunculated ascending-colon lesion was removed completely and retrieved in one oriented piece. Moderately differentiated glands extend 0.6 mm into submucosa; the invasive front is 2 mm from the deep cut edge. Both lateral mucosal edges were identified histologically and are free of adenoma and carcinoma. No lymphovascular or perineural invasion is found; budding is low. No lesion remained endoscopically.
nodes.task: Which lesion-directed plan should be discussed for {patientName}'s resected ascending-colon lesion?

choices.label: Colonoscopic surveillance of the excision site
choices.temptation: Use the complete specimen rather than the cancer label
choices.rationale: The intact assessment and favorable features support endoscopic treatment with surveillance.
choices.reasonableWhen: A fully assessed invasive polyp has favorable features and clear edges.

choices.label: Endoscopic full-thickness scar excision
choices.temptation: Treat all submucosal cancer as local residual
choices.rationale: No outstanding local margin question is established.
choices.reasonableWhen: A specialist-defined unresolved local-clearance problem.

choices.label: Oncologic ascending-colon resection
choices.temptation: Treat invasion as automatic colectomy
choices.rationale: No adverse feature puts this fully assessed lesion in the regional resection group.
choices.reasonableWhen: Adverse histology or an involved invasive margin.

nodes.explanation: Assess the whole intact specimen, including lateral and deep clearance, depth, grade, vascular/neural invasion and budding. These findings support a favorable fully excised submucosally invasive lesion for which endoscopic treatment with surveillance can be discussed; a visually clear scar alone would not establish that conclusion.

gate.cueAttack: Added explicit nonpedunculated morphology, complete excision and histologically assessed clear lateral margins. No visual-to-histologic margin substitution remains. Retained the concrete surveillance, local scar excision and regional resection alternatives.
steps: Integrate depth and adverse-feature observations with complete deep and lateral histologic clearance.
Choose surveillance rather than another local excision or regional oncologic resection in this fully assessed favorable specimen.
gate.difficulty: Fair moderate: the independent review found the intended favorable-risk reasoning reasonable once lateral clearance and morphology were supplied. No extra difficulty is manufactured.
gate.decidingObservation: An intact nonpedunculated specimen with clear assessed deep and lateral margins, superficial submucosal depth, low budding and no lymphovascular invasion.
gate.consequence: Unnecessary colectomy or reverse undertreatment of adverse disease.
gate.deletionTest: Every pathology feature establishes a relevant favorable-risk or completeness criterion. Visual clearance is corroborative and does not substitute for the added histologic lateral assessment.
gate.counterfactual: If lymphovascular invasion were identified while all margins remained clear, regional oncologic resection would become the best offered lesion-directed plan for a surgically suitable patient.
gate.sequence: Standalone. No preserved PASS malignant-polyp variant is edited or used as teaching feedback.

revisedCases.name: Elaine Porter
revisedCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 66-year-old woman, attends clinic after partial cecal-polyp removal at an outside center.

nodes.title: Advanced resection before colectomy
nodes.objective: Choose expert endoscopic assessment for a large lesion without demonstrated deep invasion.
nodes.update: The original 26-mm lesion had a uniform granular surface. Cautery removed one part; carbon tattoo was injected beneath the remainder. On repeat inspection, residual tissue fails to lift at that site. Removed tissue contains adenoma. No ulcerated or depressed focus is described.
nodes.task: Which referral should guide {patientName}'s next treatment plan?

choices.label: Advanced-endoscopy referral for completion-resection planning
choices.temptation: Recognize a treatment-related confounder of the lift sign.
choices.rationale: Prior cautery and tattoo beneath the residual lesion can produce fibrosis. Expert completion planning is warranted; nonlifting alone does not prove deep invasion.
choices.reasonableWhen: A scarred residual lesion without documented deep invasive features requires advanced assessment.

choices.label: Colorectal-surgery referral for oncologic resection planning
choices.temptation: Treat the nonlifting sign as sufficient proof of invasive cancer.
choices.rationale: This lift test was performed after interventions that can scar the submucosa; the original granular morphology and lack of an invasive focus matter.
choices.reasonableWhen: Optical deep invasion or expert assessment establishes a lesion unsuitable for curative endoscopic treatment.

choices.label: Diagnostic-endoscopy referral for repeat biopsy planning
choices.temptation: Try to settle the lift finding with another small tissue sample.
choices.rationale: Another limited sample may miss invasion and does not solve the scarred completion-resection problem.
choices.reasonableWhen: Representative tissue confirmation is needed to direct an established nonendoscopic treatment pathway.

nodes.explanation: Interpret a lift test in its procedural history. Tattoo and cautery beneath a residual lesion can cause fibrosis, so this nonlift does not independently establish deep invasion. Advanced completion-resection planning addresses the actual problem without assuming either cancer or easy routine snare removal.

gate.cueAttack: Converted all three answers to parallel referral plans. Removed standard repeat snaring and the cautious assessment versus committed operation contrast. The temporal relation between injury, tattoo and nonlift remains raw evidence.
gate.stage: Three referral plans for the residual lesion before definitive treatment.
steps: Interpret nonlifting after cautery and sublesional tattoo as a confounded finding, not proof of deep invasion.
Use the residual lesion's complexity and available original morphology to choose expert completion-resection planning.
gate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: anchoring on a later nonlift despite its procedural cause competes with expert endoscopic referral.
gate.decidingObservation: The lift failure arose at a site already treated with cautery and tattoo beneath the lesion.
gate.consequence: Unnecessary regional resection or repeated superficial sampling rather than definitive expert planning.
gate.deletionTest: Original morphology and prior interventions determine how to interpret nonlift; residual tissue establishes a completion problem. The adenoma sample cannot exclude an unsampled invasive focus.
gate.counterfactual: If the untreated lesion had a depressed ulcerated invasive focus before any injection, biopsy or cautery, oncologic resection planning would become the best offered referral.
gate.sequence: Standalone; the large-polyp referral draft cannot supply this answer as prior feedback.

revisedCases.name: Nathan Cole
revisedCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 35-year-old man with FAP and a prior ileorectal anastomosis, attends clinic to review outside rectal surveillance records.

nodes.title: Rectal removal for uncontrolled FAP burden
nodes.objective: Integrate rectal clearance, continence and restorative goals when choosing FAP operative extent.
nodes.update: Years after colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis for FAP, the retained rectum now contains a confluent adenoma field left after repeated endoscopic clearing attempts. Submitted fragments contain high-grade dysplasia; no invasive carcinoma is present in those fragments. Pelvic MRI shows no extrarectal extension or suspicious regional nodes. Continence is normal. After counseling about further surgery, he prioritizes maintaining intestinal continuity over a permanent end ileostomy.
nodes.task: Which next operative plan should be discussed for {patientName}'s retained rectum?

choices.label: Completion proctectomy with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis
choices.temptation: Update operative extent from current rather than prior burden
choices.rationale: The earlier rectal-sparing premise no longer holds; removing the uncontrolled rectum addresses the new disease while permitting restoration.
choices.reasonableWhen: A retained rectum develops disease no longer manageable endoscopically.

choices.label: Continue IRA with repeated endoscopic clearing
choices.temptation: Carry forward an earlier appropriate choice unchanged
choices.rationale: Repeated residual high-grade field disease defeats the original rectal-retention premise.
choices.reasonableWhen: A limited rectal burden remains endoscopically clearable.

choices.label: Completion proctectomy with end ileostomy
choices.temptation: Remove the rectum without using the preserved function
choices.rationale: This is an option, but the supplied function and restorative goal favor pouch planning.
choices.reasonableWhen: Poor continence or a preference to avoid pouch-related function.

nodes.explanation: Failure of endoscopic control requires reconsideration of the retained rectum. Fragment histology and MRI do not exclude microscopic invasion throughout the field. Completion proctectomy with IPAA can address the rectal burden while respecting preserved function and the stated continuity goal; final pathology still matters.

gate.cueAttack: Removed the claim that MRI shows no invasive cancer and the ambiguous desire for restoration in a patient who already has IRA. Separate fragment histology from extrarectal MRI observations; the preference now concerns future continuity versus end ileostomy.
gate.stage: Three plans for the retained rectum after IRA surveillance failure.
steps: Infer from persistent confluent dysplasia after repeated clearing that rectal preservation is no longer endoscopically controlled.
Combine the need for rectal removal with preserved continence and the stated future functional goal to choose restorative completion surgery.
gate.difficulty: Fair moderate: two clinical constraints determine extent and reconstruction. The revised case does not imply imaging excludes microscopic invasive disease.
gate.decidingObservation: The retained field persists after repeated clearing and contains high-grade dysplasia in submitted tissue.
gate.consequence: Continued uncontrolled rectal neoplasia or a reconstruction inconsistent with function and goals.
gate.deletionTest: Prior IRA identifies the retained organ; failed clearing and dysplasia establish its problem; continence and future continuity distinguish reconstruction. MRI is limited to its observed extrarectal scope.
gate.counterfactual: If the retained rectal adenomas were sparse, fully clearable and without high-grade dysplasia, continued IRA with endoscopic clearing and surveillance would become the best offered plan.
gate.sequence: New standalone post-IRA visit. The exact PASS prophylactic-IRA question and its original header remain unchanged in their own case.

revisedCases.name: Felix Turner
revisedCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 68-year-old man, attends clinic after an outside diagnostic laparoscopy was stopped to arrange colorectal and urologic surgery.

nodes.title: Plan en-bloc resection while preserving uninvolved bladder
nodes.objective: Use the location and extent of an adherent colon cancer to plan en-bloc bladder resection without automatically sacrificing the whole bladder.
nodes.update: Biopsy confirms sigmoid adenocarcinoma and distant staging is negative. The outside exploration record describes a firm focal attachment to the bladder dome, with the neck, trigone and ureteric entries separate from the tumor. The remainder of the bladder wall is uninvolved and would retain a substantial reservoir after dome removal. No peritoneal deposits were found. The patient is being considered for curative surgery, and the attachment has not been divided.
nodes.task: Which operative plan best fits {patientName}'s recorded anatomy, subject to confirmation of clear margins at surgery?

choices.label: Sigmoid colectomy with en-bloc partial cystectomy
choices.temptation: Match the organ extent to the involved dome while preserving the tumor interface.
choices.rationale: A focal dome attachment can be removed en bloc with a bladder portion while retaining uninvolved neck, trigone and reservoir; the plan still requires an achievable clear margin.
choices.reasonableWhen: The attached bladder portion can be removed with negative margins and useful remaining bladder.

choices.label: Sigmoid colectomy with en-bloc total cystectomy
choices.temptation: Equate any bladder adherence with a need to remove the whole bladder.
choices.rationale: The represented attachment is focal at the dome; the record does not show neck/trigone involvement or loss of a usable remaining bladder requiring total removal.
choices.reasonableWhen: Extent or location prevents clear-margin partial resection with a usable bladder.

choices.label: Sigmoid colectomy with separation of the bladder attachment
choices.temptation: Assume focal attachment can be peeled away to preserve bladder.
choices.rationale: An adherent cancer interface should not be divided to decide whether the adhesion is malignant; partial bladder resection preserves an en-bloc specimen.
choices.reasonableWhen: No true tumor-organ attachment exists and an uninvolved plane is established without dividing an adherent cancer interface.

nodes.explanation: First preserve the adherent tumor-organ interface. Then use the involved anatomy to choose the planned bladder extent: a focal dome attachment with separate neck/trigone and a usable remnant supports en-bloc partial cystectomy, provided a clear margin is achievable. Adherence does not itself establish histologic invasion, and total cystectomy is not automatic.

gate.cueAttack: Replaced two attachment-division near-duplicates with three distinct operative extents. The task is a conditional surgical plan, not a guarantee of final margin status. No endoscopic mucosal-negative claim is used to exclude outer-wall involvement.
gate.stage: Three combined colorectal/bladder operative plans at the same planning stage.
steps: Infer that the firm cancer-bladder interface must remain en bloc regardless of whether pathology later shows invasion.
Use dome-limited attachment, separate neck/trigone and a usable remnant to distinguish partial from total cystectomy planning.
gate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: either preserving all bladder by interface division or overextending en-bloc surgery to total cystectomy is a credible resident error.
gate.decidingObservation: The attachment is confined to the dome, with uninvolved neck/trigone and substantial uninvolved bladder remaining.
gate.consequence: Tumor-plane violation or unnecessary loss of the bladder.
gate.deletionTest: Attachment establishes the en-bloc requirement; its location and remaining reservoir determine partial versus total extent. Curative intent and negative distant staging define the operative goal.
gate.counterfactual: If the attachment instead involved the bladder neck and trigone such that no clear-margin partial resection could retain a usable bladder, the offered en-bloc total cystectomy plan would become appropriate.
gate.sequence: Standalone. The meaning now includes bladder extent, so the prior concept version is retained without FSRS migration.

revisedCases.name: Thomas Hale
revisedCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 66-year-old man, attends clinic after outside resections of synchronous right-colon and sigmoid cancers.

nodes.title: Reassess a low node yield
nodes.objective: Distinguish negative sampled nodes from an adequate pathologic regional assessment.
nodes.update: Two synchronous colon cancers were removed in separately labeled right-colon and sigmoid specimens. The right-colon report lists 17 negative regional nodes. The sigmoid report lists five negative regional nodes; that tumor extends through muscularis propria into pericolic fat with clear margins. No metastases were found on preoperative staging. Both submitted mesenteric specimens remain available to pathology.
nodes.task: Which pathology plan should next improve {patientName}'s regional-stage assessment for these two resections?

choices.label: Request an additional node search in the sigmoid specimen
choices.temptation: Keep each primary linked to its own submitted regional specimen.
choices.rationale: The sigmoid basin has only five assessed nodes. The 17 nodes assigned to the other primary do not repair that specimen-specific deficit.
choices.reasonableWhen: Fewer than 12 nodes are reported in the specimen for the cancer being staged.

choices.label: Request an additional node search in the right-colon specimen
choices.temptation: Focus on the larger node-bearing specimen while overlooking which basin is undersampled.
choices.rationale: The right-colon specimen already has 17 reported nodes; the identified low count belongs to the sigmoid specimen.
choices.reasonableWhen: The right-colon specimen rather than the sigmoid specimen has fewer than 12 assessed nodes.

choices.label: Accept the combined 22-node assessment for both primaries
choices.temptation: Pool all negative nodes from the operation.
choices.rationale: Separate primary tumors require their own regional specimen provenance; a pooled total does not establish adequate assessment for the five-node sigmoid basin.
choices.reasonableWhen: Each primary has an adequate separately assigned regional-node assessment and no additional pathology deficit is identified.

nodes.explanation: Assign nodes to the primary and specimen from which they came before assessing the count. Seventeen right-colon nodes cannot be transferred to the sigmoid basin. Additional pathology evaluation should target the sigmoid specimen with five assessed nodes; this does not itself prove nodal metastasis or require repeat colectomy.

gate.cueAttack: Replaced PET and anatomically awkward mesenteric MRI with three pathology-disposition plans. A pooled adequate-looking count now competes with a genuinely inadequate specimen-specific count; retained tissue is background feasibility for either targeted search rather than a uniquely named key action.
gate.stage: Three pathology plans for regional staging after completed resection.
steps: Separate nodes by the two labeled primaries rather than pool the operation's total.
Identify the five-node sigmoid specimen as needing additional pathology retrieval before relying on its node-negative assessment.
gate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: counting 22 negative nodes across two specimens obscures the undersampled cancer's own basin.
gate.decidingObservation: The five sigmoid nodes and 17 right-colon nodes were assigned to separate primary-specific specimens.
gate.consequence: Overconfidence in an inadequately assessed sigmoid regional stage.
gate.deletionTest: Two primaries and specimen labels create the provenance problem; both node counts distinguish the proper search from the competing plans. Submitted-tissue availability makes either pathology request possible.
gate.counterfactual: If the counts were reversed, with five right-colon nodes and 17 sigmoid nodes, the offered additional search in the right-colon specimen would become best.
gate.sequence: Standalone with a distinct patient; the exact PASS tumor-deposit question retains its original patient and wording.

revisedCases.name: Martin Shaw
revisedCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 70-year-old man, attends clinic while the founder reviews outside multidisciplinary records for sigmoid adenocarcinoma with metastases.

nodes.title: Initial treatment of an asymptomatic metastatic primary
nodes.objective: Distinguish symptom control from prophylactic primary resection when distant disease is not curatively resectable.
nodes.update: The outside multidisciplinary team records diffuse bilobar liver and pulmonary metastases not amenable to curative local treatment. At colonoscopy an adult instrument could not pass the sigmoid tumor, but a pediatric instrument passed it. He reports daily formed stools without pain, vomiting, bleeding or transfusion need. CT shows no upstream colonic dilation.
nodes.task: Which initial treatment sequence best fits {patientName}'s current metastatic-primary record?

choices.label: Systemic treatment planning with the primary left in place
choices.temptation: Distinguish a narrow endoscopic lumen from a clinically obstructing primary.
choices.rationale: The record lacks clinical or radiographic obstruction and other primary-related complications. For incurable metastatic disease in this setting, systemic treatment generally precedes prophylactic primary surgery.
choices.reasonableWhen: Metastatic disease is incurable and the primary is not causing obstruction, significant bleeding or perforation.

choices.label: Sigmoid colectomy followed by systemic treatment planning
choices.temptation: Treat failure of the adult scope to pass as a surgical obstruction indication.
choices.rationale: The smaller scope passed, bowel function continues and CT shows no upstream dilation; prophylactic colectomy would delay treatment of the dominant metastatic disease.
choices.reasonableWhen: Primary-related perforation or another surgically managed complication requires resection before systemic treatment.

choices.label: Diverting colostomy followed by systemic treatment planning
choices.temptation: Decompress preemptively because the adult scope did not pass.
choices.rationale: No symptomatic or radiographic obstruction requiring diversion is established.
choices.reasonableWhen: A clinically obstructing unresectable primary requires decompression and diversion is the selected feasible route.

nodes.explanation: The adult scope's nonpassage does not alone establish bowel obstruction. Ongoing bowel function, absent obstructive symptoms and no upstream dilation define the present primary-related burden. With incurable metastases and no primary complication, initial systemic treatment planning is generally preferred to prophylactic colectomy or diversion.

gate.cueAttack: Removed the fitness endorsement and patent-lumen interpretation. Replaced stenting with a parallel diversion-first sequence. Endoscope caliber now creates a credible concern that must be interpreted against bowel function and CT.
gate.stage: Three initial treatment sequences for incurable metastatic colon cancer.
steps: Determine whether the instrument-level narrowing represents a clinical obstruction in the current record.
Choose the systemic-first sequence for the uncomplicated primary rather than a prophylactic resection or diversion-first sequence.
gate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: instrument nonpassage can be mistaken for a mandatory local intervention despite contrary functional and radiographic observations.
gate.decidingObservation: A pediatric instrument passed, stools continue, and CT shows no proximal dilation or other primary complication.
gate.consequence: Unnecessary local intervention and delayed metastatic treatment, or failure to respond if a true complication develops.
gate.deletionTest: Metastatic resectability establishes treatment intent; scope caliber creates the competing concern; symptoms and dilation establish whether that concern is currently a complication. No affirmative treatment-fitness sentence supplies the answer.
gate.counterfactual: If the primary perforated with generalized contamination, a local resection-first sequence would supersede systemic-first planning among these choices.
gate.sequence: Standalone; the revised reconstruction question uses a distinct retrospective admission case and does not inherit this explanation.

revisedCases.name: Martin Shaw
revisedCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 70-year-old man, attends clinic after an outside admission; the founder reviews the recorded operation for his metastatic sigmoid cancer.

nodes.title: Choose reconstruction after emergency sigmoid resection
nodes.objective: Use the intraoperative physiology and contamination to choose a concrete reconstruction strategy after resection of a perforated sigmoid cancer.
nodes.update: The founder reviews the operative decision recorded during his outside admission for a perforated sigmoid primary with unresectable liver and lung metastases. Before admission he requested treatment of reversible acute complications. At the recorded decision point, the perforated sigmoid segment had been resected and the remaining bowel ends were viable. Diffuse fecal contamination had been encountered. Despite fluids, antibiotics and resection, norepinephrine was still required and the bowel was edematous. The operative team judged fascial closure feasible without a planned open abdomen.
nodes.task: At that outside intraoperative decision point, which reconstruction plan best fits {patientName}'s recorded findings?

choices.label: Close the rectal stump and create an end colostomy
choices.temptation: Interpret continuing circulatory support and contamination when deciding whether to create an anastomosis.
choices.rationale: Ongoing vasopressor need with fecal contamination and edematous bowel favors avoiding a new colorectal anastomosis. A concrete Hartmann reconstruction is supported here; no universal rule for every perforation is asserted.
choices.reasonableWhen: After left-sided perforation resection, current physiology and local conditions make primary anastomosis inappropriate and the abdomen can be closed.

choices.label: Create a colorectal anastomosis and a diverting loop ileostomy
choices.temptation: Assume proximal diversion makes a high-risk anastomosis acceptable regardless of current physiology.
choices.rationale: Diversion does not remove an anastomosis or its failure risk. The continuing vasopressor need and adverse local conditions favor not constructing it at this recorded point.
choices.reasonableWhen: Resuscitation has restored stable physiology and local bowel conditions support a primary anastomosis, with diversion selected for the residual risk.

choices.label: Create a colorectal anastomosis without proximal diversion
choices.temptation: Transfer preadmission fitness into a septic operative decision.
choices.rationale: The relevant observations are the current vasopressor need, contamination and edema, not earlier cancer-treatment eligibility.
choices.reasonableWhen: Physiology, perfusion, contamination and anastomotic conditions are favorable enough for primary anastomosis without diversion.

nodes.explanation: Review the physiology at the actual reconstruction point. Persistent vasopressor need plus fecal contamination and bowel edema favor avoiding a colorectal anastomosis; closing the stump and forming an end colostomy is a concrete plan. Diversion cannot erase the risk of an anastomosis already constructed. This scoped decision does not prescribe Hartmann reconstruction for every perforated cancer.

gate.cueAttack: Rebuilt the failed item at one past intraoperative moment after resection. All answers are specific reconstruction operations; no stent, delayed source control, vague staged plan or supplied definitive-source-control cue remains.
gate.stage: Three concrete reconstruction plans after the same completed sigmoid resection.
steps: Interpret ongoing norepinephrine need after resuscitation together with fecal contamination and bowel edema as adverse conditions for a new anastomosis.
Choose stump closure and end colostomy rather than assume that proximal diversion or earlier cancer-treatment fitness makes an anastomosis suitable.
gate.difficulty: Fair moderate: protected anastomosis is the nearest real competitor. No invented pressor-dose, lactate or timeline threshold is used, and prior systemic-treatment fitness supplies no inference.
gate.decidingObservation: At the reconstruction point vasopressor support remained necessary and bowel edema with diffuse fecal contamination was documented.
gate.consequence: Anastomotic failure risk from constructing an anastomosis under unfavorable current conditions.
gate.deletionTest: Metastatic context and the stated goals establish why the acute complication was treated; viable ends establish that reconstruction is the decision. Current physiology and local findings distinguish the operations, while feasible closure excludes an unstated open-abdomen stoma-delay question.
gate.counterfactual: If resuscitation instead restored stable physiology without vasopressors and the viable bowel was well perfused without edema or diffuse contamination, a colorectal anastomosis with selected protective diversion would become a reasonable offered reconstruction rather than a mandatory end colostomy. That counterfactual permits the alternative; it does not claim diversion is universally required.
gate.sequence: Standalone retrospective clinic chart review. No uncomplicated-primary question or its feedback precedes the reconstruction decision.

revisedCases.name: George Sutton
revisedCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 68-year-old man, attends clinic with records from two outside colonoscopies.

nodes.title: Integrate baseline and first surveillance
nodes.objective: Choose USMSTF second-surveillance timing from both the baseline adenoma and the first follow-up.
nodes.update: At baseline, a 14-mm tubular adenoma was completely removed in one piece during a high-quality examination. The first surveillance colonoscopy, performed three years later, was also complete and adequately prepared and found no adenoma or serrated lesion. He has no prior cancer, hereditary syndrome or relevant family history.
nodes.task: Under USMSTF guidance, when should {patientName}'s next colonoscopy be planned after this normal first surveillance examination?

choices.label: Colonoscopy in five years
choices.temptation: Combine the baseline and first-surveillance findings
choices.rationale: A normal first surveillance examination after an advanced baseline adenoma supports a five-year next interval.
choices.reasonableWhen: Advanced adenoma at baseline followed by a normal high-quality first surveillance.

choices.label: Colonoscopy in three years
choices.temptation: Repeat the baseline advanced-adenoma interval unchanged
choices.rationale: The normal first surveillance modifies the next interval.
choices.reasonableWhen: Advanced adenoma or another corresponding higher-risk finding persists at first surveillance.

choices.label: Colonoscopy in ten years
choices.temptation: Erase baseline risk after one normal follow-up
choices.rationale: The advanced baseline finding continues to matter when selecting the next interval.
choices.reasonableWhen: A low-risk baseline followed by normal first surveillance can support a longer interval.

nodes.explanation: Second-surveillance planning uses two examinations. A normal first follow-up modifies, but does not erase, the advanced baseline adenoma history.

gate.cueAttack: Added the missing three-year baseline-to-first-surveillance interval. Retained the reviewed two-examination decision and three parallel timing choices without introducing extraneous chronology.
steps: Classify the size-defined baseline adenoma and verify that the normal first surveillance occurred at its appropriate interval.
Apply the serial-surveillance recommendation rather than reuse either the baseline-only or latest-examination-only interval.
gate.difficulty: Fair moderate, consistent with independent review: interpreting both examinations is consequential; the newly stated first interval removes ambiguity rather than manufacturing difficulty.
gate.decidingObservation: A completely removed 14-mm baseline adenoma followed three years later by a normal high-quality first surveillance examination.
gate.consequence: Over- or under-surveillance from ignoring one examination.
gate.deletionTest: Each examination determines a different part of the serial-surveillance recommendation, and the added interval establishes that this is the appropriate first surveillance rather than an arbitrary early examination.
gate.counterfactual: Replace the first surveillance result with a new advanced adenoma: three years becomes the appropriate offered interval.
gate.sequence: Standalone; exact PASS count/provenance surveillance item remains untouched.
